knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Completeness of a Finsler Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness is with respect to the distance induced on the manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Finsler manifold \((M,g)\) with induced distance \(d\) is metrically complete if the metric space \((M,d)\) is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Finsler manifold is metrically complete when it is complete as a metric space under its induced distance.
assumptions_latex: d\text{ is the induced distance on }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (M,g)\text{ is metrically complete}\iff (M,d)\text{ is a complete metric space.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Global Optimality of Burer–Monteiro Second-Order Critical Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benign-landscape theorem for a compact smooth Burer–Monteiro feasible manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M=\{Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}:\mathcal A(YY^\top)=b\}\) be a smooth compact feasible manifold. If \(p(p+1)/2>m\), then, for generic \(C\), every \(Y\in\mathcal M\) satisfying the first- and second-order necessary optimality conditions for \(\min_{Y\in\mathcal M}\langle CY,Y\rangle\) is a global optimizer. Furthermore, \(X=YY^\top\) is a global optimizer of the original SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth compact Burer–Monteiro feasible manifold, factor width strictly exceeding the triangular dimension threshold ensures that, for generic cost matrices, every point satisfying first- and second-order necessary conditions is globally optimal and maps to a global SDP solution.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M=\{Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}:\mathcal A(YY^\top)=b\}\text{ is a smooth compact manifold}
Y\in\mathcal M\text{ satisfies first- and second-order necessary optimality conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y\text{ is a global optimizer of the factorized problem and }YY^\top\text{ is a global optimizer of the SDP}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diffeomorphism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines diffeomorphisms and diffeomorphic manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map F:\mathcal M_1\to\mathcal M_2 is a diffeomorphism if it is bijective and both F and F^{-1} are smooth. The manifolds \mathcal M_1 and \mathcal M_2 are diffeomorphic if there exists a diffeomorphism from \mathcal M_1 onto \mathcal M_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diffeomorphism is a bijection between smooth manifolds whose forward and inverse maps are both smooth. Two manifolds are diffeomorphic when such a map exists between them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a diffeomorphism}\iff F\text{ is bijective and }F,F^{-1}\text{ are smooth.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Immersion and Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for smooth maps between smooth manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be smooth manifolds and let \(f:M\to N\) be smooth. The map \(f\) is an immersion if \(\mathrm Df(p):T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N\) is injective for every \(p\in M\). An immersion \(f\) is an embedding if \(f:M\to f(M)\) is a homeomorphism, where \(f(M)\) has the relative topology inherited from \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth map is an immersion when its differential is injective everywhere. It is an embedding when it is also a homeomorphism from its domain onto its image with the relative topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is an immersion}\iff \forall p\in M,\ \mathrm Df(p)\text{ is injective};\quad f\text{ is an embedding}\iff f\text{ is an immersion and }f:M\to f(M)\text{ is a homeomorphism}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Definiteness Criterion for a Rank-One Finsler Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between positivity of a differential rank-one subtraction and a strict dual-norm bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Finsler manifold and \(f\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb{R})\). The tensor \(\widetilde g(x,y)=g(x,y)-df(x)\otimes df(x)\) is positive definite if and only if \(\lVert df(x)\rVert_y<1\) for every vector \(y\) in its stated domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the rank-one tensor formed from the differential of a smooth function preserves positive definiteness exactly when the corresponding norm of the differential is strictly less than one for every vector y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(x,y)-df(x)\otimes df(x)\succ0\iff \forall y,\ \lVert df(x)\rVert_y<1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chart and Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a chart on an arbitrary set before imposing atlas compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a set. A \(d\)-dimensional chart on \(\mathcal M\) is a pair \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\), where \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal M\) and \(\varphi:\mathcal U\to V\) is a bijection onto an open set \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). For \(x\in\mathcal U\), the components of \(\varphi(x)\) are the coordinates of \(x\) in this chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A d-dimensional chart on a set is a bijection from a subset of the set onto an open subset of Euclidean d-space. The components of the image of a point are its coordinates in that chart.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ is a }d\text{-dimensional chart, and }\varphi(x)\text{ gives the coordinates of each }x\in\mathcal U.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix manifolds, matrix quotient manifolds, and structure spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the general matrix-manifold terminology and records representative embedded and quotient families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal M\) is \(\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) or a submanifold of \(\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), a quotient manifold \(\mathcal M/\!\sim\) is called a matrix quotient manifold. A matrix manifold is any manifold constructed from \(\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) by taking embedded submanifolds and quotient manifolds. The term structure space denotes either an embedding space for an embedded submanifold or a total space for a quotient manifold. Examples include Stiefel, Grassmann, oblique, generalized Stiefel, flag, and symplectic manifolds; specifically, the generalized Stiefel family satisfies \(X^TBX=I\) with \(B=B^T\succ0\), while the symplectic family satisfies \(X^TJX=J\) with \(J=\begin{bmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{bmatrix}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix manifolds arise from matrix spaces through embedded-submanifold and quotient constructions. The ambient embedding space or quotient total space is called a structure space. Standard families include Stiefel, Grassmann, oblique, generalized Stiefel, flag, and symplectic manifolds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M/\!\sim\text{ is termed a matrix quotient manifold under the stated construction.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Manifold Structure, Manifold Chart, and Coordinate Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to a fixed smooth manifold structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximal atlas \(\mathcal A^+\) on a set \(\mathcal M\) that induces a second-countable Hausdorff topology is a manifold structure on \(\mathcal M\); any atlas generating \(\mathcal A^+\) suffices to specify it. For the manifold \((\mathcal M,\mathcal A^+)\), an atlas of the manifold is an atlas whose generated maximal atlas is \(\mathcal A^+\). A chart of the manifold is a chart belonging to \(\mathcal A^+\); its domain is a coordinate domain. If its domain \(\mathcal U\) contains \(x\in\mathcal M\), it is a chart around \(x\), and \(\mathcal U\) is a coordinate neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold structure is a maximal atlas inducing a Hausdorff, second-countable topology, and it may be specified by any generating atlas. Charts belonging to that maximal atlas are manifold charts; their domains are coordinate domains, and a domain containing a point is a coordinate neighborhood of that point.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A^+\text{ is a maximal atlas on }\mathcal M
\text{the induced topology is Hausdorff and second-countable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A^+\text{ is a manifold structure, and charts in }\mathcal A^+\text{ define coordinate domains and coordinate neighborhoods.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Natural Manifold Structure of a Finite-Dimensional Vector Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatible linear-coordinate charts induced by choices of basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal E be a d-dimensional real vector space and let (e_i)_{i=1}^d be a basis. If x=\sum_{i=1}^d x^i e_i, then the coordinate map \psi:\mathcal E\to\mathbb R^d defined by \psi(x)=(x^1,\ldots,x^d)^T is a chart. The coordinate charts arising from all bases are mutually compatible and define a natural d-dimensional smooth-manifold structure on \mathcal E.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinates relative to any basis identify a finite-dimensional real vector space with Euclidean space. All basis-coordinate charts are compatible, giving the vector space its natural linear-manifold structure.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal E\text{ is a }d\text{-dimensional real vector space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi(x)=(x^1,\ldots,x^d)^T\text{ is a chart, and all basis-coordinate charts form a compatible atlas defining a }d\text{-dimensional smooth manifold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Immersed Submanifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an immersed submanifold through the smooth, full-rank inclusion map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal M and \overline{\mathcal M} be manifolds such that \mathcal M\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M} as sets, and let i:\mathcal M\to\overline{\mathcal M} be the inclusion map. Then \mathcal M is an immersed submanifold of \overline{\mathcal M} if i is smooth and \operatorname{rank}\mathrm Di(x)=\dim\mathcal M for every x\in\mathcal M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold contained as a set in another manifold is an immersed submanifold when its inclusion map is smooth and has rank equal to the dimension of the contained manifold at every point.
assumptions_latex: i:\mathcal M\to\overline{\mathcal M}\text{ is the inclusion map}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is an immersed submanifold of }\overline{\mathcal M}\iff i\text{ is smooth and }\operatorname{rank}\mathrm Di(x)=\dim\mathcal M\quad\forall x\in\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a differentiable equivalence between two manifolds; the extract does not state any relationship between the indices r and s.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential Map on a Finsler Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The domain consists of tangent vectors whose corresponding geodesics exist through time one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Finsler manifold and \(x\in M\). For \(X\in O_x\subseteq T_xM\), let \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\) be the geodesic satisfying \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma(0)=X\). Then the exponential map is \(\exp_x:O_x\to M\), defined by \(\exp_x(X)=\gamma(1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map at x sends each tangent vector in its domain to the time-one endpoint of the geodesic beginning at x with that initial velocity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exp_x:O_x\to M,\qquad \exp_x(X)=\gamma(1).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular and Critical Points and Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surjectivity-based classification for a smooth map between manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be smooth manifolds and let \(f:M\to N\) be smooth. A point \(p\in M\) is regular if \(\mathrm Df(p):T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N\) is surjective, and critical otherwise. A point \(q\in N\) is a critical value if \(f(p)=q\) for some critical point \(p\in M\); otherwise \(q\) is a regular value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain point is regular when the differential is surjective there and critical otherwise. A codomain point is a critical value when it is the image of a critical point; otherwise it is a regular value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\text{ is regular}\iff \mathrm Df(p)\text{ is surjective};\quad q\text{ is a critical value}\iff \exists p\in M:\ f(p)=q\text{ and }\mathrm Df(p)\text{ is not surjective}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\varphi:\mathcal U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a chart on \(\mathcal M\), then \(\varphi^{-1}:V\to\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal M\) is a local parameterization of \(\mathcal M\). Consequently, families of local parameterizations and families of charts are equivalent descriptions, and a manifold may be defined using either representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of a chart is a local parameterization. Thus families of charts and families of local parameterizations give equivalent ways to describe a manifold.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:\mathcal U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is a chart on }\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi^{-1}:V\to\mathcal U\text{ is a local parameterization, and chart families are equivalent to local-parameterization families.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connectedness and Components of a Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterization of manifold connectedness and the structure of its components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A manifold \mathcal M is connected if it cannot be expressed as the disjoint union of two nonempty open subsets. Equivalently, every pair x,y\in\mathcal M can be joined by a piecewise smooth curve segment. Every connected component of \mathcal M is open and therefore inherits a natural differentiable structure as an open submanifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold is connected exactly when it cannot be separated into two nonempty open sets; equivalently, every two points can be joined by a piecewise smooth curve. Each connected component is open and inherits an open-submanifold structure.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is a smooth manifold under the stated Hausdorff and second-countable convention}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M\text{ connected}\iff\forall x,y\in\mathcal M\ \exists\text{ a piecewise smooth curve segment joining }x\text{ and }y;\quad\text{each connected component is an open submanifold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Manifolds and Riemannian metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates local Euclidean topology from tangent-space and metric structure and retains the extract's smooth embedding assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A $d$-dimensional topological manifold $\mathcal X$ is a space in which every $x\in\mathcal X$ has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$. If $\mathcal X$ is differentiable, its tangent space at $x$ is denoted $T_x\mathcal X$. A Riemannian metric is a smoothly varying family of inner products $g_x$ on $T_x\mathcal X$; it induces notions of length, distance, angle, and volume. Under sufficient smoothness, a Riemannian manifold admits an isometric embedding into a Euclidean space of possibly higher dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold is locally Euclidean. On a differentiable manifold, each point has a tangent space. A Riemannian metric assigns smoothly varying inner products to these tangent spaces, inducing distance, angles, and volume; sufficiently smooth Riemannian manifolds can be embedded isometrically in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X\text{ is differentiable when }T_x\mathcal X\text{ is invoked}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathcal X,g)\text{ has locally Euclidean topology and geometry induced by }\{g_x\}_{x\in\mathcal X}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate vector fields form a smooth local frame
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes smoothness and pointwise linear independence of the vector fields induced by a chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) be a chart on a \(d\)-dimensional manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(W_1,\ldots,W_d\) be its coordinate vector fields. Then \(W_i\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal U)\) for every \(i\), and for every \(x\in\mathcal U\), the vectors \(W_1(x),\ldots,W_d(x)\) are linearly independent. Thus, they form a smooth local frame on \(\mathcal U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinate vector fields associated with a chart are smooth, and their values are linearly independent at every point of the chart domain; hence they form a smooth local frame.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ is a chart on }\mathcal M
W_1,\ldots,W_d\text{ are the associated coordinate vector fields}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_1,\ldots,W_d\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal U),\qquad \forall x\in\mathcal U,\ \{W_1(x),\ldots,W_d(x)\}\text{ is linearly independent}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate vector fields induced by a chart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the coordinate vector fields on a chart domain and records their coordinate representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) be a chart on a \(d\)-dimensional manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(x\in\mathcal U\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), define
\[
W_i(x)=\left[t\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(x)+t e_i)\right].
\]
Then \(\theta_x^\varphi(W_i(x))=e_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a chart on a d-dimensional manifold, the ith coordinate vector at x is the tangent vector of the curve obtained by varying only the ith chart coordinate. Its chart-coordinate representation is the ith standard basis vector.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ is a chart on }\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_i(x)=\left[t\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(x)+t e_i)\right],\qquad \theta_x^\varphi(W_i(x))=e_i.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Charts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth-manifold chart with Euclidean coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a topological manifold of dimension \(n\). A coordinate chart on \(M\) is a pair \((U,\varphi)\), where \(U\subseteq M\) is open and \(\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a homeomorphism onto an open set. The components \(x^i=\pi_i\circ\varphi\) are the local coordinate functions, and each \(p\in U\) is represented by \(\varphi(p)=(x^1(p),\ldots,x^n(p))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate chart identifies an open part of an n-dimensional manifold homeomorphically with an open subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((U,\varphi)\) supplies local Euclidean coordinates on \(M\).

notation.meaning: coordinate chart with domain U and coordinate map phi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Open Submanifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Manifold structure induced on an open subset by restricting ambient charts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a manifold and let \(\mathcal V\subseteq M\) be open in its atlas topology. For every chart \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) with \(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V\ne\varnothing\), form \((\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V,\varphi|_{\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V})\). These restricted charts form an atlas on \(\mathcal V\), making \(\mathcal V\) an open submanifold of \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open subset of a manifold is an open submanifold when equipped with the atlas obtained by restricting the ambient charts to that subset.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal V\subseteq M\text{ is open in the atlas topology}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V,\varphi|_{\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V}):\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V\ne\varnothing\}\text{ forms an atlas making }\mathcal V\text{ an open submanifold of }\mathcal M.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth manifold structure on tangent-space linear maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs local coordinates using manifold charts and local tangent frames.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\dim \mathcal M=m\) and \(\dim \mathcal N=n\), then \(\mathcal L(T\mathcal M,T\mathcal N)=\{(x,y,L):x\in\mathcal M,\ y\in\mathcal N,\ L:T_x\mathcal M\to T_y\mathcal N\text{ linear}\}\) is a smooth manifold. Given charts \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\), \((\mathcal V,\psi)\) and local frames, \(\Phi(x,y,L)=(\varphi(x),\psi(y),\operatorname{Mat}(L))\) is a chart on \(\pi^{-1}(\mathcal U\times\mathcal V)\), where \(\pi(x,y,L)=(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The collection of all linear maps between tangent spaces of two manifolds forms a smooth manifold. Local coordinates consist of coordinates for the two base points together with the matrix of the linear map in chosen local frames.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M,\mathcal N\text{ are smooth manifolds of dimensions }m,n
(\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ and }(\mathcal V,\psi)\text{ are charts with chosen local frames}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L(T\mathcal M,T\mathcal N)\text{ is a smooth manifold with charts }\Phi(x,y,L)=(\varphi(x),\psi(y),\operatorname{Mat}(L)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate representation and smoothness of a manifold map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the local Euclidean representation of a manifold map and chart-independent smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathcal M_1\to\mathcal M_2, where \dim\mathcal M_i=d_i, and let x\in\mathcal M_1. For charts \varphi_1 and \varphi_2 around x and F(x), respectively, \widehat F=\varphi_2\circ F\circ\varphi_1^{-1} is a coordinate representation of F, defined in general on a subset of \mathbb R^{d_1}. The map F is smooth at x when \widehat F is C^\infty at \varphi_1(x); this condition is independent of the chosen charts. It is smooth when it is smooth at every point of its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given charts around a point and its image, composing a manifold map with the charts gives its local Euclidean coordinate representation. The map is smooth at the point exactly when this representation is infinitely differentiable there; the definition is independent of the charts. A map is smooth if it is smooth everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is smooth at }x\iff \varphi_2\circ F\circ\varphi_1^{-1}\text{ is }C^\infty\text{ at }\varphi_1(x),\text{ independently of the charts.}

knowledge_statements.title: Compatible Atlases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth compatibility and maximal atlases on finite-dimensional manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An atlas on an \(n\)-dimensional topological manifold \(M\) is a family \(\mathcal A=\{(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}\) of charts satisfying \(M=\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha\). It is smoothly compatible if, whenever \(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\neq\varnothing\), the transition maps \(\varphi_\beta\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}\) and \(\varphi_\alpha\circ\varphi_\beta^{-1}\) are smooth on their open Euclidean domains. A smooth structure is a maximal smoothly compatible atlas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible atlas covers the manifold by charts whose overlap transformations are smooth; its maximal extension defines a smooth structure.
assumptions_latex: Each \((U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\) is a coordinate chart on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\) determines a smooth structure precisely through smooth transition maps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compatibility of Coordinate Charts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes both the disjoint-domain case and all conditions required on a nonempty overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two charts $(\mathcal U,\varphi)$ and $(\mathcal V,\psi)$ on $M$ are compatible if they have the same dimension $d$ and either $\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V=\varnothing$, or $\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V\neq\varnothing$, the sets $\varphi(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V)$ and $\psi(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V)$ are open in $\mathbb R^d$, and $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V)\to\psi(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V)$ is a diffeomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two charts of the same dimension are compatible when their domains are disjoint or, on a nonempty overlap, both coordinate images are open and the transition map is smoothly invertible with a smooth inverse.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal U,\varphi)\text{ and }(\mathcal V,\psi)\text{ are charts on }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal U\cap\mathcal V=\varnothing\;\lor\;\left[\varphi(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V),\psi(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal V)\text{ are open in }\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}\text{ is a diffeomorphism}\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Atlas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a smooth atlas through coverage and smooth compatibility of overlapping charts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(C^\infty\) atlas of a set \(\mathcal M\) into \(\mathbb R^d\) is a collection of charts \(\{(\mathcal U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}_\alpha\) such that \(\bigcup_\alpha\mathcal U_\alpha=\mathcal M\), and whenever \(\mathcal U_\alpha\cap\mathcal U_\beta\neq\varnothing\), both \(\varphi_\alpha(\mathcal U_\alpha\cap\mathcal U_\beta)\) and \(\varphi_\beta(\mathcal U_\alpha\cap\mathcal U_\beta)\) are open in \(\mathbb R^d\), while the transition map \(\varphi_\beta\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(\varphi_\alpha(\mathcal U_\alpha\cap\mathcal U_\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth atlas is a collection of charts covering the set such that every pair of overlapping charts has open coordinate images of the overlap and a smooth change-of-coordinates map on that overlap.
assumptions_latex: \{(\mathcal U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}_\alpha\text{ is a collection of }d\text{-dimensional charts on }\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcup_\alpha\mathcal U_\alpha=\mathcal M\quad\text{and all nonempty chart overlaps have open coordinate images and }C^\infty\text{ transition maps.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Atlases and Generated Maximal Atlas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of smooth atlases of the same dimension on the same set and the maximal atlas they generate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A,\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2\) be \(d\)-dimensional smooth atlases on the same set \(\mathcal M\). The atlases \(\mathcal A_1\) and \(\mathcal A_2\) are equivalent if \(\mathcal A_1\cup\mathcal A_2\) is an atlas. Define \(\mathcal A^+\) to be the collection of all charts \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) such that \(\mathcal A\cup\{(\mathcal U,\varphi)\}\) is an atlas. Then \(\mathcal A^+\) is the maximal atlas generated by \(\mathcal A\), and \(\mathcal A_1\) and \(\mathcal A_2\) are equivalent if and only if they generate the same maximal atlas. A maximal atlas on \(\mathcal M\) is a differentiable structure on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two smooth atlases of the same dimension on the same set are equivalent when their union is an atlas. All charts compatible with an atlas form its generated maximal atlas. Two atlases are equivalent exactly when they generate the same maximal atlas, also called a differentiable structure.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A,\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2\text{ are }d\text{-dimensional smooth atlases on the same set }\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A_1\sim\mathcal A_2\iff\mathcal A_1^+=\mathcal A_2^+,\qquad \mathcal A^+\text{ is a maximal atlas and hence a differentiable structure on }\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Coordinate Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate representation of differentials and tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth, let \(p\in M\), and choose charts \((U,\varphi)\) at \(p\) and \((V,\psi)\) at \(F(p)\). The differential is represented in coordinates by \(D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))\). Thus a tangent vector with coordinate column \(v\) is mapped to the coordinate column \(D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))v\). Under chart changes, these columns transform by the corresponding transition-map Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local charts turn manifold differentials into ordinary Jacobian multiplication, with transition Jacobians governing changes of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([dF_p(v)]_\psi=D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))[v]_\varphi\).

notation.meaning: coordinate column of a tangent vector in chart phi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: C-s Maps Between Manifolds in Local Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuity as the C-zero case and positive-order regularity through source and target charts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be \(m\)- and \(n\)-dimensional \(C^r\) manifolds. A map \(f:M\to N\) is of class \(C^0\) if it is continuous. For \(s\in\mathbb Z\) with \(1\le s\le r\), a continuous map \(f\) is of class \(C^s\) at \(p\in M\) if there exist \(C^r\) charts \((U,\varphi)\) and \((V,\psi)\) containing \(p\) and \(f(p)\), respectively, such that \(f(U)\subseteq V\) and \(\psi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\to\mathbb R^n\) is of class \(C^s\) at \(\varphi(p)\). The map is of class \(C^s\) if this holds at every \(p\in M\). The composition \(\psi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}\) is a local coordinate representation of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map between C-r manifolds is C-zero precisely when it is continuous. For positive orders through r, it is C-s at a point when suitable source and target charts give a C-s Euclidean coordinate representation there; it is globally C-s when this holds everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }C^0\iff f\text{ is continuous};\quad f\text{ is }C^s\iff f\text{ is continuous and is }C^s\text{ in suitable local coordinates at every }p\in M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Energy extrema and zeros of an irrotational vector field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three curvature-and-rank criteria relating critical points or extrema of the energy to zeros of the field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be an irrotational vector field on an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, and let $f=\tfrac12g(X,X)$. (i) If $x_0$ is critical for $f$ and $\operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)_{x_0}=n$, then $X(x_0)=0$. (ii) Suppose $\operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)\le n-2$. If $x_0$ is a local minimum of $f$ and the indicated sectional curvature $K_{X_{x_0}}$ is strictly negative, then $X(x_0)=0$. If $x_0$ is a local maximum of $f$ and $K_{X_{x_0}}$ is strictly positive, then $X$ vanishes identically on a neighborhood of $x_0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the energy of an irrotational field, a critical point at which the covariant derivative has full rank must be a zero. Under rank at most n minus two, a local energy minimum with strictly negative indicated sectional curvature is a zero, while a local maximum with strictly positive indicated sectional curvature forces the field to vanish in a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(df_{x_0}=0\land\operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)_{x_0}=n\bigr)\Rightarrow X(x_0)=0;\quad \operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)\le n-2\Rightarrow\begin{cases}x_0\text{ local min},\ K_{X_{x_0}}<0\Rightarrow X(x_0)=0,\\x_0\text{ local max},\ K_{X_{x_0}}>0\Rightarrow X\equiv0\text{ near }x_0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every nonzero value of a projective vector field lies in the positive Q region, then the field vanishes on a neighborhood of any maximum point of its energy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a neighborhood }U\ni x_0\text{ such that }X|_U\equiv0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Killing Fields as Generators of Local Isometries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow characterization of Killing vector fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X\in\mathcal X(M)$ have local flow $T_t(x)$ defined for $t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ and $x\in D\subset M$. Then $X$ is a Killing vector field if and only if every local flow map $T_t:D\to M$ is a local isometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth vector field is Killing exactly when the maps in its local flow are local isometries.
assumptions_latex: $T_t(x)$ is the local flow generated by $X$, defined for $t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ and $x\in D\subset M$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is Killing}\iff \forall t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon),\quad T_t\text{ is a local isometry}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic behavior of a nonnegative conformal-factor orbit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complete nonconstant orbit of a conformal vector field on a compact Riemannian manifold, with conformal factor nonnegative along the orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold, let $X$ be a conformal vector field with conformal factor $\varphi$, and let $t\mapsto T_t(x_0)$ be a maximal nonconstant integral curve defined for all $t\in\mathbb R$, with $T_0(x_0)=x_0$ and $\varphi(T_t(x_0))\ge 0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. Then $\int_0^\infty \varphi(T_u(x_0))\,du$ converges and $\lim_{t\to\infty}T_t(x_0)$ does not exist. Moreover, if $\lim_{t\to\infty}\varphi(T_t(x_0))$ exists, then the zeros of $\varphi$ are not isolated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact Riemannian manifold, suppose a conformal vector field has a maximal nonconstant integral curve defined for every real time and its conformal factor is nonnegative along that curve. The conformal factor has a convergent improper integral along the forward orbit, while the orbit has no forward limit. If the conformal factor along the orbit has a forward limit, then the zeros of the conformal factor are not isolated.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is conformal with conformal factor }\varphi
t\mapsto T_t(x_0)\text{ is a maximal nonconstant integral curve defined for all }t\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_0^\infty \varphi(T_u(x_0))\,du<\infty,\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}T_t(x_0)\text{ does not exist};\quad \text{if }\lim_{t\to\infty}\varphi(T_t(x_0))\text{ exists, then the zeros of }\varphi\text{ are not isolated.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth tensor field of order $k$ on $\mathcal M$ is a map $T:\mathfrak X(\mathcal M)^k\to\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)$ that is $\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)$-linear in each argument. It is symmetric when its value is invariant under reordering its inputs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Torse-Forming Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a local torse-forming map relative to a specified vector field, retaining the source's tangent-plane formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X\in\mathcal X(M)$. A local diffeomorphism $F:D\subset M\to M$ is a local torse-forming map with respect to $X$ if, for every $x\in D$ and every $u\in T_xM$,
\[
dF(x)u\in\operatorname{span}\{u,X(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local diffeomorphism F from D into M is local torse forming with respect to X when, for every x in D and every tangent vector u at x, dF(x)u belongs to the plane spanned by u and X(x).
assumptions_latex: $F:D\subset M\to M$ is a local diffeomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is local torse forming with respect to }X\iff (\forall x\in D)(\forall u\in T_xM)\;dF(x)u\in\operatorname{span}\{u,X(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpositive Killing curvature trichotomy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and mutually exclusive alternatives for the energy of a Killing field on a complete manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a Killing vector field on a complete Riemannian manifold (M,g), and suppose the Killing curvature is everywhere nonpositive. Then f=\tfrac12 g(X,X) is convex, and exactly one of the following holds: (i) the zero set of X is a nonempty closed totally convex submanifold of even codimension; (ii) the union of the images of integral curves of X that are nonconstant geodesics is a nonempty closed totally convex set; or (iii) f has no minimum point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete manifold with everywhere nonpositive Killing curvature, the energy of a Killing field is convex. Exactly one alternative occurs: the zero set is a nonempty closed totally convex submanifold of even codimension; the nonconstant geodesic integral curves have a nonempty closed totally convex union of images; or the energy has no minimum point.
assumptions_latex: X\in\mathfrak X(M)\text{ is a Killing vector field}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex, and exactly one of }\begin{cases}Z(X)\ne\varnothing\text{ is a closed totally convex submanifold of even codimension},\\\bigcup\{\operatorname{im}\gamma:\dot\gamma=X\circ\gamma,\ \gamma\text{ is a nonconstant geodesic}\}\ne\varnothing\text{ is closed and totally convex},\\\operatorname*{argmin}_{M}f=\varnothing\end{cases}\text{ holds}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nullspace of the p-energy second variation and conjugate points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's inherited notation for the p-energy second variation, its nullspace, the geodesic velocity, and its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in(-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)\cup(1,\infty)\), \(W_1\in N_p\) if and only if \(W_1\) is a Jacobi field. If \(p=1\) and \(w_1\in T_\gamma\Omega\), then \(w_1^\perp=w_1-\|V\|^{-2}g(w_1,V)V\) belongs to \(N_1\) if and only if \(w_1^\perp\) is a Jacobi field. In these regimes, \(E_{p**}\) is degenerate if and only if \(x\) and \(y\) are conjugate along \(\gamma\), and \(\operatorname{nullity}(E_{p**})\) equals their multiplicity as conjugate points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated nonzero values of p other than 1, a field is in the nullspace of the p-energy second variation exactly when it is a Jacobi field. For p=1, this equivalence concerns the component orthogonal to the geodesic velocity. The second variation is degenerate exactly when the endpoints are conjugate along the geodesic, and its nullity is their conjugate-point multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_1\in N_p\iff W_1\text{ is Jacobi}\quad(p\ne0,1);\qquad w_1^\perp\in N_1\iff w_1^\perp\text{ is Jacobi};\qquad E_{p**}\text{ is degenerate}\iff x,y\text{ are conjugate along }\gamma.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonvanishing Energy and One-Form Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the inherited torse-forming energy notation for f, X, a, and omega.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold of finite volume. If $a$ is strictly positive and concave and $\omega=-\frac{1}{3}\frac{da}{a}$, then $f$ has no zeros and
\[
\omega(Y)=-\frac{a}{2f}g(X,Y)\qquad\text{for every }Y\in\mathfrak X(M).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete finite-volume Riemannian manifold, if a is strictly positive and concave and omega equals minus one third of da divided by a, then f is nowhere zero and omega(Y) equals −a g(X,Y)/(2f) for every vector field Y.
assumptions_latex: $(M,g)$ is a complete Riemannian manifold with finite volume.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $f(x)\neq 0$ for all $x\in M$, and $\omega(Y)=-\frac{a}{2f}g(X,Y)$ for every $Y\in\mathfrak X(M)$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive divergence forces omega-limit points to be zeros
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-orbit asymptotics for a conformal vector field with strictly positive divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let X be a conformal vector field on (M,g) with \operatorname{div}X>0, and let T_t denote its flow. For every x_0 for which the forward orbit
\[
\mathbb O(x_0)=\{T_t(x_0):t\in[0,\infty)\}
\]
is defined, every point in its omega-limit set is a zero of X:
\[
\Omega(x_0)\subseteq\{x\in M:X(x)=0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a conformal vector field has strictly positive divergence, every omega-limit point of any defined forward orbit is a zero of the vector field.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a conformal vector field on }(M,g)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega(x_0)\subseteq\{x\in M:X(x)=0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature characterization of convex affine-field energy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient pointwise condition for convexity of the energy of an affine vector field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be an affine vector field on a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ and let $f=\tfrac12g(X,X)$. Then $f$ is convex if and only if $R(X,Y,X,Y)\le g(\nabla_YX,\nabla_YX)$ for every $Y\in\mathfrak X(M)$. If $f$ is convex, its critical points coincide with its global minimizers and with the zeros of $X$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The energy of an affine vector field is convex exactly when its curvature term is bounded above by the squared covariant-derivative term in every direction. In that case, the source identifies critical points, global minimizers, and zeros of the field.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is an affine vector field on }(M,g)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff R(X,Y,X,Y)\le\|\nabla_YX\|_g^2\quad\forall Y\in\mathfrak X(M);\qquad \operatorname{Crit}(f)=\operatorname*{argmin}_M f=\{x:X(x)=0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz continuity and bounded covariant derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates intrinsic Lipschitz continuity of a tensor field to a uniform bound on its covariant derivative, with distinct differentiability assumptions in each direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $T$ be an order-$k$ tensor field on a Riemannian manifold. If $T$ is differentiable and $L$-Lipschitz, then for every $x\in\mathcal M$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_k,s\in T_x\mathcal M$,
$$|\nabla T(x)(u_1,\ldots,u_k,s)|=|(\nabla_sT)(u_1,\ldots,u_k)|\le L\|s\|_x\prod_{i=1}^k\|u_i\|_x.$$
Conversely, if $T$ is continuously differentiable and this bound holds with constant $L$ for all such arguments, then $T$ is $L$-Lipschitz continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable L-Lipschitz tensor field has covariant derivative bounded by L. Conversely, a continuously differentiable tensor field whose covariant derivative is bounded by L is L-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: $T$ is a tensor field of order $k$.
For the forward implication, $T$ is differentiable and $L$-Lipschitz.
For the converse, $T$ is continuously differentiable and the stated derivative bound holds for every $x\in\mathcal M$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_k,s\in T_x\mathcal M$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ differentiable and }L\text{-Lipschitz}\Rightarrow\|\nabla T\|\le L;\qquad T\in C^1\text{ and }\|\nabla T\|\le L\Rightarrow T\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local frame
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition on a finite-dimensional smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be an \(n\)-dimensional manifold and \(x\in\mathcal M\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of vector-field energy along a field line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient monotonicity conditions for ordinary one-dimensional convexity of energy along an integral curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\alpha:I\to M$ be a field line of $X$ on $(M,g)$ and let $f=\tfrac12g(X,X)$. If $\alpha$ is a geodesic reparametrized by $s=h(t)$ with associated coefficient $\mu$ and $\mu\circ\alpha$ is nondecreasing on $I$, then $f\circ\alpha$ is convex on $I$. Alternatively, if $\alpha$ is neither a geodesic nor a reparametrized geodesic and $g(\nabla_XX,X)\circ\alpha$ is nondecreasing on $I$, then $f\circ\alpha$ is convex on $I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Energy is convex in the trajectory parameter under either of two conditions: the coefficient associated with a reparametrized geodesic is nondecreasing, or, outside both geodesic cases, the derivative of energy along the trajectory is nondecreasing.
assumptions_latex: \alpha:I\to M\text{ is an integral curve of }X

\bigl(\alpha\text{ is a reparametrized geodesic and }\mu\circ\alpha\text{ is nondecreasing}\bigr)\lor\bigl(\alpha\text{ is neither geodesic nor reparametrized geodesic and }g(\nabla_XX,X)\circ\alpha\text{ is nondecreasing}\bigr)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\circ\alpha:I\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consequences of concurrent-field energy convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four corollaries concerning critical points, upper boundedness, nonexistence, and closed geodesics; their distinct conditional scopes are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a concurrent vector field X on (M,g), with f=\tfrac12 g(X,X), the function f has at most one critical point; if such a point exists, it is a global minimum and a zero of X. Also, f is not bounded above. A complete finite-volume Riemannian manifold, in particular a compact one, admits no concurrent vector field. If (M,g) admits a concurrent vector field, then it has no closed geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The energy of a concurrent field has at most one critical point, which if present is a global minimum and a zero of the field, and the energy is unbounded above. Complete finite-volume manifolds admit no concurrent fields, and manifolds admitting one have no closed geodesics.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the first two clauses, }X\text{ is concurrent and }f=\tfrac12 g(X,X)
\text{For the nonexistence clause, }(M,g)\text{ is complete and }\operatorname{vol}(M)<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\operatorname{Crit}(f)|\le1;\quad x_*\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\Rightarrow x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\text{ and }X_{x_*}=0;\quad f\text{ is not bounded above};\quad ((M,g)\text{ complete},\ \operatorname{vol}(M)<\infty)\Rightarrow M\text{ admits no concurrent field};\quad M\text{ admits a concurrent field}\Rightarrow M\text{ has no closed geodesics}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Energy zeros at limit points of conformal-flow orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of limiting energy zeros by accumulated conformal factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let X be a conformal vector field on (M,g) admitting a nonconstant complete orbit T_t(x_0),\ t\in\mathbb R, with T_0(x_0)=x_0; let f be its energy and \varphi its conformal factor. (i) If (s_k) is unbounded and T_{s_k}(x_0)\to x, then
\[
f(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lim_{k\to\infty}\int_0^{s_k}\varphi(T_u(x_0))\,du=-\infty.
\]
(ii) If T_t(x_0)\to x as t\to\infty, so \Omega(x_0)=\{x\}, then
\[
f(x)=0,\qquad \int_0^\infty\varphi(T_u(x_0))\,du=-\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonconstant complete orbit of a conformal vector field, a subsequential limit is a zero of the field energy exactly when the accumulated conformal factor tends to minus infinity along that subsequence. If the entire forward orbit converges to one point, that point has zero energy and the accumulated conformal factor over the positive half-line is minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a conformal vector field on }(M,g)
T_t(x_0):\mathbb R\to M\text{ is a nonconstant orbit with }T_0(x_0)=x_0
(s_k)\subset\mathbb R\text{ is unbounded and }T_{s_k}(x_0)\to x\text{ in part (i)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=0\iff\lim_{k\to\infty}\int_0^{s_k}\varphi(T_u(x_0))\,du=-\infty;\quad T_t(x_0)\to x\Rightarrow f(x)=0\text{ and }\int_0^\infty\varphi(T_u(x_0))\,du=-\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parallelizable manifolds and the sphere obstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition with stated positive examples and the failure boundary on the two-sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth \(n\)-manifold \(\mathcal M\) is parallelizable if there exist smooth vector fields \(W_1,\ldots,W_n\) on all of \(\mathcal M\) such that \(W_1(x),\ldots,W_n(x)\) is a basis of \(T_x\mathcal M\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\). The manifolds \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(S^1\) are parallelizable. The sphere \(S^2\) is not parallelizable because every smooth vector field on \(S^2\) vanishes somewhere, so no pair of global smooth vector fields forms a basis at every point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold is parallelizable when it admits a global smooth frame. Euclidean space and the circle are parallelizable, whereas the two-sphere is not because every smooth vector field on it has a zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\text{ is parallelizable}\iff\exists W_1,\ldots,W_n\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal M)\ \forall x\in\mathcal M:\ (W_1(x),\ldots,W_n(x))\text{ is a basis of }T_x\mathcal M;\quad \mathbb R^n,S^1\text{ are parallelizable, while }S^2\text{ is not}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth one-forms and metric duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Module-theoretic definition, differential example, and Riemannian musical correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth one-form on \(\mathcal M\) is an \(\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\)-linear map \(X:\mathfrak X(\mathcal M)\to\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\). Thus, in particular, \(X(gV)=gX(V)\) for all \(g\in\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\) and \(V\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal M)\). For a smooth function \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), its differential is the smooth one-form satisfying \((\mathrm Df(V))(x)=\mathrm Df(x)[V(x)]\). If \(\mathcal M\) is Riemannian, every smooth vector field \(U\) defines the one-form \(V\mapsto\langle U,V\rangle\), and every smooth one-form arises uniquely in this way. Under this musical isomorphism, \(\mathrm Df\) corresponds to \(\operatorname{grad}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth one-form is a smooth-function-linear map from smooth vector fields to smooth scalar fields. Differentials are one-forms, and a Riemannian metric gives a one-to-one correspondence between smooth one-forms and smooth vector fields; df corresponds to grad f.
assumptions_latex: For the musical correspondence, \(\mathcal M\) has a Riemannian metric \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega^1(\mathcal M)\cong\mathfrak X(\mathcal M),\qquad X(V)=\langle U,V\rangle,\qquad \mathrm Df\leftrightarrow\operatorname{grad}f.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical points and geodesic orbits of conformal-field energy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the criticality alternative, the reparametrized-geodesic field-line condition, and the Killing-field boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a conformal vector field on $(M,g)$ with conformal factor $\varphi$, and let $f=\frac12g(X,X)$. Every critical point of $f$ is a zero of $\varphi$ or a zero of $f$. The critical set of $f$ contains every field line $\alpha:I\to M$ of $X$ that becomes a geodesic under the reparametrization $s=a+b\int_{t_0}^{t}\exp\!\left(\int_{t_0}^{r}(\varphi\circ\alpha)(u)\,du\right)dr$. Moreover, the critical set contains all orbits of $X$ if and only if $X$ is a Killing vector field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical point of the energy of a conformal vector field must have either zero conformal factor or zero energy. Field lines satisfying the stated geodesic reparametrization lie in the critical set, and all field orbits lie there exactly when the vector field is Killing.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a conformal vector field with conformal factor }\varphi
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Crit}(f)\subseteq\{\varphi=0\}\cup\{f=0\};\quad \alpha(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\text{ for each field line satisfying the stated geodesic reparametrization};\quad \text{all orbits of }X\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\iff X\text{ is Killing}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Energy identities for a conformal vector field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the conformal factor and records the gradient and flow-direction derivatives of the field energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(M,g)$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Riemannian connection $
abla$, and let $X\in\mathcal X(M)$ satisfy $g(
abla_YX,Z)+g(
abla_ZX,Y)=\varphi g(Y,Z)$ for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal X(M)$, where $\varphi= rac{2}{n}\operatorname{div}X$. For $f= rac12g(X,X)$, one has $df(Y)=g(
abla_YX,X)=g(-
abla_XX+\varphi X,Y)$ for every $Y$, hence $\operatorname{grad}f=-
abla_XX+\varphi X$ and $df(X)=\varphi f$. In particular, every zero of $X$ is a critical point of $f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a conformal vector field, the gradient of its energy equals minus its covariant acceleration plus the conformal factor times the field. The energy derivative along the field is the conformal factor times the energy, and every zero of the field is an energy critical point.
assumptions_latex: (M,g)\text{ is an }n\text{-dimensional Riemannian manifold with connection }\nabla
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{grad}f=-\nabla_XX+\varphi X,\qquad df(X)=\varphi f,\qquad X(x)=0\Rightarrow \operatorname{grad}f(x)=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature consequences at extrema of conformal-field energy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives distinct positive-curvature minimum and negative-curvature maximum conclusions in even dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a conformal vector field on an even-dimensional Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, and let $f=\frac12g(X,X)$. If $x_0$ is a local minimum of $f$ and the sectional curvature $K_{X_0}$ at $x_0$ is strictly positive, then $X(x_0)=0$. If $x_0$ is a local maximum of $f$ and $K_{X_0}$ at $x_0$ is strictly negative, then $X$ vanishes identically on a neighborhood of $x_0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an even-dimensional Riemannian manifold, a positive-sectional-curvature local minimum of a conformal field's energy is a zero of the field. At a negative-sectional-curvature local maximum, the field vanishes throughout a neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a conformal vector field on }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[x_0\in\operatorname{locmin}f\land K_{X_0}>0\bigr]\Rightarrow X(x_0)=0;\qquad \bigl[x_0\in\operatorname{locmax}f\land K_{X_0}<0\bigr]\Rightarrow \exists U\ni x_0\;\forall x\in U,\ X(x)=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Irrotational vector fields and their energy identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and intrinsic identities stated in the extract, excluding its derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(M,g)$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection $
abla$, and let $X\in\mathfrak X(M)$. The field $X$ is irrotational if and only if $g(
abla_YX,Z)=g(
abla_ZX,Y)$ for all $Y,Z\in\mathfrak X(M)$, equivalently if and only if $(
abla X)_x$ is self-adjoint with respect to $g_x$ for every $x\in M$; equivalently, $X$ is locally a potential field. An irrotational field with $\operatorname{div}X=0$ is harmonic. If $X$ is irrotational and $f=	frac12g(X,X)$, then $df(Y)=g(
abla_YX,X)=g(
abla_XX,Y)$ and $\operatorname{grad}f=
abla_XX$. Hence every zero of $X$ is critical for $f$, and every affinely parametrized integral orbit of $X$ that is a geodesic lies in the critical set of $f$ and satisfies $\operatorname{rank}(
abla X)_\alpha\le n-1$. If $Y_x\mapsto g(
abla_{Y_x}X,Y_x)$ is positive definite at every $x$, every critical point of $f$ is a zero of $X$. Moreover, $\operatorname{Hess}f(Y,Y)=g(
abla_X(
abla X)(Y),Y)+R(X,Y,X,Y)+g(
abla_YX,
abla_YX)$ for every $Y\in\mathfrak X(M)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Irrotational fields have self-adjoint covariant derivative and are locally potential fields; divergence-free irrotational fields are harmonic. For an irrotational field, the gradient of its squared-norm energy is its covariant acceleration. Zeros and geodesic integral orbits therefore yield critical points, subject to the stated rank property, and positive definiteness of the covariant-derivative quadratic form makes every critical point a zero. The extract also gives the intrinsic Hessian formula for this energy.
assumptions_latex: (M,g)\text{ is an }n\text{-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection }\nabla
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
X	ext{ irrotational},\ f=	frac12g(X,X)\Longrightarrow \operatorname{grad}f=
abla_XX,\quad \operatorname{Hess}f(Y,Y)=g(
abla_X(
abla X)(Y),Y)+R(X,Y,X,Y)+\|
abla_YX\|_g^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cotangent spaces, covector fields, and differentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cotangent spaces and bundles, one-forms and their evaluation, and the critical-point criterion expressed through the differential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth manifold \(\mathcal M\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\), the cotangent space is \(T_x^*\mathcal M=(T_x\mathcal M)^*\), the space of linear maps \(\mu_x:T_x\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\); its elements are covectors. The cotangent bundle is \(T^*\mathcal M=\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal M}T_x^*\mathcal M\). A smooth section \(\mu:x\mapsto\mu_x\) is a covector field or one-form, equivalently a \((0,1)\)-tensor. For each smooth vector field \(\xi\), it defines a scalar field by \((\mu[\xi])(x)=\mu_x[\xi_x]\). If \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth, then \(\mathrm Df(x)\in T_x^*\mathcal M\), and \(x\) is a critical point of \(f\) if and only if \(\mathrm Df(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cotangent space at a point is the dual of its tangent space, and the union of these spaces is the cotangent bundle. Smooth sections are one-forms, which evaluate vector fields pointwise to give scalar fields. The differential of a smooth scalar function is a one-form and vanishes at a point exactly when that point is critical.
assumptions_latex: \mu\text{ is a smooth section of }T^*\mathcal M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_x^*\mathcal M=(T_x\mathcal M)^*,\qquad (\mu[\xi])(x)=\mu_x[\xi_x],\qquad x\text{ is critical for }f\iff \mathrm Df(x)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariant derivative of a tensor field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total and directional covariant derivatives and parallel tensor fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a connection $
abla$ and a smooth tensor field $T$ of order $k$, its total covariant derivative is defined by
$$(
abla T)(U_1,\ldots,U_k,V)=V igl(T(U_1,\ldots,U_k) igr)-\sum_{i=1}^kT(U_1,\ldots,U_{i-1},
abla_VU_i,U_{i+1},\ldots,U_k).$$
The directional derivative is defined by $(
abla_VT)(U_1,\ldots,U_k)=(
abla T)(U_1,\ldots,U_k,V)$. The field $T$ is parallel if $
abla T=0$. If $T$ is symmetric, then $
abla_VT$ is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The total covariant derivative differentiates the evaluated tensor and subtracts the contribution from differentiating each input. Fixing the final direction gives the directional derivative. A tensor is parallel when its total covariant derivative vanishes, and directional differentiation preserves symmetry.
assumptions_latex: $\mathcal M$ is a smooth manifold equipped with a connection $\nabla$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla T\in\mathfrak X^{k+1}(\mathcal M),\qquad \nabla_VT\in\mathfrak X^k(\mathcal M).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consequences of a dense complete field line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit-set and energy-variation consequences asserted for a vector field admitting a dense field line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\dim M\ge2$ and let $X$ be a vector field on $(M,g)$ admitting a field line $\alpha:\mathbb R\to M$, $\alpha(0)=x_0$, whose image is dense in $M$. Then $\Omega(x_0)=M\setminus\alpha(\mathbb R)$. If $\alpha$ is a geodesic reparametrized by $s=h(t)$ with coefficient $\mu$, then for every $x\in M\setminus\alpha(\mathbb R)$ there is a sequence $s_k\to+\infty$ or $s_k\to-\infty$ for which, respectively, $\left(\int_{t_0}^{s_k}\mu(\alpha(u))\,du\right)_k$ or $\left(\int_{s_k}^{t_0}\mu(\alpha(u))\,du\right)_k$ converges; moreover, $X$ has no zero on $M$. If $\alpha$ is neither a geodesic nor a reparametrized geodesic, then for every such $x$ there is a sequence $s_k\to+\infty$ or $s_k\to-\infty$ for which the corresponding sequence of integrals of $g(\nabla_XX,X)\circ\alpha$ over $[t_0,s_k]$ or $[s_k,t_0]$ converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vector field on a manifold of dimension at least two with a complete dense trajectory, the stated omega-limit set is the complement of that trajectory. Reparametrized-geodesic dense trajectories yield convergent subsequences of integrals of the proportional-acceleration coefficient and imply that the field has no zeros. Other dense trajectories yield analogous convergent subsequences for integrals of the energy derivative.
assumptions_latex: \alpha:\mathbb R\to M\text{ is an integral curve of }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega(x_0)=M\setminus\alpha(\mathbb R),\quad\text{with the stated branch-dependent convergent integral sequences, and in the reparametrized-geodesic branch }Z(X)=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz continuity of a Riemannian vector field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The comparison uses the unique minimizing geodesic within the injectivity-radius regime and is imposed componentwise on a disconnected manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector field \(V\) on a connected Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz continuous if, for all \(x,y\in\mathcal M\) such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\), \[\left\|\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{0\leftarrow1}V(y)-V(x)\right\|\le L\operatorname{dist}(x,y),\] where \(\gamma\) is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). If \(\mathcal M\) is disconnected, the condition is required on each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector field is L-Lipschitz when field values at sufficiently close points, compared by parallel transport along their unique minimizing geodesic, differ by at most L times their Riemannian distance. The condition is imposed separately on each connected component.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a vector field on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\).
\(x,y\) belong to one connected component and satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\).
\(\gamma\) is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left\|\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{0\leftarrow1}V(y)-V(x)\right\|\le L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobi Field and Initial-Value Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the curvature-sign convention appearing in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma\) be a geodesic on an \(n\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold and let \(V=\dot\gamma\). A vector field \(J\) along \(\gamma\) is a Jacobi field if \[\frac{\nabla^2J}{dt^2}-R(V,J)V=0.\] The solution space has dimension \(2n\), and each Jacobi field is uniquely determined by \(J(0)\) and \(\frac{\nabla J}{dt}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Jacobi field along a geodesic is a vector field satisfying the stated curvature-dependent second-order covariant equation. On an n-dimensional manifold its solution space has dimension 2n, and a solution is uniquely determined by its initial value and initial covariant derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma\) is a geodesic on an \(n\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\) is a Jacobi field iff \(\nabla_t^2J-R(V,J)V=0\); the solution space has dimension \(2n\), with each solution uniquely determined by \((J(0),\nabla_tJ(0))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zeros detected by extrema of affine-field energy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and source-stated sectional-curvature conditions under which critical points or extrema force vanishing of an affine vector field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be an affine vector field on an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, and let $f=\tfrac12g(X,X)$. If $x_0$ is critical for $f$ and $\operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)_{x_0}=n$, then $X(x_0)=0$. Suppose $\operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)\le n-2$. If $x_0$ is a local minimum of $f$ and the sectional curvature denoted by $K_{X(x_0)}$ in the source is strictly positive, then $X(x_0)=0$. If $x_0$ is a local maximum of $f$ and the corresponding sectional curvature $K_{X(x_0)}$ is strictly negative, then $X$ vanishes identically in a neighborhood of $x_0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full rank at a critical point forces the affine vector field to vanish there. Under rank at most n minus two, the source's positive or negative sectional-curvature conditions at a local energy extremum yield pointwise or local identical vanishing, respectively.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is an affine vector field on }(M,g)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(df_{x_0}=0\land\operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)_{x_0}=n\bigr)\Rightarrow X(x_0)=0;\quad \operatorname{rank}(\nabla X)\le n-2\Rightarrow\begin{cases}x_0\text{ local min},\ K_{X(x_0)}>0\Rightarrow X(x_0)=0,\\x_0\text{ local max},\ K_{X(x_0)}<0\Rightarrow X\equiv0\text{ near }x_0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Energy calculus for an affine vector field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential and Hessian identities and their immediate geometric consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(M,g)$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold and let $X$ be affine, meaning $
abla_Y
abla X=R(Y,X)$ for every $Y\in\mathfrak X(M)$. For $f=	frac12g(X,X)$, one has $df(Y)=g(
abla_YX,X)$ and $\operatorname{Hess}f(Y,Y)=-R(X,Y,X,Y)+g(
abla_YX,
abla_YX)$. Hence every zero of $X$ is critical for $f$, and every geodesic orbit of $X$ lies in the critical set. If $Y_x\mapsto g(
abla_{Y_x}X,Y_x)$ is positive definite at every $x$, every critical point of $f$ is a zero of $X$. The existence of a geodesic orbit $\alpha$ implies $\operatorname{rank}(
abla X)|_\alpha\le n-1$. If $M$ is compact, then $X$ is of Killing type.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Lipschitz tensor field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines tensor-field Lipschitz continuity by comparing values after parallel transport along radial exponential curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An order-$k$ tensor field $T$ on a Riemannian manifold is $L$-Lipschitz continuous if, for every $(x,s)$ in the domain of the exponential map and all $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in T_x\mathcal M$,
$$\left|T(\operatorname{Exp}_x(s))(P_su_1,\ldots,P_su_k)-T(x)(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\right|\le L\|s\|_x\prod_{i=1}^k\|u_i\|_x,$$
where $P_s$ is parallel transport from $t=0$ to $t=1$ along $\gamma(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(ts)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tensor field is L-Lipschitz when its value changes by at most L times the geodesic displacement and the product of the input norms after the inputs are parallel-transported along the corresponding exponential curve.
assumptions_latex: $\mathcal M$ is a Riemannian manifold with its Riemannian connection.
$T$ is a tensor field of order $k$.
$(x,s)$ lies in the domain of the exponential map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|T(\operatorname{Exp}_x(s))(P_su_1,\ldots,P_su_k)-T(x)(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\right|\le L\|s\|_x\prod_{i=1}^k\|u_i\|_x.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Bundle Structure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Spaces, Tangent Bundle, and Vector Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent vectors represented by curve velocities, the tangent-bundle construction, its possible global nontriviality, and vector fields as sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a $k$-dimensional differentiable manifold. For $x\in M$, $T_xM$ is the $k$-dimensional vector space of tangent vectors represented by velocities $\dot\gamma(0)$ of differentiable curves $\gamma$ in $M$ with $\gamma(0)=x$. The tangent bundle is $TM:=\bigsqcup_{x\in M}T_xM=\{(x,\xi):x\in M,\ \xi\in T_xM\}$ and is a manifold of dimension $2k$. In general, $TM$ need not be globally diffeomorphic to $M\times\mathbb R^k$. A vector field is a section $f:M\to TM$ satisfying $f(x)\in T_xM$ for every $x\in M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each point of a k-dimensional differentiable manifold, tangent vectors are represented by velocities of curves through that point. The disjoint union of the tangent spaces is the 2k-dimensional tangent bundle, which need not be globally a product with R^k. A vector field assigns each point a vector in its tangent space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: TM=\bigsqcup_{x\in M}T_xM\text{ is a }2k\text{-dimensional manifold and need not be globally diffeomorphic to }M\times\mathbb R^k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cotangent Space, Differential, and Cotangent Bundle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of cotangent geometry and canonical coordinates on the cotangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $x$ on a $k$-dimensional manifold $M$, the cotangent space is $T_x^*M:=(T_xM)^*$, the space of linear maps $T_xM\to\mathbb R$. If $g\in C^1(M,\mathbb R)$, its differential at $x$ is the covector $dg|_x$ defined by $dg|_x(\xi)=\left.\frac{d}{d\alpha}\right|_{\alpha=0}g(\gamma(\alpha))$ for any curve $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma(0)=\xi$; this value is independent of the chosen curve. In local coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$, $dg|_x(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^k g_{x_i}(x)\xi_i$, and $(dx_1,\ldots,dx_k)$ is a basis of $T_x^*M$. The cotangent bundle $T^*M:=\bigcup_{x\in M}T_x^*M$ is a $2k$-dimensional manifold, with the base coordinates and covector components furnishing canonical local coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cotangent space at a point is the dual of the tangent space. The differential of a continuously differentiable scalar function is the covector that returns its directional derivative, independently of the curve representing the tangent direction. Coordinate differentials form a local cotangent basis, and the union of the cotangent spaces is a 2k-dimensional manifold with canonical local coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_x^*M=(T_xM)^*,\quad dg|_x(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^k g_{x_i}(x)\xi_i,\quad \dim(T^*M)=2k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quotient construction and linear structure of a tangent space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tangent space from curve classes and its chart-induced vector-space operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth \(d\)-manifold \(\mathcal M\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\), let \(C_x\) be the smooth curves through \(x\) and let \(\sim\) identify curves with equal coordinate velocity at zero. Then \(T_x\mathcal M=C_x/\!\sim=\{[c]:c\in C_x\}\). For every chart \((\mathcal U,\varphi)\) about \(x\), the map \(\theta_x^\varphi:T_x\mathcal M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\theta_x^\varphi([c])=(\varphi\circ c)'(0)\), is well defined and bijective. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_x\mathcal M=C_x/\!\sim,\qquad \theta_x^\varphi([c])=(\varphi\circ c)'(0)\text{ is bijective and induces a chart-independent linear structure}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Symplectic Form on a Cotangent Bundle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate definition and evaluation formula for the natural symplectic two-form on a cotangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a $k$-dimensional manifold and let $(x,p)=(x_1,\ldots,x_k,p_1,\ldots,p_k)$ be canonical local coordinates on $T^*M$. The canonical symplectic two-form is $\omega^2:=\sum_{i=1}^k dx_i\wedge dp_i$, where $(\omega_1\wedge\omega_2)(\xi_1,\xi_2)=\omega_1(\xi_1)\omega_2(\xi_2)-\omega_2(\xi_1)\omega_1(\xi_2)$. Thus, for tangent vectors $(y,q)$ and $(z,r)$ to $T^*M$, $\omega^2((y,q),(z,r))=\sum_{i=1}^k(y_ir_i-q_iz_i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In canonical position-covector coordinates on a cotangent bundle, the natural symplectic two-form is the sum of dx_i wedge dp_i. Applied to tangent vectors (y,q) and (z,r), it equals the sum of y_i r_i minus q_i z_i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \omega^2=\sum_{i=1}^k dx_i\wedge dp_i,\qquad \omega^2((y,q),(z,r))=\sum_{i=1}^k(y_ir_i-q_iz_i).

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Vector Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth sections of the tangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector field on a smooth manifold \(M\) is a section \(X:M\to TM\) of the tangent-bundle projection, so \(\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M\) and \(X(p)\in T_pM\) for every \(p\in M\). It is smooth when \(X\) is smooth as a map into \(TM\). Equivalently, in every smooth chart with coordinates \((x^1,\ldots,x^n)\), there exist smooth functions \(X^i\) such that \(X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i\,\partial/\partial x^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth vector field assigns a tangent vector smoothly to every point, equivalently having smooth component functions in every chart.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) is smooth exactly when its coordinate components \(X^1,\ldots,X^n\) are smooth in every chart.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Torse-Forming Vector Field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, named subclasses, derivative endomorphism, and pregeodesic integral curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector field \(X\in\mathfrak X(M)\) on an \(n\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) is torse forming if there exist a function \(a:M	o\mathbb R\) and a one-form \(\omega\in\Omega^1(M)\) such that \(
abla_YX=aY+\omega(Y)X\) for every \(Y\in\mathfrak X(M)\). Consequently, \(
abla_XX=(a+\omega(X))X\), so the integral curves of \(X\) are geodesics after reparametrization. Pointwise, \((
abla X)_x=a(x)\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}+\omega_x\otimes X_x\). The stated subclasses are concircular if \(\omega=dh\), special concircular if \(\omega=0\), concurrent if \(a\) is a nonzero constant and \(\omega=0\), recurrent if \(a=0\), and parallel if \(a=0=\omega\). If \(X\equiv0\), then \(a\equiv0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A torse-forming vector field has covariant derivative equal to a scalar multiple of the differentiation direction plus a multiple of the field. Its integral curves are reparametrized geodesics, and its derivative endomorphism is a scalar identity plus a rank-at-most-one operator. Restrictions on the defining function and one-form give the listed subclasses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is torse forming}\iff\exists a:M\to\mathbb R,\ \exists\omega\in\Omega^1(M)\text{ such that }\nabla_YX=aY+\omega(Y)X\quad\forall Y\in\mathfrak X(M)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lie bracket and local commutation of vector fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the vector-field sign convention in the extract, which may be opposite to the matrix-commutator convention. Flow conclusions require sufficient regularity and sufficiently small times so that all trajectories remain in the neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable vector fields \(f,g:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \([f,g](x):=Dg(x)f(x)-Df(x)g(x)\). When sufficiently regular local flows \(\Phi_f^t\) and \(\Phi_g^t\) exist, \(\Phi_g^{-\varepsilon}\circ\Phi_f^{-\varepsilon}\circ\Phi_g^{\varepsilon}\circ\Phi_f^{\varepsilon}(x_0)=x_0+\varepsilon^2[f,g](x_0)+o(\varepsilon^2)\). If \([f,g]\equiv0\) on a neighborhood containing the relevant flow segments, then for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) the local flows commute and the loop returns to \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lie bracket is Dg(x)f(x) minus Df(x)g(x). A sufficiently regular small flow loop along f, g, −f, and −g has leading displacement ε²[f,g](x₀). If the bracket vanishes on a neighborhood containing the loop, then sufficiently small local flow loops close and the flows commute locally.
assumptions_latex: U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is an open neighborhood of }x_0
\text{For the flow claims, the local flows have sufficient regularity and remain in }U\text{ for sufficiently small }|\varepsilon|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [f,g](x)=Dg(x)f(x)-Df(x)g(x),\qquad \Phi_g^{-\varepsilon}\circ\Phi_f^{-\varepsilon}\circ\Phi_g^{\varepsilon}\circ\Phi_f^{\varepsilon}(x_0)=x_0+\varepsilon^2[f,g](x_0)+o(\varepsilon^2),\qquad [f,g]\equiv0\Rightarrow \Phi_g^t\circ\Phi_f^s=\Phi_f^s\circ\Phi_g^t\text{ locally}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential and critical point of a functional on fixed-endpoint curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tangent model, first variation, and criticality for a functional on a manifold-valued fixed-endpoint curve space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a differentiable manifold, let $x,y\in M$ (possibly $x=y$), and let $\Omega$ be the set of piecewise-$C^\infty$ regular curves $\omega:[0,1]\to M$ satisfying $\omega(0)=x$ and $\omega(1)=y$. Set $T_\omega\Omega=\{W: W\text{ is a piecewise differentiable vector field along }\omega,\ W(0)=W(1)=0\}$. If $\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times[0,1]\to M$ is a fixed-endpoint variation of $\omega$, $\bar\alpha(u)(t)=\alpha(u,t)$, and $W(t)=\partial_u\alpha(0,t)$, then, whenever the derivative exists for every such variation and depends only on $W$, the differential of $F:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ at $\omega$ is the linear functional $F_{*,\omega}:T_\omega\Omega\to\mathbb R$ defined by $F_{*,\omega}(W)=\left.\frac{d}{du}F(\bar\alpha(u))\right|_{u=0}$. The curve $\omega$ is a critical point of $F$ if this derivative is zero for every fixed-endpoint variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the space of piecewise-smooth regular curves joining two fixed manifold points, tangent directions are piecewise differentiable vector fields along a curve that vanish at both endpoints. The differential of a real-valued curve functional in such a direction is its derivative along any realizing fixed-endpoint variation, provided that derivative exists and is determined by the direction. A curve is critical when every such first variation is zero.
assumptions_latex: \left.\frac{d}{du}F(\bar\alpha(u))\right|_{u=0}\text{ exists for every admissible variation and is determined by }W
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{*,\omega}(W)=\left.\frac{d}{du}F(\bar\alpha(u))\right|_{u=0},\qquad \omega\text{ is critical}\iff F_{*,\omega}(W)=0\ \forall W\in T_\omega\Omega.
