knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Invariance Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility needed for representative-independent metric and gradient computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric–invariance compatibility requires every action map \(\Phi_a(x)=a\cdot x\) to be an isometry and the objective to be orbit invariant:
\[
g_{a\cdot x}(d\Phi_a\eta,d\Phi_a\zeta)=g_x(\eta,\zeta),\qquad f(a\cdot x)=f(x).
\]
These identities must hold for all \(a\in G\), \(x\in M\), and \(\eta,\zeta\in T_xM\). They imply \(d\Phi_a(\mathcal{H}_x)=\mathcal{H}_{a\cdot x}\) and \(\operatorname{grad}f(a\cdot x)=d\Phi_a\operatorname{grad}f(x)\), so quotient metric and gradient computations do not depend on the representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isometric group action and orbit-invariant objective make horizontal spaces and gradients transform equivariantly, ensuring representative-independent quotient computations.

\(g_M\) is a Riemannian metric and \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence Relations, Quotient Sets, Quotient Topology, and Orbit Quotients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational set-theoretic and topological quotient constructions, including equivalence relations induced by group actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary relation $\sim$ on a set $X$ is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. For $x\in X$, define $[x]=\{y\in X:x\sim y\}$, $X/{\sim}=\{[x]:x\in X\}$, and the natural projection $\pi:X\to X/{\sim}$ by $\pi(x)=[x]$; this projection is surjective. If $(X,\mathcal O)$ is a topological space, the quotient topology is $\mathcal O_\pi=\{O\subseteq X/{\sim}:\pi^{-1}(O)\in\mathcal O\}$. A left action $\phi:G\times X\to X$ induces $x\sim y$ exactly when $y=\phi(g,x)$ for some $g\in G$, and its orbit quotient is denoted $G\backslash X$. A right action $\phi:X\times G\to X$ similarly induces $x\sim y$ exactly when $y=\phi(x,g)$ for some $g\in G$, and its quotient is denoted $X/G$. The notation $X/G$ may also be used for a left-action quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Its classes form a quotient set with a surjective natural projection. A topology induces the quotient topology through inverse images, and a group action induces equivalence by belonging to the same orbit.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a set and }\sim\text{ is a binary relation on }X
\text{For the quotient topology, }(X,\mathcal O)\text{ is a topological space}
\text{For an orbit quotient, }G\text{ is a group acting on }X\text{ from the left or right}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X/{\sim}=\{[x]:x\in X\},\quad \pi(x)=[x]\text{ is surjective},\quad \mathcal O_\pi=\{O\subseteq X/{\sim}:\pi^{-1}(O)\in\mathcal O\},\quad \text{and group actions induce orbit quotients }G\backslash X\text{ or }X/G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness criterion for maps from a quotient manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes smooth maps from a quotient manifold through pullback along its canonical projection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ehresmann completeness and its consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the global horizontal-lifting property and records its fiber-bundle implication and completeness failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A submersion \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\) equipped with horizontal spaces is Ehresmann complete if, for every smooth curve \(c:I\to\mathcal M\) with nonvanishing velocity, every \(t_0\in I\), and every \(x_0\in\pi^{-1}(c(t_0))\), the curve \(c\) has a horizontal lift \(\bar c:I\to\overline{\mathcal M}\) on its whole domain satisfying \(\pi\circ\bar c=c\) and \(\bar c(t_0)=x_0\). If this property holds, then \(\pi\) is a smooth fiber bundle. The property may hold even when \(\overline{\mathcal M}\) is not complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submersion is Ehresmann complete when every regular smooth base curve has a whole-domain horizontal lift through any selected point of an initial fiber. This property makes the submersion a smooth fiber bundle but does not require the total space to be complete.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\) is a submersion equipped with horizontal spaces.
\(c:I\to\mathcal M\) is smooth and has nonvanishing velocity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ Ehresmann complete}\Rightarrow\pi\text{ is a smooth fiber bundle},\qquad \pi\text{ Ehresmann complete}\centernot\Rightarrow\overline{\mathcal M}\text{ complete}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Lifting Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise lifting of quotient tangent vectors to representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in M\), the restriction \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}:\mathcal{H}_x\to T_{[x]}(M/G)\) is a linear isomorphism. The quotient lifting interface is therefore
\[
\operatorname{lift}_x:=\bigl(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
For every \(u\in T_{[x]}(M/G)\), its lift \(u_x^{\mathcal H}=\operatorname{lift}_x(u)\) is uniquely characterized by \(u_x^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) and \(d\pi_x(u_x^{\mathcal H})=u\). Under an invariant connection, lifts at different representatives are related by the differential of the group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient tangent vector has a unique horizontal lift at each representative, obtained by inverting the quotient differential restricted to the horizontal space.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:M\to M/G\) is a regular quotient projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lift}_x=(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x})^{-1}\) is the unique horizontal right inverse of \(d\pi_x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grassmannian as a Stiefel quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a p-dimensional subspace by the equivalence class of its orthonormal basis matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $1\le p\le n$, let $\operatorname{St}(n,p)=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}:X^\top X=I_p\}$. For $X,Y\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, define $X\sim Y$ if $\operatorname{span}(X)=\operatorname{span}(Y)$. Then $X\sim Y$ if and only if $X=YQ$ for some $Q\in\mathrm O(p)$, and $[X]=\{XQ:Q\in\mathrm O(p)\}$. Hence $[X]\mapsto\operatorname{span}(X)$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{St}(n,p)/\mathrm O(p)$ to $\operatorname{Gr}(n,p)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For 1 ≤ p ≤ n, two orthonormal n-by-p basis matrices span the same p-dimensional subspace exactly when one is obtained from the other by right multiplication by a p-by-p orthogonal matrix. Thus the Grassmannian is in one-to-one correspondence with the quotient of the Stiefel manifold by this action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\sim Y\iff \exists Q\in\mathrm O(p):X=YQ,\qquad \operatorname{Gr}(n,p)\cong\operatorname{St}(n,p)/\mathrm O(p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preservation of minimizers and critical points under lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of optimization properties for an objective and its pullback through a manifold map, under property-specific hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\), let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), and define \(\bar f=f\circ\pi\). If \(\pi\) is surjective, then \(x\) is a global minimizer of \(\bar f\) if and only if \(\pi(x)\) is a global minimizer of \(f\). If \(\pi\) is continuous and open, then \(x\) is a local minimizer of \(\bar f\) if and only if \(\pi(x)\) is a local minimizer of \(f\). If \(\pi\) is smooth and \(\mathrm D\pi(x)\) is surjective at every point, then first-order criticality, and likewise second-order criticality, holds at \(x\) for \(\bar f\) if and only if it holds at \(\pi(x)\) for \(f\). All conclusions hold when \(\mathcal M\) is a quotient manifold of \(\overline{\mathcal M}\) and \(\pi\) is its canonical projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pullback through a manifold map preserves global minimizers under surjectivity, local minimizers under continuity and openness, and first- and second-order critical points under smoothness and an everywhere-surjective differential. Quotient-manifold projections satisfy all these conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal M\), \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), and \(\bar f=f\circ\pi\).
For local minimizers, \(\pi\) is continuous and open.
For first- and second-order criticality, \(\pi\) is smooth, \(\mathrm D\pi(x)\) is surjective for all \(x\in\overline{\mathcal M}\), and the corresponding derivatives exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname*{argmin}\bar f\iff\pi(x)\in\operatorname*{argmin}f;\quad x\text{ is a local minimizer of }\bar f\iff\pi(x)\text{ is a local minimizer of }f;\quad x\text{ is first- or second-order critical for }\bar f\iff\pi(x)\text{ has the corresponding criticality for }f,\) under the respective hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convergence of Algorithm 8 to a spectral invariant subspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded local convergence theorem for a Rayleigh quotient algorithm on a Grassmann manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the requirements of Algorithm 8, suppose there exists \(Y_*\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) such that \(\mathcal{Y}_*=\operatorname{span}(Y_*)\) is a spectral invariant subspace of \(B^{-1}A\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subject to all requirements of Algorithm 8, if the target span is a spectral invariant subspace of B^{-1}A, then every sufficiently nearby initial span produces an infinite sequence of iterates whose spans converge to the target subspace superlinearly, with at least quadratic order, on the Grassmann manifold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Newton iteration for a generalized Rayleigh quotient on Grass(p,n)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted horizontal projected Newton solve for symmetric A and symmetric positive-definite B.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A=A^T, B=B^T\succ0, and Y_0\in\mathbb{R}_*^{n\times p}. Define P_{BY,Y}=I-BY(Y^TBY)^{-1}Y^T. For k=0,1,\ldots, compute Z_k satisfying P_{BY_k,Y_k}\!\left(AZ_k-BZ_k(Y_k^TBY_k)^{-1}Y_k^TAY_k\right)=-P_{BY_k,Y_k}(AY_k),\quad Y_k^TBZ_k=0, and set Y_{k+1}=(Y_k+Z_k)N_k, where N_k\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} is nonsingular and chosen for normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For symmetric A and positive-definite B, solve the B-horizontal projected generalized Rayleigh-quotient Newton system, then update the full-rank representative and normalize it with a nonsingular matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{Y_k\}_{k\ge0}\subset\mathbb{R}_*^{n\times p}\text{ is generated by }Y_{k+1}=(Y_k+Z_k)N_k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection of total-space directions onto horizontal representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\eta\in T_xM\), the horizontal projection is
\[
P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta:=\eta-P_x^{\mathcal V}\eta.
\]
Equivalently, \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta\) is the unique vector in \(\mathcal{H}_x\) such that \(\eta-P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta\in\mathcal{V}_x\). It satisfies \(d\pi_x(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta)=d\pi_x(\eta)\), so removing a vertical component does not alter the represented quotient tangent vector. For an orthogonal splitting, \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\) is self-adjoint and idempotent with respect to the total-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal projection removes the vertical component of a tangent vector without changing the quotient tangent vector it represents.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}/\!\sim\), where \(\overline{\mathcal M}\) is an open subset of a Euclidean space \(\mathcal E\). Let \(\mathcal H\) be a horizontal distribution complementary to the vertical distribution \(\mathcal V\), and let \(P^h_{\bar x}:T_{\bar x}\overline{\mathcal M}\to\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) be projection parallel to \(\mathcal V_{\bar x}\). \(\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) is complementary to the vertical space \(\mathcal V_{\bar x}\).
\(P^h_{\bar x}\) projects onto \(\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) parallel to \(\mathcal V_{\bar x}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal-Curve Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique maximal horizontal lifting of quotient curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A curve \(\gamma:J\to M\) horizontally represents \(\bar\gamma:I\to M/G\) when \(J\subseteq I\), \(\pi(\gamma(t))=\bar\gamma(t)\), and
\[
\dot\gamma(t)=\operatorname{lift}_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\dot{\bar\gamma}(t)\bigr)\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma(t)}.
\]
Given \(t_0\in I\) and \(x_0\in\pi^{-1}(\bar\gamma(t_0))\), the associated first-order lifting equation has a unique maximal solution with \(\gamma(t_0)=x_0\). Conversely, every horizontal curve projects to a quotient curve whose velocity is \(d\pi_{\gamma(t)}\dot\gamma(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient curve is represented by the unique maximal lift through a chosen representative whose velocity remains horizontal and projects to the quotient velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:M\to M/G\) is a regular quotient equipped with a smooth horizontal distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique maximal curve \(\gamma\) through \(x_0\) satisfying \(\pi\circ\gamma=\bar\gamma\) and \(\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma(t)}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizontal Lift of a Vector Field Along a Curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise horizontal lifting of a smooth vector field along a quotient curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c=\pi\circ\bar c\) and let \(Z\in\mathfrak X(c)\) be smooth. Its horizontal lift along \(\bar c\) is the vector field \(\bar Z=\operatorname{lift}(Z)\) defined by \(\bar Z(t)=\operatorname{lift}_{\bar c(t)}(Z(t))\) for every \(t\). Similarly, \(\operatorname{Proj}^{\mathrm H}\) acts pointwise on vector fields along \(\bar c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizontal lift of a smooth vector field along a quotient curve is obtained by horizontally lifting it pointwise along a representative curve. Horizontal projection of fields along that representative curve is likewise defined pointwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall t,\;\bar Z(t)=\operatorname{lift}_{\bar c(t)}(Z(t))\), and \(\operatorname{Proj}^{\mathrm H}\) extends pointwise to vector fields along \(\bar c\)

children.title: Nonfree Group Actions
children.top_down_role: Orbit structures with nontrivial stabilizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonfree Group Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete singular boundary caused by changing stabilizers and orbit dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the rotation action of \(G=SO(2)\) on \(M=\mathbb{R}^2\), the stabilizer is \(G_x=\{e\}\) when \(x\neq 0\), but \(G_0=SO(2)\). Thus the action is not free. Nonzero orbits are circles of dimension one, whereas the orbit of \(0\) has dimension zero. The orbit space is identified topologically with \([0,\infty)\) by \(q(x)=\lVert x\rVert\). The map \(q\) is smooth with rank one on \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\) but is not differentiable at \(0\). Consequently, the free-action quotient theorem and regular principal-bundle representation do not extend across the exceptional orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planar rotations are free away from the origin but fix the origin. Orbit dimension changes there, and the radius quotient map ceases to be differentiable, so the regular principal-bundle quotient model fails across that orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit space is identified with \([0,\infty)\) by \(q(x)=\lVert x\rVert\); \(q\) has rank one away from \(0\) and is not differentiable at \(0\), exposing singular behavior at the exceptional orbit.

notation.meaning: Special orthogonal group in two dimensions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: planar rotation action is the canonical nonfree-action singularity example

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left and Right Group Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definition of actions of a group on a set, independent of any particular quotient-manifold model or application.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A map $\phi:G\times X\to X$ is a left group action if $\phi(e,x)=x$ and $\phi(g,\phi(h,x))=\phi(gh,x)$ for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. A map $\phi:X\times G\to X$ is a right group action if $\phi(x,e)=x$ and $\phi(\phi(x,g),h)=\phi(x,gh)$ for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A left or right group action is a map that respects the group identity and multiplication according to the corresponding left- or right-action law.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a group with identity }e
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi\text{ is a left or right group action when it satisfies the corresponding identity and multiplication-compatibility laws.}

children.title: Singular Quotient Strata
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth or stratified regions arising in quotient spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Quotient Strata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-type stratification of a proper, nonfree Lie-group quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and properly on a manifold \(M\). For a closed subgroup \(H\leq G\), define the orbit-type subset \(M_{(H)}=\{x\in M:G_x\text{ is conjugate to }H\}\), where \(G_x\) is the stabilizer of \(x\). Each connected component of \(M_{(H)}/G\), when nonempty, is a smooth stratum of the quotient \(M/G\). The quotient is singular at orbit types for which the local orbit dimension or isotropy representation differs from that of the principal orbit type; the collection of strata forms the orbit-type stratification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper nonfree group quotient decomposes into smooth pieces indexed by conjugacy classes of stabilizers; nonprincipal pieces constitute its singular strata.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a Lie group acting smoothly and properly on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M/G\) is partitioned into orbit-type strata given by connected components of \(M_{(H)}/G\).

notation.meaning: Subset having stabilizer conjugate to H

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the core orbit-type stratification claim is plausible, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the proper-action hypotheses, smoothness of the strata, or the characterization of singular orbit types.

children.title: Regular-to-Singular Transition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where smooth quotient-manifold descriptions cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-to-Singular Transition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where the principal quotient-manifold model loses regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and properly on \(M\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}\) be its open dense principal orbit-type subset. The regular quotient region is \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G\). Its transition boundary in \(M/G\) is \(\partial(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)=\overline{M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G}\setminus(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)\). Approaching this boundary, the stabilizer type ceases to be principal; consequently the orbit dimension, quotient dimension, or local slice representation may change. A single fixed-dimensional quotient-manifold chart and its associated horizontal-space construction therefore need not extend smoothly across the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular region ends where stabilizer type changes; quotient dimension or local geometry may then change, invalidating one smooth quotient-manifold model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed-dimensional smooth quotient model is generally valid only on \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G\), not across \(\partial(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the boundary identity and the claimed failure of fixed-dimensional quotient charts require a precise principal-orbit-type or slice-theorem source. The current source inventory supplies none.

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Product Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Riemannian geometry on a finite product of manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M_i,g_i)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be Riemannian manifolds and set \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k M_i\). At \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), identify \(T_xM=\prod_{i=1}^kT_{x_i}M_i\) and define the product metric by \(g_x(\xi,\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^k(g_i)_{x_i}(\xi_i,\eta_i)\). Its Levi-Civita connection acts componentwise. Hence geodesics and exponential maps are componentwise, and the induced distance satisfies \(d_M(x,y)^2=\sum_{i=1}^k d_{M_i}(x_i,y_i)^2\) whenever the component distances are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product carries the sum metric; tangent vectors, connections, geodesics, exponential maps, and squared distances decompose componentwise.
assumptions_latex: The product contains finitely many factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((M,g)\) has componentwise Riemannian geometry and \(d_M^2=\sum_i d_{M_i}^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the finite-product formulas are standard, including the componentwise connection and distance formula when all relevant points lie in connected components. No cited source with a relevant locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner Products, Induced Norms, and Metrics on a Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise metric structure before imposing smooth dependence on the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal M\), an inner product on \(T_x\mathcal M\) is a bilinear, symmetric, positive-definite map \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_x:T_x\mathcal M\times T_x\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\). It induces \(\|u\|_x=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle_x}\). A metric on \(\mathcal M\) assigns such an inner product to every \(x\in\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each point of a manifold, an inner product on the tangent space is bilinear, symmetric, and positive definite and induces the usual square-root norm. A metric assigns one such inner product at every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|u\|_x=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle_x},\qquad x\mapsto\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_x\text{ defines a metric on }\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Manifold Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential decomposition for objectives on product manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k M_i\) carry the product metric, and let \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\) be smooth. Writing \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), the Riemannian gradient is the block vector \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=(\operatorname{grad}_1f(x),\ldots,\operatorname{grad}_kf(x))\), uniquely characterized by \((g_i)_{x_i}(\operatorname{grad}_if(x),\xi_i)=D_if(x)[\xi_i]\). If \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k f_i(x_i)\), then each gradient block depends only on \(x_i\), and the Riemannian Hessian is block diagonal with diagonal blocks \(\operatorname{Hess}f_i(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a product manifold the gradient splits into blocks; for a sum of factorwise objectives, each block is independent and the Hessian is block diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Factorwise separability of \(f\) implies independent gradient blocks and a block-diagonal Riemannian Hessian.

notation.meaning: Differential with respect to factor i
Riemannian gradient block on factor i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits, and the gradient and Hessian decomposition is mathematically plausible under the product metric and factorwise separability. It lacks an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Redundant Factor Representations
children.top_down_role: Multiple factor tuples representing the same underlying object.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Factor Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique low-rank matrix factorization under invertible gauge transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r\geq1\) and define \(\pi(U,V)=UV^{\mathsf T}\) for full-column-rank matrices \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\). For every \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\), \(\pi(UQ,VQ^{-\mathsf T})=UV^{\mathsf T}\). Conversely, if \(U,V,\widetilde U,\widetilde V\) have full column rank and \(UV^{\mathsf T}=\widetilde U\widetilde V^{\mathsf T}\), then a unique \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\) satisfies \(\widetilde U=UQ\) and \(\widetilde V=VQ^{-\mathsf T}\). Thus a rank-\(r\) matrix is represented by an entire gauge orbit of factor pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-rank factor pair representing a rank-r matrix is nonunique: all equivalent pairs are related by an invertible change of latent basis.
assumptions_latex: \(U,V,\widetilde U,\widetilde V\) have \(r\) linearly independent columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(UV^{\mathsf T}=\widetilde U\widetilde V^{\mathsf T}\) exactly when \((\widetilde U,\widetilde V)=(UQ,VQ^{-\mathsf T})\) for a unique \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\).

notation.meaning: Group of invertible r-by-r real matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role exactly fits the leaf, and the stated GL(r) equivalence is standard for full-column-rank factors. No source or locator supports the converse and uniqueness claim.

children.title: Gauge Symmetry Orbits
children.top_down_role: Equivalence classes induced by transformations of redundant factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Symmetry Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbits of a representation-preserving gauge-group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act smoothly on a parameter manifold \(P\), and let \(\pi:P\to X\) satisfy \(\pi(g\cdot p)=\pi(p)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(p\in P\). The gauge-symmetry orbit through \(p\) is \(G\cdot p=\{g\cdot p:g\in G\}\). Its tangent space is the vertical space \(\mathcal V_p=T_p(G\cdot p)\), which is contained in \(\ker D\pi(p)\). If every fiber of \(\pi\) is one orbit, then the represented objects are identified with the orbit space \(P/G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge transformations move parameters without changing the represented object; their orbit is an equivalence class, and its tangent directions are representation-null directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\cdot p\subseteq\pi^{-1}(\pi(p))\) and \(T_p(G\cdot p)\subseteq\ker D\pi(p)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but X is not declared a smooth manifold and π is not assumed differentiable even though Dπ(p) and its kernel are used. A precise quotient-action source and corrected smoothness assumptions are required.

children.title: Gauge Identifiability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on recovering unique factors from an invariant representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Identifiability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between locally identifiable quotient parameters and additional degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on \(P\), let \(\pi:P\to X\) be invariant, and write \(\mathcal V_p=T_p(G\cdot p)\). Local identifiability modulo gauge at \(p\) requires \(\ker D\pi(p)=\mathcal V_p\) and locally constant orbit dimension. The gauge-identifiability boundary consists of points where either \(\ker D\pi(p)\supsetneq\mathcal V_p\) or the stabilizer dimension changes. At such points there are infinitesimal ambiguities not generated by the declared gauge action, or the quotient dimension changes, so a regular local quotient parametrization cannot be inferred from the gauge model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local identification modulo gauge fails when the representation has extra null directions or when stabilizer dimension changes, destroying a regular quotient parametrization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regular local identification modulo \(G\) fails when \(\ker D\pi(p)\neq\mathcal V_p\) or orbit dimension is not locally constant.

notation.meaning: Tangent space to the gauge orbit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but kernel equality and locally constant orbit dimension alone do not establish a regular local quotient parametrization without additional constant-rank, fiber, and group-action regularity hypotheses. A precise source is required to determine the valid criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Stratification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of fixed-rank manifold structure at lower-rank limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(0<r\leq\min(m,n)\), the set \(\mathcal M_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}X=r\}\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\). Its closure is \(\overline{\mathcal M_r}=\{X:\operatorname{rank}X\leq r\}\), and its boundary is \(\bigcup_{s=0}^{r-1}\mathcal M_s\). Along a sequence in \(\mathcal M_r\) approaching rank \(s<r\), at least \(r-s\) positive singular values tend to zero. The fixed-rank tangent-space model therefore does not extend as a constant-dimensional manifold model through the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-rank matrices form a smooth manifold, but its boundary contains lower-rank strata where singular values vanish and the manifold dimension changes.
assumptions_latex: Matrices are real and finite dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathcal M_r=\bigcup_{s<r}\mathcal M_s\), and fixed-rank smooth geometry fails across this boundary.

notation.meaning: Set of matrices of rank exactly r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the displayed boundary formula is false for the ordinary topological boundary in the ambient matrix space: that boundary contains the rank-r stratum as well. The lower-rank union is the relative frontier of the rank-r stratum in its closure. No source is supplied to resolve and support the intended formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial curvature relative to a pole
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the unique radial-geodesic property and defines radial sectional curvature away from and at the pole.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ have a pole $x_0$. Every $x\in M\setminus\{x_0\}$ is joined to $x_0$ by a unique geodesic $\gamma_x$, so $M$ is geodesically star-shaped with respect to $x_0$. For $x\ne x_0$, radial curvature at $x$ means the sectional curvature of each two-plane containing the tangent direction of $\gamma_x$ at $x$; at $x=x_0$, it means the sectional curvatures of all two-planes in $T_{x_0}M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a manifold with pole x0, every other point has a unique geodesic joining it to x0, so the manifold is geodesically star-shaped about x0. Radial curvature away from the pole is sectional curvature in planes containing the radial geodesic direction; at the pole it comprises all sectional curvatures there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in M\setminus\{x_0\},\ \exists!\,\gamma_x\text{ joining }x\text{ and }x_0;\quad K_{\mathrm{rad}}(x)\text{ consists of sectional curvatures of radial two-planes, with all two-planes allowed at }x_0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal and geodesic properties of quasiconvex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of geodesic quasiconvexity for minima, closed geodesics, and interior global maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:A\to\mathbb R$ be quasiconvex. Every local minimizer is a global minimizer unless $f$ is constant in a neighborhood of that minimizer. The set $\operatorname*{argmin}_A f$ is totally convex. The function is constant on every closed geodesic contained in $A$. If $f$ has a global maximum point in $\operatorname{int}A$, then $f$ is constant on $A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimum of a quasiconvex function is global unless the function is locally constant there. Its global-minimizer set is totally convex, it is constant along every closed geodesic, and an interior global maximum forces global constancy.

children.title: Riemannian Distance
children.top_down_role: Global distance structure relevant to manifold optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic length distance induced by a Riemannian metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a connected Riemannian manifold. For a piecewise continuously differentiable curve \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\), define its length by \(L_g(\gamma)=\int_0^1\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}\,dt\). The Riemannian distance between \(x,y\in M\) is \(d_g(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma}L_g(\gamma)\), where the infimum ranges over all such curves satisfying \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\gamma(1)=y\). This distance is finite and induces the original manifold topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riemannian distance is the infimum of metric lengths of piecewise smooth curves joining two points, and it induces the manifold topology.
assumptions_latex: Admissible curves are piecewise continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_g(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma(0)=x,\,\gamma(1)=y}L_g(\gamma)\) defines the intrinsic metric on \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the intrinsic-distance statement is standard for a connected Riemannian manifold, but no authoritative section, theorem, definition, or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuity with Respect to Riemannian Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric regularity of a real-valued function on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz continuous if there exists \(B>0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le B\,d(x,y)\qquad\forall x,y\in M.\] Any such \(B\) is a Lipschitz constant for \(f\).

assumptions_latex: d\text{ is the Riemannian distance on }M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Squared-distance convexity on a Hadamard manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers squared distance to totally geodesic submanifolds, sums for two such submanifolds, and compactly supported squared-distance averages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be simply connected and complete with sectional curvature $K\le 0$, and let $d$ be its Riemannian distance. For every closed totally geodesic submanifold $A\subseteq M$, $f_A(x)=d(x,A)^2$ is smooth and convex; if $K<0$, then $\operatorname{Hess}f_A$ is positive definite on $M\setminus A$, while for $A=\{y\}$ it is positive definite on $M$. If $A,B$ are closed totally geodesic submanifolds, then $f_A+f_B$ is convex and its minimum set is the set $C$ of midpoints of common perpendiculars joining distance-realizing pairs in $A\times B$; when $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$, $C=A\cap B$. If $K<0$, $\operatorname{Hess}(f_A+f_B)$ is positive definite if and only if $A$ and $B$ meet in at most one point. Finally, for every positive finite measure $\mu$ on $M$ with compact support, $h(x)=\int_M d(x,y)^2\,d\mu(y)$ has positive-definite Hessian and a unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a simply connected complete nonpositively curved Riemannian manifold, squared distance to a closed totally geodesic submanifold is smooth and convex. Strict negative curvature gives the stated Hessian-definiteness criteria. The sum of squared distances to two such submanifolds is minimized at the midpoints of their common distance-realizing perpendiculars, and every compactly supported positive finite squared-distance average has positive-definite Hessian and a unique minimizer.
assumptions_latex: (M,g)\text{ is a simply connected complete Riemannian manifold}
A,B\subseteq M\text{ are closed totally geodesic submanifolds where used}
\mu\text{ is a positive finite measure with compact support where used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_A\text{ and }f_A+f_B\text{ have the stated convexity, Hessian, and minimum-set properties, and }h(x)=\int_M d(x,y)^2\,d\mu(y)\text{ has positive-definite Hessian and a unique minimizer.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Function on a Riemannian Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: On a disconnected manifold, the inequality is imposed separately on each connected component, not between points in different components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathcal M$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R$, and let $L\geq 0$. The function $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz continuous if, for every connected component $C$ of $\mathcal M$,
\[
\forall x,y\in C,\qquad |f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y),
\]
where $\operatorname{dist}$ is the Riemannian distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function is L-Lipschitz on a Riemannian manifold when its change is bounded by L times Riemannian distance within each connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall C\in\pi_0(\mathcal M),\ \forall x,y\in C,\quad |f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance between closed sets and compact attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines set-to-set distance and records both nonattainment for general disjoint closed sets and attainment when one set is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a complete Riemannian manifold and let \(A,B\subseteq M\) be nonempty closed sets. Their distance is \[d(A,B):=\inf_{x\in A,\,y\in B}d(x,y).\] Disjoint closed sets can satisfy \(d(A,B)=0\), and the infimum need not be attained. If \(A\) is compact and \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), then there exist \(x_0\in A\) and \(y_0\in B\) such that \[d(A,B)=d(x_0,y_0)>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance between two nonempty closed sets is the infimum of distances between their points. Disjoint closed sets may have zero distance and may fail to attain the infimum. In a complete Riemannian manifold, if one set is compact and the other is closed and disjoint from it, the distance is positive and attained by a pair of points.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is compact and }A\cap B=\varnothing\quad\text{for the positive-attainment conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(A,B)=\inf_{x\in A,\,y\in B}d(x,y),\qquad \exists x_0\in A\,\exists y_0\in B:\ d(A,B)=d(x_0,y_0)>0\ \text{under the additional compactness and disjointness assumptions}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance to a Nonempty Closed Set on a Complete Riemannian Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines point-to-set distance and records separation, attainment, and Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold and let $A\subseteq M$ be nonempty and closed. For $x\in M$, define $d(x,A):=\inf_{y\in A}d(x,y)$. Then $d(x,A)\ge 0$ and $d(x,A)=0$ if and only if $x\in A$. For every $x\in M$, there exists $y_0\in A$ such that $d(x,y_0)=d(x,A)$. Moreover, $x\mapsto d(x,A)$ is $1$-Lipschitz: $|d(x',A)-d(x,A)|\le d(x,x')$ for all $x,x'\in M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed subset of a complete Riemannian manifold, point-to-set distance is the infimum of point-to-point distances. It vanishes exactly on the set, is attained, and is 1-Lipschitz in the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(x,A):=\inf_{y\in A}d(x,y),\quad d(x,A)=0\iff x\in A,\quad \exists y_0\in A:\ d(x,y_0)=d(x,A),\quad |d(x',A)-d(x,A)|\le d(x,x')

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Squared Distance Between Closed Totally Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product convexity, squared-distance convexity, and the geometry of an attained minimum for two closed totally convex subsets of a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A,B$ be closed totally convex subsets of a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, and define $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ by $f(x,y)=d(x,y)^2$. Then $A\times B$ is totally convex in $M\times M$, and $f$ is a $C^\infty$ convex function on $A\times B$. If $f$ attains its minimum at $(x,y)\in A\times B$, then the geodesic joining $x$ and $y$ is a common perpendicular to $A$ and $B$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two closed totally convex subsets of a Riemannian manifold, their product is totally convex and squared distance is smooth and convex on the product. Whenever its minimum is attained, a geodesic joining a minimizing pair is perpendicular to both sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\times B\text{ is totally convex in }M\times M;\quad f\in C^\infty(A\times B)\text{ is convex};\quad (x,y)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{A\times B}f\Rightarrow\text{the geodesic from }x\text{ to }y\text{ is a common perpendicular to }A\text{ and }B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of Distance Between Two Geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-map geometry on a simply connected nonpositively curved Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be simply connected with sectional curvature $K\le 0$. Let $\alpha,\beta:\mathbb R\to M$ be geodesics, where $\|\alpha'(t)\|=1$ and $\beta$ may be constant, and define $f(t)=d(\alpha(t),\beta(t))$. Then $f(t)=0$ has at most one solution. Moreover, at every $t$ such that $f(t)\ne0$, the function $f$ is $C^\infty$ and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a simply connected Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature, the distance between a unit-speed geodesic and another geodesic, which may be constant, vanishes at most once and is smooth and convex wherever it is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\{t\in\mathbb R:f(t)=0\}|\le1,\qquad f\in C^\infty\text{ and is convex at every }t\text{ with }f(t)\ne0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance and metric space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the metric axioms used by the Riemannian-distance construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\operatorname{dist}:\mathcal M\times\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is a distance if, for all \(x,y,z\in\mathcal M\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)=\operatorname{dist}(y,x)\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\geq0\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)=0\iff x=y\), and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,z)\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,y)+\operatorname{dist}(y,z)\). Equipped with such a distance, \(\mathcal M\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance is symmetric, nonnegative and zero exactly for identical points, and satisfies the triangle inequality. A set equipped with a distance is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the three metric axioms hold, then \((\mathcal M,\operatorname{dist})\) is a metric space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and \(x\in M\). For every \(v\in T_xM\) whose maximal geodesic \(\gamma_v\) with \(\gamma_v(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma_v(0)=v\) is defined at time \(1\), define \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)\). Its domain is an open star-shaped neighborhood of \(0_x\), and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{Exp}_x\) is a diffeomorphism from some neighborhood of \(0_x\) onto a normal neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map sends an initial tangent velocity to its geodesic endpoint at time one and is locally invertible near the zero vector.
assumptions_latex: The selected geodesic exists through time \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)\) and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the domain, derivative, and local-diffeomorphism claims are standard, but they are unsupported by any cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Exponential Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition on tangent vectors whose geodesics exist through time one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal O=\{(x,v)\in T\mathcal M:\gamma_v\text{ is defined on an interval containing }[0,1]\}. Then \operatorname{Exp}:\mathcal O\to\mathcal M is defined by \operatorname{Exp}(x,v)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1), with \mathcal O_x=\{v\in T_x\mathcal M:(x,v)\in\mathcal O\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map sends a tangent vector at x to the time-one value of its geodesic whenever that geodesic exists on an interval containing [0,1].
assumptions_latex: \gamma_v\text{ is defined on an interval containing }[0,1]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential map, geodesic completeness, and normal neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the local geodesic existence and scaling properties used to define the affine-connection exponential map, together with completeness and local normal-neighborhood properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal M$ be a manifold endowed with an affine connection. For every $x\in\mathcal M$ and $\xi\in T_x\mathcal M$, there is an interval about $0$ and a unique geodesic $\gamma(t;x,\xi)$ satisfying $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma(0)=\xi$, and $\gamma(t;x,a\xi)=\gamma(at;x,\xi)$ whenever both sides are defined. Wherever the time-one geodesic exists, define $\operatorname{Exp}_x(\xi)=\gamma(1;x,\xi)$. The manifold is geodesically complete when $\operatorname{Exp}_x$ is defined on all of $T_x\mathcal M$ for every $x$. Locally, $\operatorname{Exp}_x$ is a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of $0_x$ onto a neighborhood of $x$; if the tangent-space neighborhood is star-shaped, its image is a normal neighborhood of $x$. Moreover, $\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=x$ and $D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)[\xi]=\xi$ under the canonical identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initial position and velocity determine a unique local geodesic, with a scaling law where both geodesics are defined. Its time-one endpoint defines the exponential map on its natural domain. The map fixes the zero vector, has identity differential there, and is locally invertible. Full tangent-space domains characterize geodesic completeness, while star-shaped local inverse domains yield normal neighborhoods.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is a manifold endowed with an affine connection}
\text{The scaling identity and time-one evaluation are asserted only where the relevant geodesics are defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Exp}_x(\xi)=\gamma(1;x,\xi),\quad \operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=x,\quad D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M},\quad \operatorname{Exp}_x\text{ is a local diffeomorphism at }0_x;\ \mathcal M\text{ is geodesically complete iff every }\operatorname{Exp}_x\text{ has domain }T_x\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Normal Neighborhood and Associated Normal Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and local representation properties stated for an exponential-map neighborhood centered at a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\exp_x:B_\varepsilon(0)\subset T_xM\to W_x$ be a diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood $W_x$ of $x$. The set $W_x$ is called a convex normal neighborhood centered at $x$. Every point of $W_x$ can be joined to $x$ by a unique geodesic, up to an affine change of parameter, and every two points of $W_x$ are joined by a unique geodesic of length $<\varepsilon$ depending smoothly on the endpoints. If $(y^1,\ldots,y^n)$ are Cartesian coordinates on $T_xM$, then $\xi^i=y^i\circ\exp_x^{-1}$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, are normal coordinates on $W_x$. For $\gamma(t)=\exp_x(tX)$, they satisfy $\xi^i(\gamma(t))=tX^i$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential-map neighborhood W_x is called a convex normal neighborhood centered at x. Its points have the stated unique-geodesic properties, with uniqueness from x understood up to affine reparameterization. Transporting Cartesian tangent-space coordinates through the inverse exponential map gives normal coordinates, in which geodesics from x are straight lines.
assumptions_latex: $M$ is a Riemannian manifold and $x\in M$.
$\exp_x:B_\varepsilon(0)\subset T_xM\to W_x$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood $W_x$ of $x$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $W_x$ is a convex normal neighborhood with the stated geodesic uniqueness and smooth-dependence properties; moreover, $\xi^i=y^i\circ\exp_x^{-1}$ are normal coordinates and $\xi^i(\exp_x(tX))=tX^i$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Local Diffeomorphism of Exponential Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local invertibility of the exponential maps based at points near a fixed manifold point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every $x_0\in M$, there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for every $x\in U$, the exponential map $\exp_x$ maps the open ball $B_\varepsilon(0)\subset T_xM$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $W_x\subset U$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential of a Tangent Vector
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the pointwise exponential through the time-one endpoint of the associated geodesic and states its radial parameterization property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in T_xM\). If the geodesic \(\gamma_X\) satisfying \(\gamma_X(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma_X(0)=X\) is defined at time \(1\), then \(\exp_x(X):=\gamma_X(1)\). For every \(t\) for which the relevant geodesics are defined, \(\exp_x(tX)=\gamma_X(t)\), and \(\exp_x(0)=x\). In particular, local geodesic existence makes \(\exp_x(X)\) defined for all sufficiently small \(X\in T_xM\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential of a tangent vector is the time-one endpoint of its geodesic. Radial scaling traces that geodesic, the zero vector maps to the base point, and sufficiently small vectors are locally admissible.
assumptions_latex: The geodesic with initial data \(\gamma_X(0)=x\), \(\dot\gamma_X(0)=X\) is defined at every parameter value used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exp_x(X)=\gamma_X(1),\qquad \exp_x(tX)=\gamma_X(t),\qquad \exp_x(0)=x.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the coordinate chart induced by the inverse exponential map on a normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal U$ be a normal neighborhood of $y\in\mathcal M$, and fix a basis of $T_y\mathcal M$. For each $x\in\mathcal U$, let $\xi\in T_y\mathcal M$ be the unique vector satisfying $\operatorname{Exp}_y(\xi)=x$. The chart sending $x$ to the components of $\xi$ in the chosen basis is the normal-coordinate chart centered at $y$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a basis of the tangent space at a point and a normal neighborhood of that point. Mapping each nearby point to the components of its unique inverse-exponential tangent vector defines normal coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal U\text{ is a normal neighborhood of }y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\longmapsto [\operatorname{Exp}_y^{-1}(x)]\text{ in the chosen basis defines normal coordinates on }\mathcal U.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential and logarithmic maps are inverse diffeomorphisms below the injectivity radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint smoothness and invertibility of the exponential and logarithmic maps on base-point-dependent domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a Riemannian manifold, \(\mathcal T=\{(x,v)\in T\mathcal M:\|v\|_x<\operatorname{inj}(x)\}\), and \(\mathcal V=\{(x,y)\in\mathcal M\times\mathcal M:\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\}\). Then \((x,v)\mapsto(x,\operatorname{Exp}_x(v))\) is a diffeomorphism from \(\mathcal T\) to \(\mathcal V\), with smooth inverse \((x,y)\mapsto(x,\operatorname{Log}_x(y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below the pointwise injectivity radius, the exponential map smoothly identifies tangent displacements with nearby point pairs, and the logarithmic map is its smooth inverse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,v)\mapsto(x,\operatorname{Exp}_x(v))\) is a diffeomorphism \(\mathcal T\to\mathcal V\) with inverse \((x,y)\mapsto(x,\operatorname{Log}_x(y))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inverse of the exponential map on a normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold, let \(x\in M\), and let \(U\) be a normal neighborhood of \(x\) on which \(\operatorname{Exp}_x:V\to U\) is a diffeomorphism from an open set \(V\subset T_xM\). The logarithmic map based at \(x\) is \(\operatorname{Log}_x:U\to V\), defined by \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\operatorname{Exp}_x^{-1}(y)\). It is the initial velocity of the unique radial geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\), and satisfies \(\lVert\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rVert_x=d_g(x,y)\) within this normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a normal neighborhood, the logarithmic map is the inverse exponential map and returns the initial velocity of the unique minimizing radial geodesic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\operatorname{Exp}_x^{-1}(y)\) and \(\lVert\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rVert_x=d_g(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Local Riemannian logarithmic map at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the local inverse statement is plausible under the intended normal-neighborhood convention. A source is needed to support that convention and the minimizing-distance identity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Logarithmic Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique minimum-norm inverse selection for the exponential map; continuity on the full domain is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x\in\mathcal M, define \operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{v\in\mathcal O_x}\|v\|_x\quad\text{subject to}\quad\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=y, on the domain where this minimizer is uniquely defined. The resulting map need not be continuous on its full domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic map at x assigns to y the unique minimum-norm tangent vector whose exponential image is y. It is defined only where that selection is unique and need not be continuous on its full domain.
assumptions_latex: \{v\in\mathcal O_x:\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=y\}\text{ has a unique minimum-norm element}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{v\in\mathcal O_x,\,\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=y}\|v\|_x

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth families generated by the geodesic flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and let \(D\subset TM\times\mathbb R\) be the maximal domain of the geodesic flow. A geodesic family is the smooth map \(\Gamma:D\to M\) such that, for every \((x,v)\in TM\), the curve \(t\mapsto\Gamma(x,v,t)\) on its maximal interval satisfies \(\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0\), \(\Gamma(x,v,0)=x\), and \(\partial_t\Gamma(x,v,0)=v\). Uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value problem makes this family well defined, and whenever time \(1\) belongs to the domain, \(\Gamma(x,v,1)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geodesic flow smoothly assigns to each initial point and velocity its unique maximal geodesic; its time-one endpoint is the exponential map.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the maximal existence domain of the geodesic equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) smoothly parametrizes all maximal geodesics by their initial data in \(TM\).

notation.meaning: Geodesic family or geodesic flow projected to M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Minimality of Geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the local length-minimizing property of every geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma\) be a geodesic on \(\mathcal M\). For every \(t\in\operatorname{dom}(\gamma)\), there exists a neighborhood \(I\) of \(t\) in \(\operatorname{dom}(\gamma)\) such that, for all \(a,b\in I\) with \(a<b\), the restriction \(\gamma|_{[a,b]}\) is a minimizing curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every geodesic is locally minimizing: near each parameter value, each restricted segment between two nearby parameter values is minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists I\ni t\;\forall a,b\in I,\quad a<b\Longrightarrow \gamma|_{[a,b]}\text{ is minimizing}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesics and completeness of a diagonal product metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-specific structural theorem for a Riemannian plane with coefficient g_{11} depending only on x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(\mathbb{R}^2,ds^2=g_{11}(x)\,dx^2+dy^2)\) be the stated Riemannian manifold. Its geodesics are graphs of certain functions, vertical straight lines, or constant curves. Horizontal and vertical straight lines are mutually orthogonal geodesics and totally geodesic submanifolds. Moreover, \(M\) is complete if and only if \((\mathbb{R},g_{11}(x)\,dx^2)\) is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated Riemannian metric on the plane, geodesics are suitable graphs, vertical straight lines, or constant curves. Horizontal and vertical lines are orthogonal totally geodesic submanifolds, and the plane is complete exactly when its one-dimensional metric factor is complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Geo}(M)\text{ consists of graph geodesics, vertical straight lines, and constant curves; coordinate lines are orthogonal and totally geodesic; }M\text{ is complete}\iff \left(\mathbb{R},g_{11}(x)dx^2\right)\text{ is complete.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Velocity Scaling and Geodesic Reparameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling the initial velocity produces the corresponding linear reparameterization of a geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_X:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to M\) be a geodesic satisfying \(\gamma_X(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma_X(0)=X\). For every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\), the curve \(t\mapsto\gamma_X(\lambda t)\), defined for \(|t|<\varepsilon/|\lambda|\), is the geodesic with initial data \((x,\lambda X)\). Consequently, \(\gamma_{\lambda X}(t)=\gamma_X(\lambda t)\) on that interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a geodesic's initial velocity by a nonzero scalar rescales its parameter by the same scalar on the resulting valid interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\lambda X}(t)=\gamma_X(\lambda t)\quad\text{for all }|t|<\varepsilon/|\lambda|.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: g-connected domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization is within a homotopy class of curves constrained to remain in the domain, not necessarily within the corresponding ambient-manifold class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain $D\subset M$ is $g$-connected if, for every $p,q\in D$, each homotopy class of curves in $D$ joining $p$ to $q$ contains a geodesic lying entirely in $D$ whose length is minimal among the curves in that class. Such a geodesic need not minimize length in the corresponding homotopy class of curves in $M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is g-connected when every homotopy class of internal curves between two points has a shortest representative that is a geodesic remaining in the domain. That representative need not be shortest in the corresponding ambient-manifold homotopy class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall[\gamma]_{D,p,q}\ \exists\gamma_*\in[\gamma]_{D,p,q}:\ \gamma_*\subset D,\ \gamma_*\text{ is geodesic},\ L(\gamma_*)=\inf_{\eta\in[\gamma]_{D,p,q}}L(\eta).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Length-Minimizing Geodesic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a geodesic between two points of an equality-constraint surface through global arc-length minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=\{x:h(x)=0\}\subset E^n\). A smooth curve \(x:[0,T]\to\Omega\) is a geodesic connecting \(x(0)\) and \(x(T)\) if it minimizes \(\int_0^T\|\dot{x}(t)\|\,dt\) among all smooth curves in \(\Omega\) with the same endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geodesic connecting two points of the surface is a smooth surface-valued curve having minimum arc length among smooth curves with those endpoints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed geodesics relative to a closed totally convex subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the flat-cylinder alternative and the strict-negative-curvature consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature $K\leq 0$, let $A\subseteq M$ be closed and totally convex, and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ be a closed geodesic. Then $\gamma$ is freely homotopic to a closed geodesic contained in $A$. If $\gamma$ is not entirely contained in $A$, all points of $\gamma$ are at the same distance from $A$, and the deformation occurs along a flat finite-length cylinder whose meridians are perpendicular to $\gamma$. Consequently, if $K<0$, then every closed geodesic of $M$ is contained in $A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every closed geodesic is freely homotopic to a closed geodesic in a closed totally convex set. If it is not already in the set, it remains at constant distance from it and the deformation spans a flat cylinder. Strictly negative curvature therefore forces every closed geodesic into the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesics, completeness, and distance on a Riemannian line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit coordinate representation and global consequences for the one-dimensional Riemannian manifold \((\mathbb R,g)\). Uniqueness refers to the connecting geodesic with fixed endpoint parameter values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)\) be \(C^\infty\), let \(\Gamma(x)=\tfrac12g(x)^{-1}g'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\log\sqrt{g(x)}\), and let \(F'(x)=\sqrt{g(x)}\). A curve \(x(t)\) satisfies the geodesic equation \(\ddot x+\Gamma(x)\dot x^2=0\) if and only if \(F(x(t))=C_1t+C_2\). It is constant when \(C_1=0\) and strictly monotone when \(C_1\ne0\); consequently, no nonconstant geodesic is closed, and two distinct endpoints with fixed endpoint parameter values determine at most one connecting geodesic. The manifold \((\mathbb R,g)\) is geodesically complete if and only if \(F(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R\); under completeness, every two distinct points admit exactly one such connecting geodesic. Moreover, \(d(x_1,x_2)=\left|\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\sqrt{g(x)}\,dx\right|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a primitive of the square root of a smooth positive metric turns geodesics on the real line into affine curves. Nonconstant geodesics are strictly monotone and cannot be closed. With endpoint parameter values fixed, distinct endpoints determine at most one connecting geodesic. The Riemannian line is geodesically complete exactly when the primitive is onto the real line; completeness then guarantees existence and uniqueness. Distance is the absolute integral of the metric square root between the endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a geodesic}\iff F(x(t))=C_1t+C_2;\quad (\mathbb R,g)\text{ is geodesically complete}\iff F(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R;\quad d(x_1,x_2)=\left|\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\sqrt{g(x)}\,dx\right|.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Piecewise-Minimizing-Geodesic Interpolation of a Continuous Curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The constructed curve interpolates finitely many sampled values of the original continuous curve; it need not equal the original curve between sample times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M$ be continuous on a Riemannian manifold. There exist finitely many times
\[
0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1
\]
such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(c(t_i),c(t_{i+1}))<\operatorname{inj}(c(t_i))
\]
for $i=0,\ldots,n-1$. Joining each consecutive pair by a minimizing geodesic produces a piecewise regular curve $\gamma$ with $\gamma(t_i)=c(t_i)$. Moreover, there exist $s_i\in T_{\gamma(t_i)}\mathcal M$ such that
\[
\gamma(t_{i+1})=\operatorname{Exp}_{\gamma(t_i)}(s_i),\qquad \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\|s_i\|=L(\gamma).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous manifold-valued curve has finitely many sampled points that can be joined successively by minimizing geodesics. The resulting piecewise-geodesic interpolant has segment-vector norms summing to its length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists n\geq1,\ 0=t_0<\cdots<t_n=1,\ \gamma,\ s_i\in T_{\gamma(t_i)}\mathcal M:\ \operatorname{dist}(c(t_i),c(t_{i+1}))<\operatorname{inj}(c(t_i)),\ \gamma(t_i)=c(t_i),\ \gamma(t_{i+1})=\operatorname{Exp}_{\gamma(t_i)}(s_i),\ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\|s_i\|=L(\gamma)

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric and geodesic completeness for connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A connected Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) is geodesically complete if every maximal geodesic \(\gamma:(a,b)\to M\) extends to a geodesic defined on all of \(\mathbb R\). Equivalently, for every \(p\in M\), the exponential map \(\exp_p\) is defined on all of \(T_pM\). By the Hopf–Rinow theorem, these conditions are equivalent to completeness of the metric space \((M,d_g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connected Riemannian manifold is complete when every geodesic exists for all time; equivalently, every exponential map has full tangent-space domain and the induced metric space is complete.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is geodesically complete}\iff \operatorname{dom}(\exp_p)=T_pM\ \forall p\in M\iff (M,d_g)\text{ is complete}.\)

Let $(M,g)$ be a Finsler manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a proper $C^\infty$ function. Define
\[
\bar g(x,y)=g(x,y)\exp\!\left(\lVert df(x)\rVert_y^2\right).
\]
Then $(M,\bar g)$ is a complete Finsler manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a Finsler manifold admits a proper smooth real-valued function, multiplying its Finsler metric by the exponential of the squared indicated norm of the function's differential produces a complete Finsler manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (M,\bar g)\text{ is a complete Finsler manifold}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hopf–Rinow Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of metric and geodesic completeness conditions, including the minimizing-geodesic consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. The following are equivalent: (i) $(M,d_g)$ is complete; (ii) every closed and bounded subset of $M$ is compact; (iii) $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete; (iv) for some $x\in M$, $\exp_x$ is defined on all of $T_xM$; and (v) every maximal geodesic is defined on $\mathbb{R}$. Under these equivalent conditions, every pair of points in $M$ can be joined by a minimizing geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected Riemannian manifold, metric completeness, compactness of closed bounded sets, geodesic completeness, global definition of one exponential map, and extension of every maximal geodesic over the real line are equivalent. Completeness also guarantees a minimizing geodesic between every pair of points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{(i)}\iff\mathrm{(ii)}\iff\mathrm{(iii)}\iff\mathrm{(iv)}\iff\mathrm{(v)},\qquad \forall p,q\in M\;\exists\text{ a minimizing geodesic from }p\text{ to }q.

children.title: Geodesic Reachability
children.top_down_role: Connectivity of manifold points through admissible geodesic segments.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hopf–Rinow reachability by globally minimizing geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be connected and complete. For every \(p,q\in M\), there exists \(v\in T_pM\) such that \(q=\exp_p(v)\) and the radial geodesic \(\gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv)\), \(0\le t\le1\), minimizes length between its endpoints. Consequently, \(L(\gamma)=\lVert v\rVert_g=d_g(p,q)\), so every point is reachable from every other point by a minimizing geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected complete Riemannian manifold, every pair of points is joined by a length-minimizing geodesic obtained from the exponential map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists v\in T_pM:\ q=\exp_p(v),\quad L(t\mapsto\exp_p(tv))=\lVert v\rVert_g=d_g(p,q).\)

notation.meaning: Riemannian length of the curve γ

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated minimizing-geodesic reachability theorem is a standard Hopf–Rinow consequence and fits the container, but it has no cited authoritative source or theorem/section locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Admissible direction on a Riemannian feasible set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility of a tangent direction through a forward exponential-map segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_0\in S\subseteq M$. A nonzero vector $X\in T_{x_0}M$ is an admissible direction for $S$ at $x_0$ if there exists $\delta>0$ such that $\exp_{x_0}(tX)\in S$ for every $t\in[0,\delta)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero tangent vector at a feasible point is admissible when its sufficiently short forward geodesic segment remains inside the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is admissible at }x_0\iff \exists\delta>0\ \forall t\in[0,\delta),\ \exp_{x_0}(tX)\in S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior and boundary characterization of admissible directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-stated characterization for a smooth inequality-defined feasible set on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S=\{x\in M:\psi_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}$ and $I(x_0)=\{i:\psi_i(x_0)=0\}$. If $x_0\in\operatorname{Int}S$, every nonzero $X\in T_{x_0}M$ is admissible. If $x_0\in\partial S$, then a nonzero $X\in T_{x_0}M$ is admissible if and only if $d\psi_i(x_0)[X]\le0$ for every $i\in I(x_0)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior feasible point every nonzero tangent direction is admissible. At a boundary point, the source states that admissibility is equivalent to having nonpositive directional derivative for every active inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_0\in\operatorname{Int}S\Rightarrow X\text{ is admissible};\qquad x_0\in\partial S\Rightarrow\bigl(X\text{ is admissible}\iff d\psi_i(x_0)[X]\le0\ \forall i\in I(x_0)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sectional-curvature regimes relevant to comparison geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) and constants \(\kappa_-\le\kappa_+\), the two-sided curvature regime \(\kappa_-\le\sec_M\le\kappa_+\) means that every point \(p\in M\) and every two-dimensional subspace \(\sigma\subset T_pM\) satisfy \(\kappa_-\le\sec_p(\sigma)\le\kappa_+\). The special regimes \(\sec_M\le0\), \(\sec_M=0\), and \(\sec_M\ge0\) are respectively nonpositive, flat, and nonnegative sectional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature regime imposes uniform lower and upper bounds on sectional curvature over every tangent two-plane; sign regimes arise by comparison with zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_-\le\sec_M\le\kappa_+\iff \kappa_-\le\sec_p(\sigma)\le\kappa_+\quad\forall p\in M,\ \forall\sigma\in\operatorname{Gr}_2(T_pM).\)

notation.meaning: sectional curvature of the tangent two-plane σ at p
set of two-dimensional linear subspaces of the tangent space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sectional-curvature regimes are precise and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Injectivity Radius
children.top_down_role: Local scale governing uniqueness of exponential-map representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Injectivity Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and global injectivity radii of the exponential map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in M\), the injectivity radius is \[\operatorname{inj}(p):=\sup\{r>0:\exp_p|_{B(0,r)}:B(0,r)\subset T_pM\to M\text{ is a diffeomorphism onto its image}\}.\] The global injectivity radius is \(\operatorname{inj}(M):=\inf_{p\in M}\operatorname{inj}(p)\). If \(0<r<\operatorname{inj}(p)\), each point of \(\exp_p(B(0,r))\) has a unique radial geodesic from \(p\), and this geodesic minimizes distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The injectivity radius is the largest tangent-ball radius on which the exponential map is one-to-one and nonsingular; the global radius is the infimum over base points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<r<\operatorname{inj}(p)\Longrightarrow \exp_p|_{B(0,r)}\text{ is a diffeomorphism onto its image}.\)

notation.meaning: open radius-r ball for the norm induced by g_p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise and global definitions are standard and locally appropriate, but the definition and its uniqueness/minimality consequence lack an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On any Riemannian manifold, the pointwise injectivity radius varies continuously with the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{inj}:\mathcal M\to(0,\infty]\) is continuous.

children.title: Convexity Radius
children.top_down_role: Local scale associated with geodesically convex neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius of strongly geodesically convex metric balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An open set \(U\subset M\) is strongly geodesically convex if every \(x,y\in U\) are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic in \(M\) whose image lies in \(U\). For \(p\in M\), define \[\operatorname{conv}(p):=\sup\{r>0:B_g(p,s)\text{ is strongly geodesically convex for every }0<s<r\}.\] The global convexity radius is \(\operatorname{conv}(M):=\inf_{p\in M}\operatorname{conv}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convexity radius at a point is the largest scale below which all centered metric balls contain a unique minimizing geodesic between every two of their points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<s<\operatorname{conv}(p)\Longrightarrow B_g(p,s)\text{ is strongly geodesically convex}.\)

notation.meaning: open Riemannian metric ball centered at p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-convexity and convexity-radius definitions fit the terminal container, but no source or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Curvature–Radius Interactions
children.top_down_role: Structural influence of curvature on injectivity or convexity scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature–Radius Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conservative local scale combining curvature and injectivity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) have sectional curvature bounded above by \(K\ge0\), and define \(r_K=+\infty\) when \(K=0\) and \(r_K=\pi/(2\sqrt K)\) when \(K>0\). If \(0<r<\min\{\operatorname{inj}(M)/2,r_K\}\), then every metric ball \(B_g(p,r)\) is strongly geodesically convex. Thus positive curvature and loss of injectivity jointly limit a uniform radius on which minimizing geodesics are unique and remain inside the ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform strongly convex neighborhood scale is bounded jointly by half the global injectivity radius and, under positive curvature, a curvature-dependent radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_g(p,r)\text{ is strongly geodesically convex for every }p\in M.\)

notation.meaning: curvature-controlled radius, infinite for K=0 and π/(2√K) for K>0

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim is relevant to curvature–radius interactions, but the uniform strong-convexity bound, including the factors 1/2 and π/(2√K), requires direct verification against a theorem with matching completeness and curvature hypotheses.

children.title: Cut-Locus Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure where minimizing-geodesic behavior changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Locus Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut locus defined by terminal minimizing radial geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\in M\). For a unit vector \(v\in T_pM\), let \(c(v):=\sup\{t>0:s\mapsto\exp_p(sv),\ 0\le s\le t,\text{ minimizes distance from }p\}\). The cut locus of \(p\) is \[\operatorname{Cut}(p):=\{\exp_p(c(v)v):\lVert v\rVert_g=1,\ c(v)<+\infty\}.\] Before the cut time, the radial geodesic is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(p\); beyond it, that radial segment is not minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut locus consists of endpoints where radial geodesics cease to remain uniquely minimizing; each direction has a corresponding cut time, possibly infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<t<c(v)\Longrightarrow s\mapsto\exp_p(sv),\ 0\le s\le t,\text{ is uniquely minimizing}.\)

notation.meaning: cut time in the unit tangent direction v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-time definition is standard but uncited. The plain statement also suggests every cut point is where uniqueness fails, whereas a cut point may arise through conjugacy while its minimizing geodesic remains unique; an authoritative source is needed to settle and restate the exact boundary behavior.

children.title: Nonunique Minimizing Geodesics
children.top_down_role: Regions admitting multiple minimizing geodesic connections.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Minimizing Geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity branch of the cut-locus alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be complete and \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\). Then either at least two distinct minimizing geodesics join \(p\) to \(q\), or \(q\) is conjugate to \(p\) along a minimizing geodesic. In the first case there exist distinct \(v,w\in T_pM\) with \(\lVert v\rVert_g=\lVert w\rVert_g=d_g(p,q)\) and \(\exp_p(v)=\exp_p(w)=q\). Hence the inverse logarithm at \(p\) is set-valued at \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a cut point, minimizing geodesics either become nonunique or encounter conjugacy; in the nonunique case, distinct tangent vectors exponentiate to the same endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\{\text{minimizing geodesics from }p\text{ to }q\}\ge2\quad\text{or}\quad q\text{ is conjugate to }p.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-point alternative is a theorem rather than merely a generic property. It also lacks a source locator supporting the precise alternative and the claimed logarithm behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexistence of nonconstant closed geodesics

children.title: Distance-Smoothness Failure Boundary
