knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Smoothness Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness boundary for distance and squared-distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\) in a complete Riemannian manifold. The function \(q\mapsto d_g(p,q)\) is smooth on \(M\setminus(\{p\}\cup\operatorname{Cut}(p))\), while \(q\mapsto \tfrac12d_g(p,q)^2\) is smooth on \(M\setminus\operatorname{Cut}(p)\). If \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\) admits two distinct minimizing geodesics from \(p\), then \(d_g(p,\cdot)\) and \(\tfrac12d_g(p,\cdot)^2\) are not differentiable at \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance is smooth away from its base point and cut locus, while squared distance is smooth away from the cut locus; multiple minimizers force nondifferentiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\notin\{p\}\cup\operatorname{Cut}(p)\Longrightarrow d_g(p,\cdot)\text{ is smooth near }q;\) multiplicity at a cut point implies nondifferentiability.

notation.meaning: distance from the fixed point p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smoothness domains and nondifferentiability under multiple minimizers fit the failure-boundary leaf, but these nontrivial claims have no cited theorem, section, or page.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential of a Smooth Map Between Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tangent map, its realization by curves, immersion and submersion characterizations, and its vector-space specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N be smooth, x\in\mathcal M, and \xi_x\in T_x\mathcal M. The differential of F at x is the linear map \mathrm DF(x):T_x\mathcal M\to T_{F(x)}\mathcal N defined by (\mathrm DF(x)[\xi_x])f=\xi_x(f\circ F) for every smooth function germ f at F(x). If a curve \gamma realizes \xi_x, then F\circ\gamma realizes \mathrm DF(x)[\xi_x]. Moreover, F is an immersion, respectively a submersion, if and only if \mathrm DF(x) is injective, respectively surjective, for every x\in\mathcal M. If \mathcal N=\mathcal E is a vector space and F=\sum_iF^ie_i, then \mathrm DF(x)[\xi_x]=\sum_i(\xi_xF^i)e_i; if \mathcal N=\mathbb R, this is \xi_xF. When \mathcal M and \mathcal N are linear manifolds, \mathrm DF(x)[\xi_x]=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{F(x+t\xi_x)-F(x)}{t}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The differential of a smooth manifold map sends a tangent vector to the derivation obtained by differentiating pullbacks of smooth functions. It is linear and can be realized by composing a representing curve with the map. Pointwise injectivity or surjectivity characterizes immersions or submersions, and in vector spaces the definition reduces to ordinary directional differentiation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm DF(x)[\xi_x]\in T_{F(x)}\mathcal N,\qquad (\mathrm DF(x)[\xi_x])f=\xi_x(f\circ F),\qquad \mathrm DF(x)\text{ is linear}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent vectors and vector fields as derivations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of curve-realized tangent vectors with point derivations and of smooth vector fields with global derivations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivation at \(x\in\mathcal M\) is an \(\mathbb R\)-linear map \(\xi_x:\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\xi_x(fg)=\xi_x(f)g(x)+f(x)\xi_x(g).\] Every smooth curve \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma(0)=x\) defines a derivation by \(f\mapsto\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_{t=0}\), and every derivation at \(x\) is realized by such a curve. Thus point derivations and tangent vectors at \(x\) are equivalent. A global derivation is an \(\mathbb R\)-linear map \(\mathcal D:\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\to\mathfrak F(\mathcal M)\) satisfying \(\mathcal D(fg)=\mathcal D(f)g+f\mathcal D(g)\); global derivations are exactly the operators \(f\mapsto\xi f\) induced by smooth vector fields \(\xi\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point derivation is a linear functional on smooth functions satisfying the Leibniz rule, and point derivations are exactly tangent vectors realized by curves. Global derivations satisfying the analogous rule are exactly the operators induced by smooth vector fields.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_x\mathcal M\cong\operatorname{Der}_x(\mathfrak F(\mathcal M),\mathbb R),\qquad \mathfrak X(\mathcal M)\cong\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak F(\mathcal M))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Vectors and the Tangent Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curve-derivative definition of tangent vectors at a point of a smooth manifold and the resulting tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold and \(p\in M\). A map \(\xi:\mathfrak F_p(M)\to\mathbb R\) is a tangent vector at \(p\) if there exists a curve \(\gamma\) on \(M\) with \(\gamma(0)=p\) such that \[\xi f=\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_{t=0}\qquad\text{for every }f\in\mathfrak F_p(M).\] This tangent vector is denoted by \(\dot\gamma(0)\). The set of all tangent vectors at \(p\), denoted by \(T_pM\), is the tangent space of \(M\) at \(p\); if \(\dim M=n\), then \(T_pM\) is an \(n\)-dimensional vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent vector at a point p of a smooth manifold is a map on the local smooth functions obtained by differentiating those functions along a curve through p. It is written as the curve's velocity at zero. All such tangent vectors form the tangent space T_pM, whose dimension equals the dimension of M.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in T_pM\iff \exists\gamma\text{ on }M\text{ with }\gamma(0)=p\text{ and }\xi f=\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_{t=0}\ \forall f\in\mathfrak F_p(M);\qquad \dim M=n\Rightarrow \dim T_pM=n.

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold Differentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic differential of a smooth map between manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth and \(p\in M\). The differential of \(F\) at \(p\) is the linear map \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\) defined by \[dF_p(v):=(F\circ\gamma)'(0),\] where \(\gamma:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to M\) is any smooth curve satisfying \(\gamma(0)=p\) and \(\gamma'(0)=v\). This value is independent of the representing curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The differential sends a tangent velocity at the source to the velocity of its image under the map, independently of the curve representing that velocity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\text{ is a well-defined linear map}.\)

notation.meaning: tangent space of M at p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential of a Smooth Map Between Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic curve-based definition of the differential of a smooth manifold map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) and \(\mathcal M'\) be smooth manifolds, \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M'\) a smooth map, and \(x\in\mathcal M\). \(x\in\mathcal M\) and \(v=[c]\in T_x\mathcal M\), where \(c\) is smooth and \(c(0)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm DF(x):T_x\mathcal M\to T_{F(x)}\mathcal M'\) is the linear map satisfying \(\mathrm DF(x)[v]=[t\mapsto F(c(t))]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-Curve Representation of a Manifold Differential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a manifold differential as the ordinary derivative of an ambient-space-valued curve, including the scalar-field specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N\) be smooth, where \(\mathcal N\) is an embedded submanifold of a linear space \(\mathcal E\), and identify each \(T_y\mathcal N\) with its corresponding subspace of \(\mathcal E\). knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Space Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative represented as a tangent-space covector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. At \(p\in M\), its tangent-space derivative is the covector \(df_p\in T_p^*M\) satisfying \[df_p[v]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_{t=0}\] for every \(v\in T_pM\) and every smooth curve \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma(0)=p\) and \(\gamma'(0)=v\). If \(M\) has metric \(g\), the Riemannian gradient is uniquely determined by \(df_p[v]=g_p(\operatorname{grad}f(p),v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar function's derivative is a covector on the tangent space; a Riemannian metric uniquely represents that covector by the gradient vector.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth manifold and \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(df_p\in T_p^*M;\quad df_p[v]=g_p(\operatorname{grad}f(p),v)\text{ when }g\text{ is specified}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covector representation and metric duality with the Riemannian gradient fit the representation container, but neither claim has an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unilateral geodesic directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the right directional derivative along a chosen geodesic and states the opposite-direction criterion for bilaterality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\), \(x\in A\), and let \(\gamma\) be a geodesic with \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma(0)=X_x\). If the limit exists, the unilateral directional derivative is
\[
Df(x;X_x):=\lim_{t\searrow0}\frac{f(\gamma(t))-f(x)}{t}.
\]
It is bilateral if and only if \(Df(x;-X_x)\) exists and
\[
Df(x;-X_x)=-Df(x;X_x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unilateral directional derivative is the right derivative of the function along a geodesic starting at x with initial velocity X_x. It is bilateral exactly when the derivative in the opposite direction exists and is its negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Df(x;X_x)=\lim_{t\searrow0}\frac{f(\gamma(t))-f(x)}{t},\qquad Df(x;X_x)\text{ is bilateral}\iff Df(x;-X_x)\text{ exists and }Df(x;-X_x)=-Df(x;X_x).

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Representations of Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chart-matrix representation of the intrinsic differential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth, let \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^m)\) be a chart near \(p\), and let \(y=(y^1,\ldots,y^n)\) be a chart near \(F(p)\). Relative to the coordinate tangent bases, \(dF_p\) is represented by the Jacobian \[J_{y\circ F\circ x^{-1}}(x(p))=\left[\frac{\partial(y^\alpha\circ F)}{\partial x^i}(p)\right]_{\alpha,i}.\] Under new charts, this matrix changes by left and right multiplication with the corresponding transition-map Jacobians, while \(dF_p\) itself is chart independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In source and target charts, the intrinsic differential is represented by the ordinary Jacobian; coordinate changes transform its matrix but not the underlying linear map.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are charts at \(p\) and \(F(p)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([dF_p]_{x,y}=J_{y\circ F\circ x^{-1}}(x(p)).\)

ordinary Jacobian matrix of a coordinate map h

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate representation of a Fréchet derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinate criterion for continuous differentiability and basis-independent representation of the differential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (e_1,\ldots,e_m) and (e'_1,\ldots,e'_n) be bases of \mathcal E and \mathcal F, and let \widehat F:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n be the coordinate expression of F. Then F is continuously differentiable if and only if all partial derivatives \partial_i\widehat F^j exist and are continuous. knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Metric Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian metric used to identify tangent vectors and covectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. A Riemannian metric on \(M\) is a family \(g=(g_x)_{x\in M}\) such that each \(g_x:T_xM\times T_xM\to\mathbb R\) is a symmetric positive-definite bilinear form and, for all smooth vector fields \(X,Y\), the function \(x\mapsto g_x(X_x,Y_x)\) is smooth. It induces the norm \(\|\xi\|_x=\sqrt{g_x(\xi,\xi)}\) and the musical isomorphism \(g_x^\flat:T_xM\to T_x^*M\), defined by \(g_x^\flat(\xi)[\eta]=g_x(\xi,\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian metric is a smoothly varying inner product on tangent spaces; it induces tangent norms and identifies tangent vectors with cotangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_x^\flat:T_xM\to T_x^*M\) is a linear isomorphism for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: tangent space of the manifold at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian curve length and reparameterization invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For piecewise smooth regular curves on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold and let $\omega:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise $C^\infty$ regular curve. Its length is $L(\omega)=\int_a^b\|\dot\omega(t)\|_g\,dt$. If $h:[c,d]\to[a,b]$ is surjective, monotone, and piecewise $C^\infty$, then $L(\omega\circ h)=L(\omega)$; in particular, reversing the parameter preserves length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The length of a piecewise smooth regular curve is the integral of its Riemannian speed. Length is unchanged by a surjective monotone piecewise-smooth reparameterization, including reversal of orientation.
assumptions_latex: h:[c,d]\to[a,b]\text{ is surjective, monotone, and piecewise }C^\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(\omega)=\int_a^b\|\dot\omega(t)\|_g\,dt,\qquad L(\omega\circ h)=L(\omega)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian metric, induced distance, and gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes coordinate representations and the nonzero-gradient steepest-ascent characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Riemannian metric on a manifold \(\mathcal M\) is a smoothly varying family of inner products \(g_x\) on \(T_x\mathcal M\), inducing \(\|\xi_x\|_x=\sqrt{g_x(\xi_x,\xi_x)}\). In a chart, \(g_x(\xi_x,\zeta_x)=\widehat\xi_{\widehat x}^{T}G_{\widehat x}\widehat\zeta_{\widehat x}\), where \(G_{\widehat x}\) is symmetric positive definite. Curve length and, on connected \(\mathcal M\), Riemannian distance are \(L(\gamma)=\int_a^b\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}\,dt\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma:x\leadsto y}L(\gamma)\). For smooth \(f\), \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\) is uniquely determined by \(g_x(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi)=Df(x)[\xi]\) for every \(\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\), and locally \(\widehat{\operatorname{grad}f}(\widehat x)=G_{\widehat x}^{-1}\operatorname{Grad}\widehat f(\widehat x)\). If \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\ne0\), its normalization maximizes \(Df(x)[\xi]\) over unit tangent vectors, with maximum \(\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smoothly varying tangent-space inner product defines a Riemannian metric and norm. Its local matrix is symmetric positive definite. Integrating tangent speed defines curve length, whose infimum over joining curves defines Riemannian distance on a connected manifold. The Riemannian gradient represents the differential through the metric, has coordinate form inverse-metric times Euclidean gradient, and, when nonzero, points in the unit steepest-ascent direction with norm equal to the steepest slope.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is a smooth manifold equipped with a smoothly varying positive-definite inner product }g
\mathcal M\text{ is connected for the distance definition, and Hausdorff for the stated metric properties}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ induces the tangent norm, curve length, Riemannian distance, and the unique gradient satisfying }g_x(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi)=Df(x)[\xi].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. For each \(x\in M\), the Riemannian gradient \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\in T_xM\) is the unique tangent vector satisfying \[g_x\bigl(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\bigr)=\mathrm df(x)[\xi]\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in T_xM.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=(g_x^\flat)^{-1}(\mathrm df(x))\). Thus the differential is metric-independent, whereas its representing tangent vector is determined by \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Gradient and Its Metric Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the metric-dependent gradient of a smooth real-valued function and records its representation for a constant positive-definite metric on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold, let $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be smooth, and let $x\in M$. The Riemannian gradient $\operatorname{grad}f(x)$ is the unique vector in $T_xM$ such that
\[
\mathrm{D}f(x)[\xi]=g_x\bigl(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in T_xM.
\]
For $M=\mathbb{R}^n$ equipped with the constant metric $g_x(a,b)=a^TGb$, where $G\in\operatorname{Sym}(n)$ is positive definite, this definition gives
\[
\operatorname{grad}f(x)=G^{-1}\nabla f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Riemannian gradient is the unique tangent vector representing the differential through the Riemannian metric. On Euclidean space with a constant metric defined by a symmetric positive-definite matrix G, it is G inverse times the Euclidean gradient.
assumptions_latex: For the Euclidean specialization, $M=\mathbb{R}^n$ and $G\in\operatorname{Sym}(n)$ is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{D}f(x)[\xi]=g_x\bigl(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\bigr)\quad\forall\xi\in T_xM,\qquad g_x(a,b)=a^TGb\Longrightarrow\operatorname{grad}f(x)=G^{-1}\nabla f(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Dependence on Metric Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation law for gradients under two Riemannian metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) and \(h\) be Riemannian metrics on \(M\). For each \(x\in M\), let \(A_x:T_xM\to T_xM\) be the unique \(g_x\)-self-adjoint positive-definite operator satisfying \(h_x(u,v)=g_x(A_xu,v)\) for all \(u,v\in T_xM\). Then every smooth \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \[\operatorname{grad}_{h}f(x)=A_x^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_{g}f(x).\] Consequently, changing the metric generally changes the gradient vector and steepest-descent direction, while leaving \(\mathrm df(x)\) and the critical-point condition \(\mathrm df(x)=0\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one metric equals another through a positive-definite operator, their gradients differ by the inverse operator; critical points remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are Riemannian metrics on the same smooth manifold \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_{h}f(x)=A_x^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_{g}f(x)\), and \(\operatorname{grad}_{h}f(x)=0\iff\operatorname{grad}_{g}f(x)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian gradient and critical points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the intrinsic definition, coordinate components, elementary calculus rules, and critical-point characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth function \(f\) on a Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\), \(\operatorname{grad}f\) is the unique vector field satisfying \(g(X,\operatorname{grad}f)=df(X)=X(f)\) for every smooth vector field \(X\). In local coordinates, \((\operatorname{grad}f)^i=g^{ij}\partial_jf\). It obeys linearity, the product and chain rules, and, wherever \(f_2\ne0\), the quotient rule: \(\operatorname{grad}(f_1f_2)=f_1\operatorname{grad}f_2+f_2\operatorname{grad}f_1\), \(\operatorname{grad}(f_1/f_2)=(f_2\operatorname{grad}f_1-f_1\operatorname{grad}f_2)/f_2^2\), and \(\operatorname{grad}(\varphi\circ f)=(\varphi'\circ f)\operatorname{grad}f\). A point \(x\) is critical exactly when \(df_x=0\), equivalently \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Riemannian gradient is the metric-dual vector field of the differential. Its coordinate components are obtained by raising the index of the differential; it satisfies the usual linear, product, quotient, and chain rules. Critical points are exactly its zeros.
assumptions_latex: f_2\ne0\text{ wherever the quotient rule is applied}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(X,\operatorname{grad}f)=df(X)\ \forall X,\qquad df_x=0\iff\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded Gradient Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient formula for an embedded submanifold with its induced metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a smooth embedded submanifold of a Euclidean space \(E\), equipped with the induced metric, and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) admit a smooth extension \(\bar f\) to a neighborhood of \(M\). If \(P_x:E\to T_xM\) is the orthogonal projector, then \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla\bar f(x).\] This expression is independent of the chosen extension because any two extensions have ambient gradients whose difference is orthogonal to \(T_xM\). Equivalently, \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\rangle=\mathrm df(x)[\xi]\) for every \(\xi\in T_xM\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an embedded manifold with induced metric, project the ambient Euclidean gradient orthogonally onto the tangent space.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subset E\) is a smooth embedded submanifold with the induced Euclidean metric.
\(\bar f\) is a smooth local extension of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla\bar f(x)\), independently of the extension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Gradient Descent on the Unit Sphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sphere-specific gradient-descent iteration using an embedded gradient formula and normalization retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathrm{S}^{d-1}\to\mathbb{R} admit a smooth extension \bar f to \mathbb{R}^d. Given x_0\in\mathrm{S}^{d-1}, define for k\ge 0
\[
\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)=(I_d-x_kx_k^\top)\nabla\bar f(x_k),\qquad
x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\alpha_k\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)),
\]
where
\[
R_x(v)=\frac{x+v}{\lVert x+v\rVert}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth function on the unit sphere with a smooth ambient extension, Riemannian gradient descent projects the ambient gradient onto the tangent space, takes a scaled negative-gradient step, and retracts to the sphere by normalizing the resulting vector.
assumptions_latex: \bar f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is a smooth extension of }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=\frac{x_k-\alpha_k(I_d-x_kx_k^\top)\nabla\bar f(x_k)}{\left\lVert x_k-\alpha_k(I_d-x_kx_k^\top)\nabla\bar f(x_k)\right\rVert}\in\mathrm{S}^{d-1}\quad(k\ge0).

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Gradient Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizontal-lift representation of gradients on a Riemannian quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:\bar M\to M=\bar M/G\) be a Riemannian quotient map, with horizontal space \(\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) orthogonal to the vertical space \(\ker\mathrm D\pi(\bar x)\). For smooth \(f:M\to\mathbb R\), define the invariant lift \(\bar f=f\circ\pi\). Then \(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)\) is horizontal and is the unique horizontal lift of the quotient gradient: \[\mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)]=\operatorname{grad}f(\pi(\bar x)).\] More generally, if an ambient representative is first obtained, its horizontal projection represents the quotient gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Riemannian quotient, the gradient of the invariant lifted objective is horizontal and projects to the quotient gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\bar M\to M\) is a Riemannian submersion defining a smooth quotient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)\in\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) and \(\mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)]=\operatorname{grad}f(\pi(\bar x))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Hessian as the Hessian of the Exponential Pullback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of the intrinsic Hessian with the Euclidean Hessian in exponential coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold, let \(f\in C^2(\mathcal M)\), and let \(x\in\mathcal M\). Endow \(T_x\mathcal M\) with the inner product \(g_x\). Then \[\operatorname{Hess}f(x)=\operatorname{Hess}(f\circ\operatorname{Exp}_x)(0_x),\] where the right-hand side is the Euclidean Hessian of the locally defined pullback on \(T_x\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Riemannian Hessian at a point equals the Euclidean Hessian at the tangent-space origin of the function pulled back by the exponential map.
assumptions_latex: \(T_x\mathcal M\) is endowed with \(g_x\), and \(f\circ\operatorname{Exp}_x\) is considered on a neighborhood of \(0_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)=\operatorname{Hess}(f\circ\operatorname{Exp}_x)(0_x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric affine connection making a noncritical function linear affine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes the existence of a symmetric linear connection relative to which a smooth function without critical points has vanishing covariant Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((M,g)\) be an \(n\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be of class \(C^\infty\). If \(f\) has no critical points, then there exists a symmetric linear connection \(\bar\nabla\) on \(M\) such that
\[
\operatorname{Hess}_{\bar\nabla}f=0.
\]
Hence \(f\) is linear affine with respect to \(\bar\nabla\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every smooth function without critical points on a Riemannian manifold is linear affine with respect to some symmetric linear connection; its covariant Hessian for that connection vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a symmetric linear connection }\bar\nabla\text{ on }M\text{ such that }\operatorname{Hess}_{\bar\nabla}f=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent representations of a Riemannian affine function on the real line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies componentwise when the domain is a union of open intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval or a union of open intervals, let $g\in C^\infty(I)$ be a positive Riemannian metric, set $\Gamma=(\log\sqrt g)'$, and let $f\in C^2(I)$. Then $f$ is affine with respect to $g$ precisely when $\operatorname{Hess}_g f=f''-\Gamma f'=0$. On each connected component of $I$, this is equivalent to $f'/\sqrt g$ being constant and to $f(x)=C\int^x\sqrt{g(s)}\,ds+D$ for constants $C,D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable function on a Riemannian real line, vanishing covariant Hessian is equivalent, on each interval component, to a constant metric-normalized derivative and to an affine expression in Riemannian arc-length coordinates.
assumptions_latex: I\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ is an open interval or a union of open intervals}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Hess}_g f=0\iff \frac{f'}{\sqrt g}\text{ is constant componentwise}\iff f(x)=C\int^x\sqrt{g(s)}\,ds+D\text{ componentwise}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: At a zero of a smooth vector field, its covariant derivative agrees with its differential for every choice of connection.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall u\in T_x\mathcal M,\quad \nabla_uV=DV(x)[u]\in T_x\mathcal M.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Connections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-compatible affine connections used in Riemannian calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold. A Riemannian, or metric-compatible, connection is an affine connection \(
abla\) satisfying \[X igl(g(Y,Z) igr)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ)\] for every smooth vector field \(X,Y,Z\). Equivalently, parallel transport defined by \(
abla\) preserves the metric inner product along every smooth curve. Metric compatibility alone does not generally determine the connection uniquely; uniqueness follows after imposing vanishing torsion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian connection is an affine connection that preserves the metric under covariant differentiation and parallel transport.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla g=0\), equivalently its parallel transport preserves \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariant-derivative criterion for Lipschitz operator fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an infinitesimal characterization and a curvewise consequence for continuously differentiable operator fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H(x):T_x\mathcal M\to T_x\mathcal M be linear for every x\in\mathcal M, and suppose H is continuously differentiable. Then H is L-Lipschitz continuous if and only if \|\nabla_sH\|\le L\|s\| for all (x,s)\in T\mathcal M. In that case, every smooth curve c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M from x to y satisfies \left\|\operatorname{PT}^{c}_{0\leftarrow1}\circ H(y)\circ\operatorname{PT}^{c}_{1\leftarrow0}-H(x)\right\|\le L\,\operatorname{Length}(c).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable tangent-space operator field is L-Lipschitz exactly when every covariant directional derivative has norm at most L times the direction norm. Consequently, its transported variation along any smooth curve is bounded by L times the curve length.
assumptions_latex: \forall x\in\mathcal M,\ H(x):T_x\mathcal M\to T_x\mathcal M\text{ is linear}
c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\text{ is smooth with }c(0)=x,\ c(1)=y

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Hessians
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariant derivative of the Riemannian gradient under the Levi-Civita connection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection \(\nabla\), and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. The Riemannian Hessian at \(x\) is the linear map \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x):T_xM\to T_xM\) defined by \[\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\xi]=\nabla_{\xi}\operatorname{grad}f.\] Its associated bilinear form is \(\operatorname{hess}f(x)[\xi,\eta]=g_x(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\xi],\eta)\). Because the Levi-Civita connection is torsion-free, this bilinear form is symmetric for every \(x\in M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Riemannian Hessian differentiates the Riemannian gradient covariantly; its metric-associated bilinear form is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\xi]=\nabla_\xi\operatorname{grad}f\) and \(\operatorname{hess}f(x)\) is symmetric.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hessian definition and symmetry statement fit the topic and stated Levi-Civita assumptions, but no source or precise locator is provided.

Under the source's convention, $f$ is convex when $\operatorname{Hess}f(x)$ is positive semidefinite for every $x\in D$, and $f$ is strictly convex when $\operatorname{Hess}f(x)$ is positive definite for every $x\in D$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sphere characterization by a Hessian equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of a round sphere through the existence of a nonconstant solution to a Riemannian Hessian equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a complete connected Riemannian manifold of dimension \(n\ge 2\), and let \(c>0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Line Convexity and Constant-Mean-Curvature Level Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two equivalences for a twice continuously differentiable Riemannian submersion whose squared gradient norm depends only on its value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:N\to\mathbb{R}\) be a \(C^2\) submersion satisfying \(\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2=h(f)\). Then (i) the restrictions of \(f\) to its gradient lines are convex if and only if \(h'(f)>0\) along those lines; and (ii) \(\Delta f\) is a function of \(f\) if and only if every level hypersurface of \(f\) has constant mean curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable submersion whose squared gradient norm depends only on the function value, its restrictions to gradient lines are convex exactly when the derivative of that gradient-norm function is positive along those lines. Its Laplacian depends only on the function value exactly when every level hypersurface has constant mean curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(f|_{\text{gradient lines}}\text{ is convex}\iff h'(f)>0\text{ along those lines}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\left(\exists\psi\;\Delta f=\psi(f)\iff\text{every level hypersurface of }f\text{ has constant mean curvature}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian characterization of strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise second-order characterization for a twice continuously differentiable function on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a Riemannian manifold and \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be of class \(C^2\). Then \(f\) is strongly convex if and only if there exists \(m>0\) such that \[\operatorname{Hess}f(X,X)\ge m\lVert X\rVert^2\quad\text{on }M\qquad\forall X\in\mathfrak X(M).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable function is strongly convex exactly when its Riemannian Hessian is uniformly bounded below by a positive multiple of the metric norm squared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strongly convex}\iff\exists m>0\;\forall X\in\mathfrak X(M),\quad \operatorname{Hess}f(X,X)\ge m\lVert X\rVert^2\text{ on }M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(M^c=\{x\in M:f(x)\le c\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strongly convex function on a Riemannian manifold, if there is no critical point at levels between a and b, then its a- and b-sublevel sets are diffeomorphic. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric and topological consequences of tangent-bundle energy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four stated consequences for the energy E on (TM,G); compactness is required only for the deformation-retract conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the energy \(E\) on \((TM,G)\): (i) \(\{z\in TM:E(z)\le 1\}\) is totally convex; (ii) \(\operatorname{Crit}(E)=\operatorname*{argmin}E\) is the zero section \(M\), and \(M\) is totally convex and totally geodesic in \((TM,G)\); (iii) if \(M\) is compact, then \(M\) is a deformation retract of \(TM\); and (iv) the field lines of \(\operatorname{grad}E\) are geodesics of \((TM,G)\) reparameterized by \(s=a+be^{2t}\), with \(a,b\) constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit sublevel of the energy is totally convex; its critical and global-minimum set is the zero section M, which is totally convex and totally geodesic. If M is compact, it is a deformation retract of TM. Gradient field lines become geodesics under the stated exponential reparameterization.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is the energy function on the Riemannian manifold \((TM,G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{E\le 1\}\text{ is totally convex};\quad \operatorname{Crit}(E)=\operatorname*{argmin}E=M;\quad M\text{ is totally convex and totally geodesic in }(TM,G);\quad M\text{ compact}\Rightarrow M\text{ deformation retracts }TM;\quad s=a+be^{2t}\text{ reparameterizes the field lines of }\operatorname{grad}E\text{ as geodesics}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal value of p-energy in terms of Riemannian distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract states the result for arbitrary endpoint pairs. For $p<0$, the expression $d(x,y)^p$ is not finite when $x=y$; the extract supplies no distinct-endpoint boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be complete, let $x,y\in M$, set $d=d(x,y)$, and let $E_p$ be the $p$-energy on regular piecewise smooth curves joining $x$ to $y$. If $p\in(-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)$, then $\max_{\omega\in\Omega}E_p(\omega)=d^p$, and this value is attained on minimizing geodesics from $x$ to $y$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete Riemannian manifold, the extract claims that p-energy has minimum d(x,y)^p for p greater than one and maximum d(x,y)^p for negative p or p between zero and one, with minimizing geodesics attaining the stated value.

For the first case, $p>1$; for the second, $p\in(-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Length, distance, and p-energy of a Riemannian curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For piecewise smooth regular curves with fixed endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold and let $\Omega$ be the set of piecewise $C^\infty$ regular curves $\omega:[0,1]\to M$ joining $x$ to $y$. Define $L(\omega)=\int_0^1\|\dot\omega(t)\|_g\,dt$ and $d(x,y)=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}L(\omega)$. For $p\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, the functional $E_p(\omega)=\int_0^1\|\dot\omega(t)\|_g^p\,dt$ is called the $p$-energy of $\omega$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For piecewise smooth regular curves joining two points of a Riemannian manifold, length is the integral of speed and distance is the infimum of length. For every nonzero real p, p-energy is the integral of speed to the pth power.
assumptions_latex: $\omega:[0,1]\to M$ is piecewise $C^\infty$, regular, and joins $x$ to $y$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E_p(\omega):=\int_0^1\|\dot\omega(t)\|_g^p\,dt\quad\text{is the $p$-energy of }\omega.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal piecewise-Jacobi decomposition of the variation space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the piecewise-Jacobi space T_1 and nodally vanishing space T_2 associated with a sufficiently fine partition of the geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1\) be the space of variation fields that are Jacobi fields on each subinterval of the chosen partition, and let \(T_2\) be the space of variation fields vanishing at every partition point. For every \(p\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0,1\}\), \[T_\gamma\Omega=T_1\oplus T_2,\qquad E_p^{**}(W_1,W_2)=0\quad(W_1\in T_1,\ W_2\in T_2).\] Moreover, \(E_p^{**}|_{T_2}\) is positive definite if \(p>1\), and negative definite if \(p\in(-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variation space is the direct sum of the piecewise-Jacobi fields and the fields vanishing at all partition points. The two subspaces are orthogonal for the p-energy Hessian. On the nodally vanishing subspace the Hessian is positive definite for p greater than one and negative definite for negative p or p strictly between zero and one.
assumptions_latex: 0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_k=1\text{ is the sufficiently fine partition used to define }T_1\text{ and }T_2
T_1=\{W:W|_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}\text{ is a Jacobi field for every }i\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_\gamma\Omega=T_1\oplus T_2,\quad E_p^{**}(T_1,T_2)=0,\quad p>1\Rightarrow E_p^{**}|_{T_2}\succ0,\quad p\in(-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)\Rightarrow E_p^{**}|_{T_2}\prec0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate-point index theorem for geodesic p-energy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts the relevant p-energy Hessian index by interior conjugate points, with multiplicity, in the preceding fixed-endpoint geodesic variational setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_\gamma\) denote the number of points \(\gamma(t)\), \(t\in(0,1)\), conjugate to \(\gamma(0)\) along \(\gamma\), each counted with its multiplicity. Then \(N_\gamma<\infty\), and for every admissible parameter, \[p>1\implies \operatorname{ind}_{-}(E_p^{**})=N_\gamma,\qquad p\in(-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)\implies \operatorname{ind}_{+}(E_p^{**})=N_\gamma.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of interior points conjugate to the initial point along the geodesic, counted with multiplicity, is finite. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and uniqueness of the induced covariant derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes covariant differentiation of order-k tensor fields along a smooth curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $c:I\to\mathcal M$ be smooth and let $\mathcal M$ carry a connection $\nabla$. There exists a unique operator $\frac{D}{dt}:\mathfrak X^k(c)\to\mathfrak X^k(c)$ such that
$$\frac D{dt}(aY+bZ)=a\frac{DY}{dt}+b\frac{DZ}{dt},$$
$$\frac D{dt}(gZ)=g'Z+g\frac{DZ}{dt},$$
and
$$\left(\frac D{dt}(T\circ c)\right)(t)=\nabla_{c'(t)}T$$
for all $Y,Z\in\mathfrak X^k(c)$, $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $g\in\mathfrak F(I)$, $T\in\mathfrak X^k(\mathcal M)$, and $t\in I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connection uniquely induces differentiation of order-k tensor fields along a smooth curve. The operator is real-linear, satisfies the scalar Leibniz rule, and agrees with the ambient covariant derivative on tensor fields restricted to the curve.
assumptions_latex: $\mathcal M$ is equipped with a connection $\nabla$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\frac D{dt}:\mathfrak X^k(c)\to\mathfrak X^k(c)\text{ satisfying the stated linearity, Leibniz, and chain rules.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariant derivative and acceleration along a curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vector fields and covariant differentiation along a manifold-valued curve for a fixed affine connection, including the induced acceleration and its coordinate representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal M,
abla)$ be a manifold with affine connection and let $\gamma:I	o\mathcal M$ be smooth. A vector field along $\gamma$ is a smooth assignment $\xi(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}\mathcal M$. There is a unique operator $ rac{D}{dt}:\mathfrak X(\gamma)	o\mathfrak X(\gamma)$ that is $\mathbb R$-linear, satisfies $ rac{D}{dt}(f\xi)=f'\xi+f rac{D\xi}{dt}$, and obeys $ rac{D}{dt}(\eta\circ\gamma)(t)=
abla_{\dot\gamma(t)}\eta$. The acceleration is $ rac{D^2\gamma}{dt^2}:= rac{D\dot\gamma}{dt}$; in local coordinates its $k$th component is $\ddot x^k+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma(t))\dot x^i\dot x^j$. Thus acceleration depends on $
abla$, whereas velocity does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth curve on a manifold with an affine connection, vector fields along the curve admit a unique covariant derivative characterized by linearity, the product rule, and compatibility with the connection. Applying it to the velocity defines acceleration, whose coordinate formula contains the Christoffel-symbol term and therefore depends on the connection, unlike velocity.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal M,\nabla)\text{ is a manifold equipped with an affine connection}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\frac{D}{dt}\text{ with the stated properties, and }\frac{D^2\gamma}{dt^2}=\frac{D\dot\gamma}{dt},\quad \left(\frac{D^2\gamma}{dt^2}\right)^k=\ddot x^k+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualitative properties of a Riemannian gradient line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The theorem uses the ascent equation $\dot\alpha=\operatorname{grad}f(\alpha)$ and extended endpoint limits where appropriate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\alpha:I\to M$, $I=(\omega_-(x),\omega_+(x))$, be a maximal gradient line of $f$, and write $T_t(x)=\alpha(t)$. Then: (i) $\alpha$ is a curve of maximal local increase of $f$, and the endpoint limits of $f(T_t(x))$ exist; (ii) $\alpha$ can be closed only when it is constant at a critical point of $f$; (iii) if $\omega_+(x)<\infty$, then $\lim_{t\nearrow\omega_+(x)}f(T_t(x))=+\infty$; and (iv) if $\omega_+(x)=\infty$ and $\lim_{t\to\infty}\alpha(t)=x_0$ exists, then $\operatorname{grad}f(x_0)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a maximal positive-gradient trajectory, the objective increases and has endpoint limits. A closed gradient trajectory must be a constant critical point. If its forward maximal time is finite, the objective diverges to positive infinity; if the trajectory exists forever and converges, its limit is a critical point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\circ\alpha\text{ has endpoint limits};\quad \alpha\text{ closed}\Rightarrow\alpha\text{ is a critical equilibrium};\quad \omega_+(x)<\infty\Rightarrow\lim_{t\nearrow\omega_+(x)}f(\alpha(t))=+\infty;\quad [\omega_+(x)=\infty,\ \alpha(t)\to x_0]\Rightarrow\operatorname{grad}f(x_0)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-nets, total boundedness, and relative compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric compactness notions for subsets of a complete Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\subset M$. For $\varepsilon>0$, a finite set $A_\varepsilon\subset A$ is an $\varepsilon$-net of $A$ if for every $x\in A$ there exists $y\in A_\varepsilon$ with $d(x,y)<\varepsilon$. The set $A$ is totally bounded if it has an $\varepsilon$-net for every $\varepsilon>0$, and it is relatively compact if $\overline A$ is sequentially compact. In a complete metric space, $A$ is totally bounded if and only if it is relatively compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-net is a finite subset whose epsilon-balls cover the given set. A set is totally bounded when it has such a net at every positive scale, and relatively compact when its closure is sequentially compact. In a complete metric space these two properties are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: $(M,d)$ is a complete metric space, in particular the metric space induced by a complete Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_\varepsilon\text{ is an }\varepsilon\text{-net}\iff A_\varepsilon\subset A\text{ is finite and }(\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A_\varepsilon)\ d(x,y)<\varepsilon;\qquad A\text{ totally bounded}\iff\overline A\text{ sequentially compact}.

knowledge_statements.title: Covariant Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariant differentiation of a vector field along a curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) carry an affine connection \(\nabla\), let \(c:I\to M\) be a smooth curve, and let \(V\) be a smooth vector field along \(c\). The covariant derivative \(DV/dt\) is the unique vector field along \(c\) that is linear in \(V\), satisfies \(D(aV)/dt=a'V+aDV/dt\) for every smooth scalar function \(a:I\to\mathbb R\), and agrees with \(\nabla_{\dot c}\widetilde V\) whenever \(V\) is the restriction of a local vector field \(\widetilde V\). In coordinates, \[(DV/dt)^k=\dot V^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(c)V^i\dot c^j.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The covariant derivative differentiates a tangent vector field along a curve while correcting coordinate derivatives by the connection coefficients.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is equipped with an affine connection \(\nabla\).
\(c:I\to M\) and the vector field \(V\) along \(c\) are smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DV/dt\) is a well-defined vector field along \(c\), independent of the chosen coordinates or extension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedded-Manifold Construction of the Induced Covariant Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the curvewise derivative from the embedded construction with the derivative induced by the embedded connection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be an embedded submanifold of a Euclidean space \(\mathcal E\), equipped with the connection induced by its embedding. If \(\mathcal M\) is a Riemannian submanifold of \(\mathcal E\), it also satisfies \(\frac d{dt}\langle Y,Z\rangle=\left\langle\frac{DY}{dt},Z\right\rangle+\left\langle Y,\frac{DZ}{dt}\right\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an embedded submanifold with its embedding-induced connection, the derivative along curves supplied by the embedded construction is exactly the induced covariant derivative. If the embedding is Riemannian, this derivative also satisfies the inner-product product rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential of a Smooth Vector Field on a Linear Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the classical directional differential of a smooth vector field and records the properties used as axioms for manifold differentiation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E\) be a linear space equipped with its smooth-calculus structure, let \(U,V,W\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal E)\), \(f\in\mathfrak F(\mathcal E)\), \(x,u,w\in\mathcal E\), and \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Then \[\mathrm DV(x)[u]=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{V(x+tu)-V(x)}{t}.\] Moreover, \(\mathrm DV(x)[au+bw]=a\mathrm DV(x)[u]+b\mathrm DV(x)[w]\), \(\mathrm D(aV+bW)(x)[u]=a\mathrm DV(x)[u]+b\mathrm DW(x)[u]\), and \(\mathrm D(fV)(x)[u]=\mathrm Df(x)[u]V(x)+f(x)\mathrm DV(x)[u]\). The map \(x\mapsto\mathrm DV(x)[U(x)]\) is a smooth vector field on \(\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The differential of a smooth vector field on a linear space is its directional difference-quotient limit. It is linear in the direction and in the vector field, satisfies the scalar-product Leibniz rule, and differentiation along a smooth vector field yields another smooth vector field.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\) is a linear space in the stated smooth-calculus setting.
\(U,V,W\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal E)\) are smooth vector fields.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The differential is given by \(\mathrm DV(x)[u]=\lim_{t\to0}(V(x+tu)-V(x))/t\), has the stated linearity and Leibniz properties, and \(x\mapsto\mathrm DV(x)[U(x)]\) is a smooth vector field.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $c:I	o\mathcal M$ be a smooth curve on a manifold equipped with a connection $
abla$. There exists a unique operator $ rac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}:\mathfrak X(c)	o\mathfrak X(c)$ such that, for all $Y,Z\in\mathfrak X(c)$, $U\in\mathfrak X(\mathcal M)$, $g\in\mathfrak F(I)$, $a,b\in\mathbb R$, and $t\in I$, it is $\mathbb R$-linear, satisfies $ rac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}(gZ)=g'Z+g rac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}Z$, and obeys $\left( rac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}(U\circ c)ight)(t)=
abla_{c'(t)}U$. If $\mathcal M$ is Riemannian and $
abla$ is metric-compatible, then $ rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\langle Y,Zangle=\left\langle rac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}Y,Zightangle+\left\langle Y, rac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}Zightangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connection induces a unique covariant derivative on vector fields along each smooth curve. It is real-linear, satisfies the scalar Leibniz rule, and agrees with the connection on restricted manifold vector fields. When the manifold is Riemannian and the connection is metric-compatible, it also satisfies the inner-product product rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian of a curve functional at a critical curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Hessian by a mixed second derivative along a two-parameter fixed-endpoint variation realizing two tangent fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\gamma$ be a critical point of $F:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and let $W_1,W_2\in T_\gamma\Omega$. Choose a two-parameter fixed-endpoint variation $\alpha:U\times[0,1]\to M$, where $(0,0)\in U\subset\mathbb R^2$, such that $\alpha(0,0,t)=\gamma(t)$ and $\partial_{u_i}\alpha(0,0,t)=W_i(t)$ for $i=1,2$. Writing $\bar\alpha(u_1,u_2)(t)=\alpha(u_1,u_2,t)$, if the mixed derivative exists for every such variation and determines a bilinear form independently of the realizing variation, the Hessian of $F$ at $\gamma$ is $F_{**,\gamma}:T_\gamma\Omega\times T_\gamma\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given by $F_{**,\gamma}(W_1,W_2)=\left.\frac{\partial^2}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}F(\bar\alpha(u_1,u_2))\right|_{(0,0)}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a critical curve, choose a two-parameter fixed-endpoint variation whose coordinate variation fields are two prescribed tangent fields. When the mixed second derivative exists for every such variation and is determined by those fields, it defines the bilinear Hessian of the curve functional.
assumptions_latex: \left.\partial_{u_1}\partial_{u_2}F(\bar\alpha(u_1,u_2))\right|_{(0,0)}\text{ exists for every admissible }\bar\alpha\text{ and determines a bilinear form}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{**,\gamma}(W_1,W_2)=\left.\frac{\partial^2}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}F(\bar\alpha(u_1,u_2))\right|_{(0,0)}\text{ is the Hessian of }F\text{ at }\gamma.

knowledge_statements.title: Curve Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic acceleration determined by a connection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) have an affine connection \(\nabla\), and let \(c:I\to M\) be a smooth curve. The covariant acceleration of \(c\) is the vector field along the curve defined by \[A_c(t)=\frac{D\dot c}{dt}(t)=\nabla_{\dot c(t)}\dot c.\] In local coordinates \((x^k)\), its components are \[A_c^k(t)=\ddot c^k(t)+\Gamma^k_{ij}(c(t))\dot c^i(t)\dot c^j(t).\] Unlike the coordinatewise second derivative alone, this expression transforms as a tangent vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curve acceleration is the covariant derivative of velocity along the curve; connection terms make it an intrinsic tangent vector.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is equipped with an affine connection \(\nabla\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_c=D\dot c/dt\) is an intrinsic vector field along \(c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intrinsic acceleration definition and coordinate expression are mathematically appropriate and correctly classified, but no supporting source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and lower semicontinuity for bounded-energy curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compactness lemma for a sequence in the curve class $\Omega$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\{\alpha_n\}\subset\Omega$ be curves with $E(\alpha_n)\le C$, all having image in a compact set $K\subset M$. Then there exist a curve $\alpha\in\Omega$ with image in $K$ and a subsequence $\{\alpha_n'\}$ such that $\alpha_n'\rightharpoonup\alpha$ weakly in $H^1$, hence $\alpha_n'\to\alpha$ in $C^0$, and $E(\alpha)\le\lim_n E(\alpha_n')=\limsup_n E(\alpha_n)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any uniformly energy-bounded sequence of curves in the class Ω whose images remain in one compact subset of the manifold has a subsequence converging weakly in H1 and uniformly to a curve in Ω. The limiting energy does not exceed the subsequential limiting energy, which can be chosen as the original limsup.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\alpha\in\Omega,\ \exists\{\alpha_n'\}:\ \alpha_n'\rightharpoonup\alpha\text{ in }H^1,\ \alpha_n'\to\alpha\text{ in }C^0,\ E(\alpha)\le\lim_nE(\alpha_n')=\limsup_nE(\alpha_n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Acceleration of a Manifold-Valued Curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines intrinsic acceleration and gives its ambient projection representation for a Riemannian submanifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $c:I\to\mathcal M$ be a smooth curve on a Riemannian manifold. Its intrinsic acceleration is $c''=\frac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}c'$. If $\mathcal M$ is a Riemannian submanifold of a linear space $\mathcal E$ with the induced Riemannian connection and $\ddot c=\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}c$ denotes extrinsic acceleration, then $c''(t)=\operatorname{Proj}_{c(t)}\!\left(\ddot c(t)\right)$ for all $t\in I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic acceleration of a smooth manifold-valued curve is the covariant derivative of its velocity. For a Riemannian submanifold with the induced connection, intrinsic acceleration is the tangential projection of ambient acceleration.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the projection formula, }\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\text{ is a Riemannian submanifold with the induced connection}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c''=\frac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}c',\qquad c''(t)=\operatorname{Proj}_{c(t)}\!\left(\ddot c(t)\right)\quad\forall t\in I\ \text{in the submanifold case}

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Acceleration Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-parameter criterion for a curve to be geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) carry an affine connection \(\nabla\), and let \(c:I\to M\) be a smooth regular curve with parameter \(t\). The curve is an affinely parameterized geodesic exactly when its covariant acceleration vanishes: \[\frac{D\dot c}{dt}=0.\] In local coordinates this is equivalent to the system \[\ddot c^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(c)\dot c^i\dot c^j=0\qquad\text{for every coordinate index }k.\] A non-affine reparameterization of the same unparameterized geodesic may instead have acceleration proportional to its velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularly parameterized curve is an affine geodesic exactly when its covariant acceleration is zero; non-affine parameterizations need not satisfy this equation.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is equipped with an affine connection \(\nabla\).
\(c:I\to M\) is a smooth regular curve with parameter \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is an affinely parameterized geodesic \(\iff D\dot c/dt=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-covariant-acceleration condition correctly characterizes affinely parameterized geodesics and distinguishes non-affine reparameterizations, but it lacks an authoritative citation and precise locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesic via Vanishing Covariant Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic definition for smooth curves on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth curve \(\gamma:I\to M\) is a geodesic if its covariant acceleration vanishes identically: \(\frac{\nabla}{dt}\dot\gamma(t)=0\) for every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth manifold-valued curve is a geodesic when its covariant acceleration vanishes throughout its parameter interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma\text{ is geodesic}\iff \frac{\nabla}{dt}\dot\gamma\equiv0.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Pullback Taylor-Model Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order Taylor models of a smooth objective pulled back to a tangent space by a retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, let \(R\) be a smooth retraction, and fix \(x\in\mathcal M\). The pullback \(\widehat f_x=f\circ R_x\) has the tangent-space model
\[
m_x(\eta)=f(x)+\langle \operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x+\tfrac12\langle \eta,H_x\eta\rangle_x,
\qquad \eta\in T_x\mathcal M,
\]
where \(H_x=\nabla^2\widehat f_x(0_x)\) is self-adjoint. As \(\eta\to0_x\),
\[
\widehat f_x(\eta)=m_x(\eta)+o(\|\eta\|_x^2).
\]
If \(R\) is second order at \(x\), then \(H_x=\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retraction pulls the objective onto a tangent space, where its quadratic Taylor model uses the pullback Hessian; for a second-order retraction this equals the Riemannian Hessian.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a smooth retraction defined near \(0_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(R_x(\eta))=m_x(\eta)+o(\|\eta\|_x^2)\), with \(H_x=\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\) when \(R\) is second order at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Restriction of the retraction to the tangent space at x.
Pullback of f to the tangent space at x.
Euclidean Hessian of the pullback at the zero tangent vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the pullback Taylor-model container and is mathematically plausible, but no citation is supplied for the second-order expansion or for identifying the pullback Hessian with the Riemannian Hessian under a second-order retraction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Retraction on a Smooth Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a retraction through its value and differential at each tangent-space origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth map \(R:TM\to M\) is a retraction on a smooth manifold \(M\) if, for every \(x\in M\), its restriction \(R_x:T_xM\to M\) satisfies \(R_x(0_x)=x\) and \(\mathrm{D}R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth tangent-bundle map is a retraction when it maps every zero tangent vector to its base point and has identity differential there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\text{ is a retraction}\iff \forall x\in M,\ R_x(0_x)=x\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{D}R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Every retraction admits a locally diffeomorphic endpoint map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a zero-section neighborhood, with a continuous-radius description relative to any chosen Riemannian metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every retraction \(R\) on a manifold \(\mathcal M\), there exists a neighborhood \(\mathcal T\) of the zero section of \(T\mathcal M\) such that \((x,v)\mapsto(x,R_x(v))\) is a diffeomorphism from \(\mathcal T\) onto its image. With respect to any Riemannian metric, \(\mathcal T\) may be chosen in the radius-controlled form stated in (10.8), with a continuous function \(\Delta:\mathcal M\to(0,\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every retraction has a neighborhood of the tangent-bundle zero section on which its base-point and endpoint map is a diffeomorphism. For any chosen Riemannian metric, such a neighborhood can be selected using a continuous positive radius function.
assumptions_latex: A Riemannian metric is chosen only to express the radius-controlled neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a zero-section neighborhood \(\mathcal T\) such that \((x,v)\mapsto(x,R_x(v))\) is a diffeomorphism onto its image, and \(\mathcal T\) may be chosen with continuous \(\Delta:\mathcal M\to(0,\infty]\) as in (10.8).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector transport associated with a retraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines general vector transport and distinguishes it from a transporter determined only by source and destination points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a smooth manifold and \(R\) a retraction. A vector transport associated with \(R\) is a smooth map \((x,u,v)\mapsto \mathrm{VT}_{(x,u)}(v)\) on \(T\mathcal M\oplus T\mathcal M\) such that, for every \((x,u)\in T\mathcal M\), \(\mathrm{VT}_{(x,u)}:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{R_x(u)}\mathcal M\) is linear, and \(\mathrm{VT}_{(x,0)}=\operatorname{Id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\). A transporter \(T\) and \(R\) induce such a transport by \(\mathrm{VT}_{(x,u)}=T_{R_x(u)\leftarrow x}\). Conversely, a general vector transport need not arise this way, since \(R_x(u)=R_x(w)\) need not imply \(\mathrm{VT}_{(x,u)}=\mathrm{VT}_{(x,w)}\); it defines a transporter only after restricting to a domain where \((x,u)\mapsto(x,R_x(u))\) has a smooth inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a smooth manifold and a retraction, a vector transport smoothly and linearly moves tangent vectors from the tangent space at x to that at the retracted point, and it is the identity for a zero step. Every endpoint-dependent transporter yields a vector transport, but a vector transport may depend on the chosen retraction step beyond its endpoint; the converse construction therefore requires local smooth invertibility of the step-to-endpoint map.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{VT}:T\mathcal M\oplus T\mathcal M\to T\mathcal M\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{VT}_{(x,u)}:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{R_x(u)}\mathcal M\) is linear for all \((x,u)\), \(\mathrm{VT}_{(x,0)}=\operatorname{Id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\), and equivalence with an endpoint-dependent transporter requires the stated smooth-invertibility restriction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Riemannian Strong Wolfe Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The global-domain and curvewise lower-bound assumptions are essential hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ on a smooth Riemannian manifold $(M,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$, and let the retraction $R$ be defined on all of $TM$. Given $x_k\in M$ and a descent direction $\eta_k\in T_{x_k}M$, suppose that $f$ is bounded below on $\{R_{x_k}(t\eta_k):t>0\}$. If $0<c_1<c_2<1$, then there exists $t_k>0$ such that $f(R_{x_k}(t_k\eta_k))\le f(x_k)+c_1t_k\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_k),\eta_k\rangle_{x_k}$ and $|\langle\operatorname{grad}f(R_{x_k}(t_k\eta_k)),\mathrm DR_{x_k}(t_k\eta_k)[\eta_k]\rangle_{R_{x_k}(t_k\eta_k)}|\le c_2|\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_k),\eta_k\rangle_{x_k}|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable objective, a globally defined retraction, a descent direction, and an objective bounded below along the positive retraction curve, some positive step satisfies the Riemannian strong Wolfe conditions whenever the two Wolfe constants lie strictly between zero and one in increasing order.
assumptions_latex: R\text{ is defined on all of }TM
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,t_k>0\text{ satisfying the Riemannian Armijo and strong-curvature inequalities.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transporters induced by a retraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives parallel-transport and differential constructions where the retraction admits a smooth local inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a retraction on \(\mathcal M\), and suppose \(E(x,v)=(x,R_x(v))\) is a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood \(\mathcal T\) of the zero section onto \(\mathcal V=E(\mathcal T)\). For \((x,y)\in\mathcal V\), write \(v=R_x^{-1}(y)\). If each fiber \(\mathcal T_x\) is star-shaped about \(0\), parallel transport along \(c(t)=R_x(tv)\) defines a transporter by \(T_{y\leftarrow x}=\operatorname{PT}^{c}_{1\leftarrow0}\). Independently, \(T_{y\leftarrow x}=DR_x(v)\) defines a transporter on \(\mathcal V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Where a retraction has a smooth local inverse, it produces transporters in two ways: by parallel transport along its radial curves when the relevant fibers are star-shaped, and by its differential without that additional condition.

\mathcal T_x\text{ is star-shaped about }0\text{ for the parallel-transport construction}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Retraction on a Manifold

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cholesky QR-Based Retraction on a Generalized Stiefel Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A retraction formula specialized to the generalized Stiefel manifold associated with a positive-definite matrix G.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G\in\operatorname{Sym}(n) satisfy G\succ0, let X\in\operatorname{St}_G(p,n), and let \eta\in T_X\operatorname{St}_G(p,n). Set Z=(X+\eta)^TG(X+\eta), compute the Cholesky factorization Z=R^TR, and define R_X^G(\eta)=(X+\eta)R^{-1}. Since the tangency condition gives Z=I_p+\eta^TG\eta\succ0, the factorization exists and R_X^G(\eta)\in\operatorname{St}_G(p,n).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a positive-definite matrix G, a point X on the associated generalized Stiefel manifold, and a tangent vector eta at X, form the G-Gram matrix of X+eta, compute its Cholesky factor, and right-normalize X+eta by the inverse factor. The tangency condition makes the Gram matrix positive definite, and the result lies on the generalized Stiefel manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z=I_p+\eta^TG\eta\succ0,\qquad R_X^G(\eta)=(X+\eta)R^{-1}\in\operatorname{St}_G(p,n),\quad Z=R^TR.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexpansive metric projection onto a closed totally convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The perpendicular endpoint defines the nearest-point retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete, simply connected, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature $K\le 0$, and let $A\subseteq M$ be closed and totally convex. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous positive local-invertibility radius for a retraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A base-point-dependent radius controlling the domain and diffeomorphic behavior of a general retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a retraction on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), defined on a neighborhood \(\mathcal O\) of the zero section, and set \(E(x,v)=(x,R_x(v))\). For \(\delta>0\), define \(V_\delta(x)=\{(x',v')\in T\mathcal M:\operatorname{dist}(x,x')<\delta,\ \|v'\|_{x'}<\delta\}\) and \(\Delta(x)=\sup\{\delta>0:V_\delta(x)\subseteq\mathcal O\text{ and }E\text{ is a diffeomorphism on }V_\delta(x)\}\). Then \(\Delta:\mathcal M\to(0,\infty]\) is positive and continuous, and for every \(x\), \(R_x\) is defined and is a diffeomorphism on the tangent-space ball of radius \(\Delta(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every retraction admits a positive, continuous base-point-dependent radius within which it is defined and diffeomorphic; this radius can be characterized through neighborhoods on which the associated tangent-to-pair map is a diffeomorphism.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction defined on a neighborhood \(\mathcal O\) of the zero section of \(T\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta(x)>0\text{ for all }x,\quad \Delta\text{ is continuous, and }R_x\text{ is defined and diffeomorphic on }\{v\in T_x\mathcal M:\|v\|_x<\Delta(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order-q model on a Riemannian manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines local approximation order using Riemannian distance and records base-point interpolation as an immediate property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R be a real-valued function on a Riemannian manifold, let x\in\mathcal M, let m_x be a real-valued function defined near x, and let q>0. The function m_x is an order-q model of f at x if there exist a neighborhood \mathcal U of x and c>0 such that \left|f(y)-m_x(y)\right|\le c\,\operatorname{dist}(x,y)^{q+1} for every y\in\mathcal U. Every order-q model satisfies m_x(x)=f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local function is an order-q model of an objective at a point when its error is bounded nearby by a constant times the Riemannian distance to that point raised to q+1. It must agree with the objective at the base point.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Map Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact geodesic retraction models within the injectivity neighborhood of a base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal M,g)\), fix \(x\in\mathcal M\). For every \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\) for which the geodesic \(\gamma_\eta\) exists on \([0,1]\),
\[
\operatorname{Exp}_x(\eta)=\gamma_\eta(1),\qquad \gamma_\eta(0)=x,\qquad \dot\gamma_\eta(0)=\eta.
\]
The exponential map satisfies \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=x\) and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\), hence is a retraction wherever defined. If \(\|\eta\|_x<\operatorname{inj}(x)\), it gives the unique minimizing radial geodesic from \(x\) to \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map sends a tangent vector to its unit-time geodesic endpoint, is a second-order retraction, and is locally one-to-one inside the injectivity radius.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a smooth Riemannian manifold.
The indicated geodesic exists through time \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=x\) and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian exponential map based at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential-map representation fits the container, but it has no cited evidence. In addition, the plain statement calls the exponential map a second-order retraction and locally one-to-one, while the displayed conclusion records only the first-order retraction identities; the injectivity-radius formulation and second-order claim require authoritative support and alignment across fields.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard first-order retraction definition on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be a smooth manifold and let \(T\mathcal M\) be its tangent bundle. A smooth map \(R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal M\), defined on an open neighborhood \(\mathcal D\subseteq T\mathcal M\) of the zero section, is a first-order retraction if, for every \(x\in\mathcal M\),
\[
R_x(0_x)=x,
\qquad
DR_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M},
\]
where \(R_x\) denotes the restriction of \(R\) to \(\mathcal D\cap T_x\mathcal M\). Equivalently, for each \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\), the curve \(t\mapsto R_x(t\eta)\) starts at \(x\) with velocity \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order retraction maps zero to its base point and has identity derivative at zero, so each tangent vector is reproduced as the initial curve velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\) is an open neighborhood of the zero section in \(T\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_x(0_x)=x\) and \(DR_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: Fiberwise restriction of R to the tangent space at x.
Zero vector in the tangent space at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is standard, well quantified, and appropriate for the First-Order Retractions container, but source_refs is empty. A specific authoritative definition or section locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retractions whose radial curves have zero covariant acceleration at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a first-order retraction on a Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal M,g)\) with Levi-Civita connection \(\nabla\). It is a second-order retraction at \(x\in\mathcal M\) if every radial retraction curve \(c_\eta(t)=R_x(t\eta)\) satisfies
\[
\left.\nabla_{\dot c_\eta}\dot c_\eta\right|_{t=0}=0
\qquad\text{for all }\eta\in T_x\mathcal M.
\]
It is second order on \(\mathcal M\) if this holds at every base point. Thus its radial curves agree with exponential-map geodesics through second order at their initial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order retraction is first order and has zero initial covariant acceleration along every radial tangent-space curve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left.\nabla_{\dot c_\eta}\dot c_\eta\right|_{t=0}=0\) for every \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: Radial curve obtained from the retraction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pullback Hessian identity for retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the Riemannian Hessian with the Hessian of the tangent-space pullback under either second-order retraction accuracy or stationarity at the point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order Taylor expansions along retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the intrinsic quadratic pullback expansion at critical points for arbitrary retractions and at arbitrary points for second-order retractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a Riemannian manifold equipped with a retraction \(R\), and let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. As \(s\to0\) in \(T_x\mathcal M\), if \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\), then \[f(R_x(s))=f(x)+\tfrac12\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[s],s\rangle_x+O(\|s\|_x^3).\] If \(R\) is a second-order retraction, then for every \(x\in\mathcal M\), \[f(R_x(s))=f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),s\rangle_x+\tfrac12\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[s],s\rangle_x+O(\|s\|_x^3).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a critical point, any retraction yields the intrinsic second-order Taylor expansion with a cubic remainder. For a second-order retraction, the full expansion also holds at every point.
assumptions_latex: For the first expansion, \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\); for the second expansion, \(R\) is second order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\Rightarrow f(R_x(s))=f(x)+\frac12\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[s],s\rangle_x+O(\|s\|_x^3)\), while a second-order \(R\) gives \(f(R_x(s))=f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),s\rangle_x+\frac12\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[s],s\rangle_x+O(\|s\|_x^3)\) for every \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Hessian as the pullback Hessian at the origin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the intrinsic Hessian with the Euclidean Hessian of the retraction pullback under either second-order retraction accuracy or criticality at the base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transport of a Retraction Through a Diffeomorphism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that transporting a retraction through a diffeomorphism and its differential yields a retraction on the source manifold.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-point projection construction for embedded Riemannian submanifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a smooth embedded submanifold, and suppose the nearest-point projection \(\pi_{\mathcal M}\) is single-valued and smooth on an open tubular neighborhood \(U\) of \(\mathcal M\). Define
\[
R_x(\eta)=\pi_{\mathcal M}(x+\eta)
\]
whenever \(x\in\mathcal M\), \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\), and \(x+\eta\in U\). Then \(R_x(0_x)=x\) and \(DR_x(0_x)=P_{T_x\mathcal M}|_{T_x\mathcal M}=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\); hence \(R\) is a local retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an embedded manifold, adding a tangent vector and projecting to the unique nearest manifold point defines a local retraction inside a tubular neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a smooth embedded submanifold.
\(\pi_{\mathcal M}\) is single-valued and smooth on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_x(\eta)=\pi_{\mathcal M}(x+\eta)\) defines a first-order retraction on its stated domain.

notation.meaning: Nearest-point projection onto the embedded manifold.
Orthogonal projection onto the tangent space at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is appropriate for Projection Retractions and states the needed local smoothness and uniqueness assumptions, but it lacks evidence for the tubular-neighborhood projection properties and derivative formula.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the submanifold carries the Riemannian metric induced by the ambient Euclidean space, its metric projection retraction is second order.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a Riemannian submanifold of the Euclidean space \(\mathcal E\).
\(R_x(v)=P_{\mathcal M}(x+v)\) is the metric projection retraction on its open single-valued domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\text{ is a second-order retraction.}
