knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Projection onto an Embedded Submanifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ambient distance, the possibly empty or multivalued metric projection, and its single-valued domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E\) be a Euclidean space and \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal E\) an embedded submanifold. For \(y\in\mathcal E\), define \(\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal M}(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal M}\|x-y\|\) and \(P_{\mathcal M}(y)=\{x\in\mathcal M:\|x-y\|=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal M}(y)\}\). The set \(P_{\mathcal M}(y)\) may be empty or contain one or more points. Define \(A=\{y\in\mathcal E:P_{\mathcal M}(y)\text{ is a singleton}\}\); this set may be neither open nor closed.

children.title: Polar Retractions
children.top_down_role: Retractions based on polar-decomposition geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar-factor retraction on the real Stiefel manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Stiefel manifold \(\operatorname{St}(p,n)=\{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}:X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p\}\), define for \(\Xi\in T_X\operatorname{St}(p,n)\)
\[
R_X^{\mathrm{pol}}(\Xi)=(X+\Xi)\bigl((X+\Xi)^{\mathsf T}(X+\Xi)\bigr)^{-1/2}
=(X+\Xi)(I_p+\Xi^{\mathsf T}\Xi)^{-1/2}.
\]
Because \(X^{\mathsf T}\Xi+\Xi^{\mathsf T}X=0\), the matrix under the inverse square root is positive definite. The result lies in \(\operatorname{St}(p,n)\), fixes \(X\) at \(\Xi=0\), and has derivative equal to the identity on \(T_X\operatorname{St}(p,n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the Stiefel manifold, the orthogonal polar factor of a tangent perturbation gives a globally defined first-order retraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_X^{\mathrm{pol}}(\Xi)\in\operatorname{St}(p,n)\), \(R_X^{\mathrm{pol}}(0)=X\), and \(DR_X^{\mathrm{pol}}(0)[\Xi]=\Xi\).

notation.meaning: Real Stiefel manifold of matrices with orthonormal columns.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polar formula is appropriate for the Stiefel-manifold leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no authoritative matrix-manifold source is cited. The plain statement's global-domain claim and the retraction derivative require specific support.

children.title: QR Retractions
children.top_down_role: Retractions based on QR-factorization interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: QR Retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thin-QR retraction on the real Stiefel manifold with fixed diagonal convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\operatorname{St}(p,n)\) and \(\Xi\in T_X\operatorname{St}(p,n)\), let \(X+\Xi=QR\) be the thin QR factorization whose triangular factor \(R\) has positive diagonal. Define
\[
R_X^{\mathrm{QR}}(\Xi)=Q=\operatorname{qf}(X+\Xi).
\]
Since \((X+\Xi)^{\mathsf T}(X+\Xi)=I_p+\Xi^{\mathsf T}\Xi\) is positive definite, \(X+\Xi\) has full column rank and the specified factorization is unique. Moreover, \(R_X^{\mathrm{QR}}(0)=X\) and \(DR_X^{\mathrm{QR}}(0)[\Xi]=\Xi\), so this is a retraction on \(\operatorname{St}(p,n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The orthonormal factor of a sign-normalized thin QR factorization of a Stiefel tangent perturbation defines a retraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_X^{\mathrm{QR}}(\Xi)=\operatorname{qf}(X+\Xi)\) is a first-order retraction.

notation.meaning: Q factor of the thin QR factorization with positive diagonal in R.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign-normalized thin-QR construction fits the QR Retractions container, but source_refs is empty. A specific source must support smoothness, uniqueness under the positive-diagonal convention, and the identity derivative at zero.

children.title: Factorization Retractions
children.top_down_role: Retractions derived from structured matrix factorizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Retractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General construction of retractions from smooth local normalization factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\subset E\) be an embedded manifold and suppose a smooth normalization map \(q:U\to\mathcal M\) is defined on a neighborhood \(U\subset E\) of \(\mathcal M\). If
\[
q(x)=x,
\qquad
Dq(x)[\eta]=\eta
\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal M\text{ and }\eta\in T_x\mathcal M,
\]
then
\[
R_x(\eta)=q(x+\eta)
\]
defines a first-order retraction wherever \(x+\eta\in U\). Maps \(q\) obtained by selecting a smooth normalized factor from a locally unique matrix factorization yield factorization retractions; loss of uniqueness or smoothness restricts their domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth factorization-based normalization that fixes manifold points and preserves tangent directions produces a retraction by normalizing each tangent perturbation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset E\) is a smooth embedded manifold.
\(q\) is smooth and satisfies the displayed value and derivative conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_x(\eta)=q(x+\eta)\) is a first-order retraction on its domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization principle is relevant to Factorization Retractions, but the broad abstraction from locally unique factorizations is uncited and may cover more than a standard named construction. A source is needed to establish the intended family and whether principle is the correct role for this exact leaf.

children.title: Retraction Validity Domains
children.top_down_role: Regions where a retraction remains well-defined for optimization use.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction Validity Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise domain conditions required for a local retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A local retraction domain is an open set \(\mathcal D\subseteq T\mathcal M\) containing the zero section such that a smooth map \(R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal M\) satisfies
\[
R_x(0_x)=x,
\qquad
DR_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}
\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal M.
\]
For a fixed base point, the valid fiber is \(\mathcal D_x=\mathcal D\cap T_x\mathcal M\). Any additional construction requirement—such as uniqueness of a projection, nonsingularity of a factor, or a fixed factorization convention—must hold throughout \(\mathcal D_x\); outside it the formula need not define a smooth single-valued map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retraction is valid on an open tangent-bundle neighborhood where its formula is smooth, single-valued, and satisfies the base-point and identity-derivative conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\subseteq T\mathcal M\) is open and contains the zero section.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal M\) is a local retraction exactly when the displayed smoothness, value, and derivative requirements hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Retraction Validity Domains container and cleanly distinguishes the tangent-bundle domain from its fibers, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Retraction Approximation Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Local fidelity of retractions to intrinsic manifold motion.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction Approximation Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local comparison orders between retractions and the Riemannian exponential map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\) on a Riemannian manifold and use a norm on \(T_x\mathcal M\). For a smooth first-order retraction \(R\), any smooth coordinate chart centered at \(x\) gives
\[
\varphi(R_x(\eta))-\varphi(\operatorname{Exp}_x(\eta))=O(\|\eta\|_x^2)
\quad\text{as }\eta\to0_x.
\]
If \(R\) is second order at \(x\), then
\[
\varphi(R_x(\eta))-\varphi(\operatorname{Exp}_x(\eta))=O(\|\eta\|_x^3).
\]
These orders are chart-independent locally because smooth coordinate changes have bounded derivatives near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order retractions match the exponential map through linear terms; second-order retractions also match its quadratic term, improving local error from quadratic to cubic.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and the exponential map are smooth near \(0_x\).
\(\varphi\) is a smooth local chart centered at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local coordinate error is \(O(\|\eta\|_x^2)\), or \(O(\|\eta\|_x^3)\) for a second-order retraction.

notation.meaning: Riemannian exponential map based at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the approximation-accuracy leaf, but the quadratic and cubic coordinate-error orders and their claimed chart independence require authoritative support. No source is supplied, so the exact hypotheses and intended pointwise meaning of the big-O bounds cannot be verified.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian Pullback Identity for a Zero-Acceleration Retraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-order pullback identity under zero initial covariant acceleration of every radial retraction curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold, let \(R\) be a retraction, fix \(x\in\mathcal M\), and let \(f\in C^2(\mathcal M)\). If \[\left.\frac{D^2}{dt^2}R_x(t\xi)\right|_{t=0}=0\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in T_x\mathcal M,\] then \[\operatorname{Hess}f(x)=\operatorname{Hess}(f\circ R_x)(0_x),\] where the right-hand side is the Euclidean Hessian on \((T_x\mathcal M,g_x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every radial curve of a retraction has zero initial covariant acceleration at the base point, the Hessian of the retraction pullback at the tangent-space origin equals the Riemannian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)=\operatorname{Hess}(f\circ R_x)(0_x)\).

children.title: Retraction Breakdown Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transitions where domain validity or local accuracy deteriorates.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction Breakdown Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure mechanisms at the boundary of projection- and factorization-based retraction formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constructive retraction formula ceases to be valid where it is no longer smooth and single-valued. For the nearest-point formula \(R_x(\eta)=\pi_{\mathcal M}(x+\eta)\), breakdown occurs when \(x+\eta\) reaches the medial or focal boundary at which the nearest point is nonunique or the projection derivative is singular. For a factorization formula \(R_x(\eta)=q(x+\eta)\), breakdown occurs when the required factorization loses rank, uniqueness, or its normalization convention. Consequently, an algorithm must restrict accepted steps to the connected domain containing \(0_x\) on which the chosen formula remains smooth and uniquely defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection retractions fail at nonunique or singular projections; factorization retractions fail when rank, uniqueness, or smooth normalization is lost.
assumptions_latex: The retraction is defined by projection or a normalized factorization.
Validity requires a smooth single-valued local formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validity boundary is reached when projection or factorization smoothness, uniqueness, or required nonsingularity fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Levi-Civita parallel transport along a prescribed piecewise-smooth curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection \(\nabla\), and let \(\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\) be piecewise smooth. For \(v\in T_{\gamma(0)}\mathcal M\), the parallel transport of \(v\) along \(\gamma\) is
\[
P_\gamma v=V(1),
\]
where \(V\) is the unique vector field along \(\gamma\) satisfying
\[
V(0)=v,
\qquad
\nabla_{\dot\gamma(t)}V(t)=0
\]
on each smooth segment. Metric compatibility implies \(P_\gamma:T_{\gamma(0)}\mathcal M\to T_{\gamma(1)}\mathcal M\) is a linear isometry, and transport along the reversed curve is its inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel transport moves a tangent vector along a curve by zero covariant derivative and preserves inner products and norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\gamma\) is a linear isometry and \(P_{\gamma^{-1}}=P_\gamma^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: Parallel vector field with prescribed initial value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and isometry properties fit Parallel Transport and are standard for the Levi-Civita connection, but source_refs is empty. A specific Riemannian-geometry definition or theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential-map characterization of Lipschitz vector fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes intrinsic Lipschitz continuity on the full domain of the exponential map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq T\mathcal M\) be the domain of \(\operatorname{Exp}\), and let \(P_s\) be parallel transport along \(\gamma(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(ts)\) from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\). A vector field \(V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz continuous if and only if \[\forall (x,s)\in\mathcal O,\qquad \left\|P_s^{-1}V(\operatorname{Exp}_x(s))-V(x)\right\|\le L\|s\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector field is L-Lipschitz exactly when, for every tangent vector in the domain of the exponential map, transporting the field value at the exponential endpoint back to the base point changes it by at most L times the tangent-vector norm.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a vector field on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz}\iff \forall(x,s)\in\mathcal O,\ \|P_s^{-1}V(\operatorname{Exp}_x(s))-V(x)\|\le L\|s\|.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent formulations of Riemannian vector-field Lipschitz continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The geodesic and exponential-map formulations apply to any vector field; the arbitrary-curve and covariant-derivative formulations additionally require continuous differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a vector field \(V\) on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz; (ii) for all same-component \(x,y\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\), \(\|\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{0\leftarrow1}V(y)-V(x)\|\le L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\), where \(\gamma\) is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\); and (iii) for every \((x,s)\) in the domain of \(\operatorname{Exp}\), \(\|P_s^{-1}V(\operatorname{Exp}_x(s))-V(x)\|\le L\|s\|\). If \(V\) is continuously differentiable, these are also equivalent to: (iv) every smooth \(c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\) satisfies \(\|\operatorname{PT}^{c}_{0\leftarrow1}V(c(1))-V(c(0))\|\le L\operatorname{Length}(c)\); and (v) \(\|\nabla_sV\|\le L\|s\|\) for all \((x,s)\in T\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz continuity of a manifold vector field is equivalently expressed by transported differences along short minimizing geodesics or exponential-map curves. For continuously differentiable fields it is also equivalent to a length bound along every smooth curve and to a uniform covariant-derivative bound.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a vector field on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\).
The minimizing-geodesic formulation uses same-component points satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\).
The exponential-map formulation quantifies over the domain of \(\operatorname{Exp}\).
The arbitrary-curve and covariant-derivative formulations additionally assume \(V\in C^1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((i)\iff(ii)\iff(iii))\), and if \(V\in C^1\), then \((i)\iff(ii)\iff(iii)\iff(iv)\iff(v)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic and Metric Properties of Parallel Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the linearity, composition, identity, inverse, and conditionally isometric properties of parallel transport along a curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t_0,t_1,t_2\in I\), parallel transport along a smooth curve \(c:I\to\mathcal M\) is linear and satisfies \(\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_2\leftarrow t_1}\circ\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_1\leftarrow t_0}=\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_2\leftarrow t_0}\), \(\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t\leftarrow t}=\operatorname{Id}\), and \((\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_1\leftarrow t_0})^{-1}=\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_0\leftarrow t_1}\). If \(\mathcal M\) is Riemannian and the connection is metric-compatible, then for all \(u,v\in T_{c(t_0)}\mathcal M\), \(\langle u,v\rangle_{c(t_0)}=\langle\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_1\leftarrow t_0}(u),\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_1\leftarrow t_0}(v)\rangle_{c(t_1)}\), and hence \((\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_1\leftarrow t_0})^*=(\mathrm{PT}^{c}_{t_1\leftarrow t_0})^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel transport is linear, composes along the curve, equals the identity when the endpoints coincide, and is inverted by transport in the reverse direction. With a metric-compatible Riemannian connection, it also preserves inner products, so its adjoint equals its inverse.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal M\text{ is a manifold with a connection}
\mathcal M\text{ is Riemannian and the connection is metric-compatible for the isometry and adjoint claims}
u,v\in T_{c(t_0)}\mathcal M\text{ for the inner-product identity}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Retraction Distance Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exponential retraction satisfies the bound with equality and \(\mu=1\); the condition also holds on compact manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A retraction \(R\) satisfies the local metric-control condition if there exist \(\mu>0\) and \(\delta_\mu>0\) such that, for every \(x\in\mathcal M\) and every \(\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\) with \(\|\xi\|\le\delta_\mu\), \[\|\xi\|\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,R_x(\xi)).\] For the exponential retraction this is an equality with \(\mu=1\), and such a bound is also available when \(\mathcal M\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally, the manifold distance traveled by a retraction must be bounded above by a fixed multiple of the tangent-step norm. The exponential retraction preserves this distance exactly, and compactness also guarantees an appropriate local bound.
assumptions_latex: R:T\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\text{ is a retraction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathcal M\ \forall\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\ (\|\xi\|\le\delta_\mu):\ \|\xi\|\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,R_x\xi)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order Taylor remainder along an exponential curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides a local quadratic function-value error bound from transported gradient variation along one exponential curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R be continuously differentiable, let \gamma(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(ts) be defined for t\in[0,1], and suppose L\ge0 satisfies \|P_{ts}^{-1}\operatorname{grad}f(\gamma(t))-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\le L\|ts\| for every t\in[0,1]. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the gradient transported back along an exponential curve differs from the initial gradient by at most L times the traveled tangent length, then the first-order Taylor error at the curve endpoint is at most L/2 times the squared step norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parallel vector fields and parallel translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines parallel vector fields and parallel translation along a curve, states uniqueness from an initial tangent vector, and records the isometry property for the Riemannian connection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a manifold endowed with an affine connection \(\nabla\), and let \(\gamma\) be a curve. A vector field \(\xi\) along \(\gamma\) is parallel if \(\frac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}\xi=0\). Given \(a\in\operatorname{dom}(\gamma)\) and \(v\in T_{\gamma(a)}\mathcal M\), there is a unique parallel vector field \(\xi\) along \(\gamma\) such that \(\xi(a)=v\). The operator \(P_\gamma^{b\leftarrow a}\) defined by \(P_\gamma^{b\leftarrow a}v=\xi(b)\) is parallel translation along \(\gamma\), and it satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm D}{\mathrm dt}\bigl(P_\gamma^{t\leftarrow a}v\bigr)=0\). If \(\mathcal M\) is Riemannian and \(\nabla\) is the Riemannian connection, then the induced parallel translation is an isometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector field along a curve is parallel when its covariant derivative vanishes. Every initial tangent vector determines a unique parallel vector field, and its value at another point of the curve defines parallel translation. For the Riemannian connection, this translation is an isometry.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a manifold endowed with an affine connection \(\nabla\).
\(\gamma\) is a curve, \(a,b\in\operatorname{dom}(\gamma)\), and \(v\in T_{\gamma(a)}\mathcal M\).
For the isometry property, \(\mathcal M\) is Riemannian and \(\nabla\) is the Riemannian connection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique parallel vector field \(\xi\) along \(\gamma\) with \(\xi(a)=v\); the map \(P_\gamma^{b\leftarrow a}v=\xi(b)\) defines parallel translation and is an isometry when \(\nabla\) is the Riemannian connection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order Riemannian Taylor remainder bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds both the cubic function-value remainder and the quadratic gradient remainder along an exponential curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R be twice continuously differentiable, let \gamma(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(ts) be defined for t\in[0,1], and suppose L\ge0 satisfies \|P_{ts}^{-1}\circ\operatorname{Hess}f(\gamma(t))\circ P_{ts}-\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\|\le L\|ts\| for all t\in[0,1]. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the transported Hessian changes at most linearly along an exponential curve, then the second-order function-value remainder is at most L/6 times the cubed step norm, and the first-order gradient remainder is at most L/2 times the squared step norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz continuity of a tangent-space operator field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses operator norm and conjugation by parallel transport along the unique minimizing geodesic; imposed componentwise when the manifold is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in\mathcal M\), let \(H(x):T_x\mathcal M\to T_x\mathcal M\) be linear. On a connected Riemannian manifold, \(H\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz continuous if, for all \(x,y\in\mathcal M\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\), \[\left\|\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{0\leftarrow1}\circ H(y)\circ\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{1\leftarrow0}-H(x)\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L\operatorname{dist}(x,y),\] where \(\gamma\) is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). On a disconnected manifold, the condition is required on each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent-space operator field is L-Lipschitz when transporting an operator from one point to another by conjugation changes it in operator norm by at most L times the Riemannian distance. The definition is applied separately on each connected component.
assumptions_latex: \(H(x):T_x\mathcal M\to T_x\mathcal M\) is linear for every \(x\in\mathcal M\).
\(x,y\) lie in the same connected component and satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\operatorname{inj}(x)\).
\(\gamma\) is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\).
The norm is the operator norm induced by the Riemannian metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left\|\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{0\leftarrow1}\circ H(y)\circ\operatorname{PT}^{\gamma}_{1\leftarrow0}-H(x)\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuously Differentiable Function on a Riemannian Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The comparison is restricted to distances below the positive injectivity radius, where the minimizing geodesic is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal M,g)\) has injectivity radius \(i(\mathcal M)>0\). A differentiable function \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz continuously differentiable if there exists \(\beta_1\ge0\) such that, for all \(x,y\in\mathcal M\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<i(\mathcal M)\), \[\left\|P_{\alpha}^{0\leftarrow1}\operatorname{grad}f(y)-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\right\|\le\beta_1\operatorname{dist}(x,y),\] where \(\alpha\) is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function on a manifold with positive injectivity radius has a Lipschitz gradient when gradients at sufficiently close points, after parallel transport along their unique minimizing geodesic, differ by at most a constant times the geodesic distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\beta_1\ge0\ \forall x,y\ (\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<i(\mathcal M)):\ \|P_{\alpha}^{0\leftarrow1}\operatorname{grad}f(y)-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\le\beta_1\operatorname{dist}(x,y)

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiated-Retraction Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector transport induced by differentiating a smooth retraction in its tangent argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\colon \mathcal D\subset T\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\) be a smooth retraction, with \(R_x(0_x)=x\) and \(\mathrm D R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\). For \(\eta,\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\) with \(\eta\in\mathcal D\), the differentiated-retraction transport is
\[
\mathcal T^R_\eta(\xi):=\mathrm D R_x(\eta)[\xi]\in T_{R_x(\eta)}\mathcal M.
\]
For each fixed \(\eta\), this map is linear in \(\xi\), and \(\mathcal T^R_{0_x}=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\). It need not be isometric or invertible when \(\eta\neq0_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiating a retraction at a tangent step produces a linear map from the original tangent space to the tangent space at the retracted point.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a smooth retraction on \(\mathcal D\subset T\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T^R_\eta=\mathrm D R_x(\eta)\) is a transport with \(\mathcal T^R_{0_x}=\operatorname{id}\).

notation.meaning: restriction of the retraction to the fiber at x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition obtained by differentiating a retraction fiber map

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector transport by differentiated retraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transport obtained from the differential of a retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a retraction on \(\mathcal M\). Define \[\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\xi_x):=DR_x(\eta_x)[\xi_x]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}R_x(\eta_x+t\xi_x)\right|_{t=0}.\] Then \(\mathcal T\) is a vector transport associated with \(R\). In particular, \(DR_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\) implies \(\mathcal T_{0_x}(\xi_x)=\xi_x\), and \[\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\eta_x)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}R_x(t\eta_x)\right|_{t=1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiating a retraction at a displacement transports tangent vectors to the tangent space at the retracted point. The transport is the identity at zero, and self-transport equals the retraction-curve velocity at time one.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a smooth retraction on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T_{\eta_x}=DR_x(\eta_x)\) is a vector transport associated with \(R\), with \(\mathcal T_{0_x}=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\) and \(\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\eta_x)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}R_x(t\eta_x)\right|_{t=1}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric conjugate-gradient iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic recurrence only; the choices of step size and conjugacy coefficient, stopping conditions, and convergence guarantees are unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a Riemannian manifold, let \(R\) be a retraction, let \(\mathcal T\) be an associated vector transport, let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), and choose \(x_0\in\mathcal M\). For each \(k\ge 0\), compute \(\alpha_k\) and set \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\alpha_k\eta_k)\); then compute \(\beta_{k+1}\) and set \(\eta_{k+1}=-\operatorname{grad}f(x_{k+1})+\beta_{k+1}\mathcal T_{\alpha_k\eta_k}(\eta_k)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General vector transport associated with a retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector transport on a manifold \(\mathcal M\) is a smooth map \(\mathcal T:T\mathcal M\oplus T\mathcal M\to T\mathcal M\), \((\eta_x,\xi_x)\mapsto\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\xi_x)\), for which there is a retraction \(R\) satisfying \(\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\xi_x)\in T_{R_x(\eta_x)}\mathcal M\), \(\mathcal T_{0_x}(\xi_x)=\xi_x\), and \(\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(a\xi_x+b\zeta_x)=a\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\xi_x)+b\mathcal T_{\eta_x}(\zeta_x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\), \(\eta_x,\xi_x,\zeta_x\in T_x\mathcal M\), and scalars \(a,b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector transport is a smooth, fiberwise-linear mechanism that moves tangent vectors from the tangent space at x to the tangent space at the retracted point R_x(eta), and it reduces to the identity when the displacement is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(R:T\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\) is the retraction associated with \(\mathcal T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T_{\eta_x}:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{R_x(\eta_x)}\mathcal M\) is linear and \(\mathcal T_{0_x}=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\).

children.title: Isometric Vector Transports

knowledge_statements.title: Isometric Vector Transports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-preserving transport along a retraction step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold, \(R\) a retraction, and \(\mathcal T_\eta\colon T_x\mathcal M\to T_{R_x(\eta)}\mathcal M\) a vector transport. The transport is isometric when, for every admissible \(x\), \(\eta\), and \(\xi,\zeta\in T_x\mathcal M\),
\[
g_{R_x(\eta)}\!\left(\mathcal T_\eta\xi,\mathcal T_\eta\zeta\right)=g_x(\xi,\zeta).
\]
Equivalently, \(\mathcal T_\eta^*\mathcal T_\eta=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\). Consequently, it preserves tangent-vector norms and angles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isometric vector transport preserves inner products, and hence norms and angles, between tangent vectors transported along the same step.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is a vector transport associated with \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{R_x(\eta)}(\mathcal T_\eta\xi,\mathcal T_\eta\zeta)=g_x(\xi,\zeta)\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian inner product on the tangent space at x
metric adjoint of the transport map

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Vector Transports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-capped scaling of a base transport used in line-search and conjugate-gradient methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a vector transport \(\mathcal T\), define the scaled transport rule for \(\eta,\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\) by
\[
\mathcal T^{\mathrm S}_\eta(\xi)=s(\eta,\xi)\mathcal T_\eta(\xi),\qquad
s(\eta,\xi)=\begin{cases}
\min\!\left\{1,\dfrac{\|\xi\|_x}{\|\mathcal T_\eta(\xi)\|_{R_x(\eta)}}\right\},&\mathcal T_\eta(\xi)\neq0,\\
1,&\mathcal T_\eta(\xi)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\|\mathcal T^{\mathrm S}_\eta(\xi)\|_{R_x(\eta)}\leq\|\xi\|_x\). Because the scale may depend on \(\xi\), this rule generally fails linearity and is not necessarily a vector transport in the strict axiomatic sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base transport can be rescaled to prevent norm growth, although direction-dependent scaling generally destroys linearity in the transported vector.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is defined along the retraction \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\mathcal T^{\mathrm S}_\eta(\xi)\|_{R_x(\eta)}\leq\|\xi\|_x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm cap is algebraically valid and the representation kind fits, but scaled-transport conventions vary and the exact nonlinear rule requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Transport Norm-Distortion Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Transport Norm-Distortion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform multiplicative bounds on tangent-vector norm distortion over an admissible step region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal T\) be a vector transport along a retraction \(R\), and let \(\Omega\subset T\mathcal M\) be an admissible step set. A two-sided norm-distortion regime with constants \(0<m\leq M<\infty\) means
\[
m\|\xi\|_x\leq\|\mathcal T_\eta\xi\|_{R_x(\eta)}\leq M\|\xi\|_x
\]
for every \((x,\eta)\in\Omega\) and \(\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\). The upper bound gives uniform boundedness; the lower bound gives injectivity and bounded inverse on the range. The isometric regime is \(m=M=1\), while a nonexpansive regime requires only the upper bound with \(M=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transport distortion is controlled by uniform lower and upper norm ratios; isometric and nonexpansive transports are special regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T_\eta\) is linear for each admissible step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m\|\xi\|_x\leq\|\mathcal T_\eta\xi\|_{R_x(\eta)}\leq M\|\xi\|_x\) uniformly on \(\Omega\).

notation.meaning: admissible set of base points and tangent steps

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard operator norm and minimum-gain bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided distortion condition and its consequences are coherent, but no source supports this precise regime formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Retraction Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local comparison between a forward retraction step and the reverse displacement at its endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a smooth retraction and \(\mathcal T\) a smooth vector transport along \(R\). For \(y=R_x(\eta)\) sufficiently near \(x\), assume the local inverse \(R_y^{-1}(x)\in T_y\mathcal M\) exists. As \(\eta\to0_x\),
\[
R_y^{-1}(x)=-\mathcal T_\eta\eta+O(\|\eta\|_x^2),
\]
where the remainder is measured in \(T_y\mathcal M\), uniformly on compact coordinate neighborhoods. Thus the reverse inverse-retraction displacement agrees to first order with the negative transported forward step. A higher-order comparison requires additional compatibility between \(R\) and \(\mathcal T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally, the reverse inverse-retraction displacement equals the negative transported forward step up to a quadratic error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{R_x(\eta)}^{-1}(x)=-\mathcal T_\eta\eta+O(\|\eta\|_x^2)\).

notation.meaning: local inverse-retraction displacement from y to x
tangent-vector remainder bounded quadratically in the step norm

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order consistency of smooth retractions and transports

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The first-order comparison is plausible, but the required local inverse, tangent-space identification, uniformity, and compatibility hypotheses need a precise source.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport Compatibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes transport axioms from invertibility and metric-compatibility properties needed by stronger comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The basic vector-transport axioms require that \(\mathcal T_\eta\colon T_x\mathcal M\to T_{R_x(\eta)}\mathcal M\) be linear in its transported argument and satisfy \(\mathcal T_{0_x}=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\). These axioms do not imply that \(\mathcal T_\eta\) is invertible, isometric, or equal to parallel transport. In particular, the differentiated-retraction transport \(\mathrm D R_x(\eta)\) becomes noninvertible wherever the fiber map \(R_x\) has a critical point. Consequently, inverse-transport identities and two-sided norm comparisons are valid only inside regions where an appropriate nonsingularity or lower-distortion condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector-transport axioms alone do not guarantee invertibility or metric preservation; inverse comparisons fail when the retraction differential becomes singular.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) satisfies only the basic vector-transport axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T_{0_x}=\operatorname{id}\) does not imply invertibility or isometry for \(\eta\neq0_x\).

notation.meaning: differential of the retraction fiber map

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identity at the zero step imposes no global nonsingularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is appropriate and the singular-differential observation is sound, but the exact vector-transport axioms and resulting boundary claims lack a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension-independent first-order complexity of Riemannian gradient descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient convergence and worst-case stationarity complexity for the constant step \(1/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be smooth on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\) and bounded below by \(f_{\mathrm{low}}\). Suppose a retraction \(R\) and a set \(S\subseteq T\mathcal M\) satisfy \[f(R_x(s))\le f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),s\rangle+\frac L2\lVert s\rVert^2\quad\forall(x,s)\in S.\] If retraction-based gradient descent uses \(\alpha_k=1/L\) and every generated \((x_k,s_k)\) lies in \(S\), then \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert=0.\] Moreover, for every integer \(K\ge1\), some \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\) satisfies \[\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert\le\sqrt{\frac{2L(f(x_0)-f_{\mathrm{low}})}{K}}.\] Hence an iterate with gradient norm at most \(\varepsilon>0\) occurs among the first \(K\) iterates whenever \[K\ge\frac{2L(f(x_0)-f_{\mathrm{low}})}{\varepsilon^2}.\] This bound is independent of \(\dim\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-bounded smooth objective satisfying the quadratic retraction-pullback bound, Riemannian gradient descent with step 1/L has gradients converging to zero and reaches epsilon first-order stationarity within 2L times the initial objective gap divided by epsilon squared iterations, independently of manifold dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{k\to\infty}\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert=0,\qquad \min_{0\le k<K}\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert\le\sqrt{\frac{2L(f(x_0)-f_{\mathrm{low}})}{K}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient decrease for bounded Riemannian gradient step sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient decrease for retraction-based gradient descent under a quadratic pullback upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be smooth on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), let \(R\) be a retraction, and suppose that for some \(S\subseteq T\mathcal M\) and \(L>0\), \[f(R_x(s))\le f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),s\rangle+\frac L2\lVert s\rVert^2\quad\forall(x,s)\in S.\] If retraction-based gradient descent generates \(s_k=-\alpha_k\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\), \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(s_k)\), with every \((x_k,s_k)\in S\) and \(\alpha_k\in[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\subset(0,2/L)\), then \[f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge c\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert^2,\] where \[c=\min\left\{\alpha_{\min}-\frac L2\alpha_{\min}^2,\;\alpha_{\max}-\frac L2\alpha_{\max}^2\right\}>0.\] For \(\alpha_k=1/L\), one may take \(c=1/(2L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the quadratic retraction-pullback bound, gradient steps whose sizes remain in a fixed interval strictly inside (0, 2/L) produce uniform sufficient decrease. The constant step 1/L gives decrease constant 1/(2L).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge c\lVert\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\rVert^2,\quad c=\min\left\{\alpha_{\min}-\frac L2\alpha_{\min}^2,\alpha_{\max}-\frac L2\alpha_{\max}^2\right\}>0

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Smoothness Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic upper model along minimizing geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a geodesically convex subset of a Riemannian manifold and let \(f\colon U\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. The function is geodesically \(L\)-smooth on \(U\) when, for every \(x\in U\) and every \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\) such that \(\gamma(t)=\exp_x(t\eta)\) remains in \(U\) for \(0\leq t\leq1\),
\[
f(\exp_x\eta)\leq f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x+\frac L2\|\eta\|_x^2.
\]
This is an intrinsic descent model along geodesics and does not by itself assert geodesic convexity of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geodesic smoothness bounds function growth along each admissible geodesic by the tangent linearization plus a quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\exp_x\eta)\leq f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x+\tfrac L2\|\eta\|_x^2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: intrinsic quadratic upper model along exponential-map curves

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic geodesic upper model fits the leaf, but terminology for geodesic L-smoothness varies and no source identifies this precise convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction-Pullback Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic smoothness model for objective pullbacks to tangent spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a retraction and define the pullback \(\widehat f_x=f\circ R_x\) on an admissible subset of \(T_x\mathcal M\). The objective has retraction-pullback \(L\)-smoothness on a set \(\Omega\subset T\mathcal M\) when, for every \((x,\eta)\in\Omega\),
\[
\widehat f_x(\eta)\leq \widehat f_x(0_x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x+\frac L2\|\eta\|_x^2.
\]
The linear term is valid because \(\mathrm D R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\), so \(\nabla\widehat f_x(0_x)=\operatorname{grad}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pullback smoothness imposes a uniform quadratic upper model after expressing the objective in tangent coordinates through a retraction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable wherever the pullbacks are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(R_x(\eta))\leq f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x+\tfrac L2\|\eta\|_x^2\).

notation.meaning: pullback of f to the tangent space at x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard tangent-space pullback upper model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pullback model and zero-step gradient identity are standard, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the stated uniform condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Hessian-Regular Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel-transport Lipschitz regularity of the Riemannian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be geodesically convex and let \(f\colon U\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. Its Riemannian Hessian is \(\rho\)-Lipschitz on \(U\) when every \(x,y\in U\), joined by the unique minimizing geodesic in \(U\), satisfy
\[
\left\|\operatorname{Hess}f(y)-P_{x\to y}\operatorname{Hess}f(x)P_{y\to x}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq \rho\,d(x,y).
\]
Here parallel transport identifies the two tangent spaces before the operators are compared. The regime controls variation of curvature of \(f\), not merely the magnitude of its Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hessian regularity means that Hessians, after parallel-transport identification, vary at most linearly with geodesic distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\operatorname{Hess}f(y)-P_{x\to y}\operatorname{Hess}f(x)P_{y\to x}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\rho d(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: parallel transport along the selected minimizing geodesic
operator norm induced by the Riemannian metric

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Lipschitz Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel-transport Lipschitz continuity of the Riemannian gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be geodesically convex and let \(f\colon U\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Its Riemannian gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(U\) when every \(x,y\in U\), joined by the unique minimizing geodesic in \(U\), satisfy
\[
\left\|\operatorname{grad}f(y)-P_{x\to y}\operatorname{grad}f(x)\right\|_y\leq Ld(x,y).
\]
Equivalently, one may transport the gradient at \(y\) back to \(T_x\mathcal M\). For twice differentiable \(f\), a uniform bound \(\|\operatorname{Hess}f\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L\) implies this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian gradient is Lipschitz when parallel-transported gradients differ by at most a constant times geodesic distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\operatorname{grad}f(y)-P_{x\to y}\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_y\leq Ld(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: parallel transport along the selected minimizing geodesic

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: intrinsic gradient Lipschitz condition under parallel transport

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Implication Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient Lipschitzness does not imply Lipschitz continuity of the Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(0<\alpha<1\) and consider the Euclidean manifold \(\mathbb R\) with
\[
f(t)=|t|^{2+\alpha}.
\]
On every bounded interval, \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable and its gradient is Lipschitz because
\[
f''(t)=(2+\alpha)(1+\alpha)|t|^\alpha
\]
is bounded there. However, the Hessian is not Lipschitz near zero, since
\[
\frac{|f''(t)-f''(0)|}{|t|}=(2+\alpha)(1+\alpha)|t|^{\alpha-1}\to\infty.
\]
Thus gradient-Lipschitz regularity, equivalently bounded Hessian in this setting, does not imply a Hessian-Lipschitz regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function |t|^(2+α) has Lipschitz gradient on bounded intervals but a Hessian that is not Lipschitz at zero.
assumptions_latex: The domain is a bounded interval containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz, but \(f''\) is not Lipschitz near \(0\).

notation.meaning: fixed Hölder exponent between zero and one

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: directly checkable one-dimensional regularity counterexample

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-to-Global Characterization with a Uniform Lipschitz Constant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The same constant must hold on every local neighborhood; the equivalence is stated under the source's standing Riemannian-manifold assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) and \(B>0\), \[|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|\le B\,d(x_1,x_2)\qquad\forall x_1,x_2\in M\] if and only if, for every \(x\in M\), there exists a neighborhood \(U_x\) such that \[|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|\le B\,d(x_1,x_2)\qquad\forall x_1,x_2\in U_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is globally B-Lipschitz exactly when every point has a neighborhood on which that same constant B applies.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Dependent Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rauch-type distortion bounds for the exponential-map differential under sectional-curvature control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) have sectional curvatures satisfying \(|K|\leq\kappa\) on the geodesic ball traversed by \(t\mapsto\exp_x(t\eta)\), and set \(r=\|\eta\|_x\). If \(\kappa>0\), assume \(r<\pi/\sqrt\kappa\). For every \(\xi\perp\eta\), Rauch comparison gives
\[
\frac{\sin(\sqrt\kappa r)}{\sqrt\kappa r}\|\xi\|_x
\leq\|\mathrm D\exp_x(\eta)[\xi]\|_{\exp_x\eta}
\leq
\frac{\sinh(\sqrt\kappa r)}{\sqrt\kappa r}\|\xi\|_x.
\]
Both factors equal \(1+O(\kappa r^2)\) as \(r\to0\), quantifying curvature-induced distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded sectional curvature controls exponential-map distortion through sine and hyperbolic-sine comparison factors, giving quadratic small-step distortion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\mathrm D\exp_x(\eta)[\xi]\|/\|\xi\|=1+O(\kappa r^2)\) as \(r\to0\).

notation.meaning: length of the radial tangent step

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Rauch comparison bounds for transverse Jacobi fields

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed comparison needs a precise Rauch theorem locator and verified curvature-domain hypotheses. As written, the displayed factors are also undefined when kappa equals zero unless their continuous-extension convention is stated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positivity and Global Existence for a Riccati-Type Metric Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion concerns the solution of the displayed nonlinear Cauchy problem for a time-dependent covariant two-tensor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((M,g_0)\) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let \(a,q\) be \((0,2)\)-tensor fields on \(M\), and suppose that \(q\) is symmetric and positive definite. If \(g(t)\) solves
\[\partial_t g+{}^Ta\,g_0^{-1}(g-g_0)+(g-g_0)g_0^{-1}a+(g-g_0)g_0^{-1}(g-g_0)=q,\qquad g(0)=2g_0,\]
then \(g(t)-g_0\) is positive semidefinite, and \(g(t)\) is a Riemannian metric on \(M\) defined for every \(t\in[t_0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated Riccati-type tensor Cauchy problem with positive-definite forcing and initial metric twice the reference metric, the solution stays above the reference metric in the semidefinite order and remains a globally defined Riemannian metric in forward time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(t)-g_0\succeq0\quad\text{and}\quad \forall t\in[t_0,\infty),\ g(t)\text{ is a Riemannian metric on }M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient orthogonality and steepest ascent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise geometric characterization under the absence of critical points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^\infty(M)\) have no critical points on the Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\). Then every level set of \(f\) is locally a hypersurface and \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\) is orthogonal to its tangent space. Moreover, for every \(x\in M\), \(df_x(v)=g_x(\operatorname{grad}f(x),v)\le \|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\) for every unit vector \(v\in T_xM\), with equality at \(v=\operatorname{grad}f(x)/\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\); hence the gradient gives the direction and orientation of steepest increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a smooth function has no critical points, its gradient is normal to each level hypersurface and its normalized gradient is the unit direction of greatest instantaneous increase.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{grad}f(x)\perp T_xf^{-1}(f(x)),\qquad \max_{\|v\|=1}df_x(v)=\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper-Function Characterization of Riemannian Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization by a proper smooth function with controlled gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is complete if and only if there exists a proper $C^\infty$ function $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $g-df\otimes df$ is positive definite. Equivalently, $(M,g)$ is complete if and only if it admits a proper $C^\infty$ function whose $g$-gradient has bounded length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian manifold is complete exactly when it admits a proper smooth function for which g minus df tensor df is positive definite; equivalently, it admits a proper smooth function with bounded gradient length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (M,g)\text{ is complete}\iff\exists f\in C^\infty(M)\text{ proper}:g-df\otimes df\succ0\iff\exists h\in C^\infty(M)\text{ proper}:\sup_{x\in M}\|\nabla h(x)\|_g<\infty.

children.title: Induced Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metrics inherited from an ambient geometric representation.

assumptions_latex: \(M\subset E\) is a smooth embedded manifold of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \((E,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_x=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_E|_{T_xM\times T_xM}\) for every \(x\in M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient Euclidean metric restricted to an embedded manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The metric induced on \(M\) by the ambient inner product is the smooth field \(g\) defined, for every \(x\in M\) and \(\xi,\eta\in T_xM\), by \[g_x(\xi,\eta)=\langle\xi,\eta\rangle_E.\] Thus each tangent space inherits its norm from \(E\), and the Riemannian gradient of a smooth function \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is characterized by \(g_x(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi)=Df(x)[\xi]\) for all \(\xi\in T_xM\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An induced metric measures tangent vectors using the inner product of the ambient space containing the manifold.
knowledge_statements.title: Induced Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The induced-metric definition and gradient characterization are mathematically standard and fit the container, but no citation or inspectable locator supports them.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient Euclidean Metric Induces a Riemannian Metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric induced on an embedded submanifold by restriction of the ambient Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be an embedded submanifold of a Euclidean space \((\mathcal E,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\). For each \(x\in\mathcal M\), define \(\langle u,v\rangle_x=\langle u,v\rangle\) for all \(u,v\in T_x\mathcal M\). Then \(\{\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_x\}_{x\in\mathcal M}\) is a Riemannian metric on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the ambient Euclidean inner product to each tangent space of an embedded submanifold yields a Riemannian metric.

\mathcal E\text{ is a Euclidean space with inner product }\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle u,v\rangle_x:=\langle u,v\rangle\quad(u,v\in T_x\mathcal M)\text{ defines a Riemannian metric on }\mathcal M.

assumptions_latex: \(M=G/H\) is a reductive homogeneous space with Lie-algebra decomposition \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak m\).
\(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathfrak m}\) is an \(\operatorname{Ad}(H)\)-invariant inner product selected by the homogeneous-space structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{aH}(dL_a\xi,dL_a\eta)=\langle\xi,\eta\rangle_{\mathfrak m}\) defines the canonical homogeneous metric.

notation.meaning: Reductive complement identified with the tangent space at the identity coset
Left action by an element of the group

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical metric in the reductive homogeneous-space sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Identify \(T_{eH}M\) with \(\mathfrak m\). The canonical homogeneous metric associated with the selected inner product is the unique \(G\)-invariant Riemannian metric \(g\) satisfying, for every \(a\in G\) and \(\xi,\eta\in\mathfrak m\), \[g_{aH}(dL_a\xi,dL_a\eta)=\langle\xi,\eta\rangle_{\mathfrak m}.\] The \(\operatorname{Ad}(H)\)-invariance makes this value independent of the representative of \(aH\). Here “canonical” refers to the distinguished reductive inner product chosen by the manifold model, not to an arbitrary ambient induced metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical homogeneous metric transports a distinguished isotropy-invariant inner product from the identity coset to every tangent space.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction correctly describes the invariant metric determined by an Ad(H)-invariant inner product, but calling that selected inner product and metric canonical is convention-dependent and requires a source specific to the intended homogeneous-space model.

children.title: Invariant Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metrics preserved by designated symmetry actions.

assumptions_latex: A Lie group \(G\) acts smoothly and transitively on a manifold \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is \(G\)-invariant exactly when \(g_{a\cdot x}(d\Phi_a\xi,d\Phi_a\eta)=g_x(\xi,\eta)\).

notation.meaning: Action map associated with a group element

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric invariance under a transitive smooth group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Riemannian metric \(g\) on \(M\) is \(G\)-invariant if every action map \(\Phi_a:M\to M\) is an isometry. Equivalently, for all \(a\in G\), \(x\in M\), and \(\xi,\eta\in T_xM\), \[g_{a\cdot x}\bigl(d\Phi_a(x)[\xi],d\Phi_a(x)[\eta]\bigr)=g_x(\xi,\eta).\] For a transitive action, such a metric is determined by its inner product at one base point, subject to invariance under that point's isotropy subgroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant metric is unchanged when tangent vectors are transported by the specified group action.
knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariance identity and isotropy characterization are standard and appropriate, but the record supplies no supporting source with a specific locator.

children.title: Metric-Family Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural differences in geometry or conditioning across the metric families.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Family Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform comparison of two metrics on the same manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated two-sided bound, the metrics \(g\) and \(h\) are uniformly equivalent. For every \(x\in M\) and \(\xi\in T_xM\), \[\sqrt m\,\|\xi\|_{g,x}\leq \|\xi\|_{h,x}\leq \sqrt L\,\|\xi\|_{g,x}.\] Thus \(L/m\) is an upper bound on their worst relative squared-norm anisotropy; it is the exact relative metric condition number when \(m\) and \(L\) are the optimal uniform comparison constants. On a compact manifold, any two smooth Riemannian metrics admit positive constants satisfying such a comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly equivalent metrics give comparable tangent norms. The ratio of chosen comparison constants bounds their relative anisotropy and is exact when those constants are optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are Riemannian metrics on the same manifold \(M\).
There exist constants \(0<m\leq L<\infty\) such that \(m g_x(\xi,\xi)\leq h_x(\xi,\xi)\leq L g_x(\xi,\xi)\) for every \(x\in M\) and \(\xi\in T_xM\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt m\,\|\xi\|_{g,x}\leq\|\xi\|_{h,x}\leq\sqrt L\,\|\xi\|_{g,x}\), and \(L/m\) bounds the relative metric condition number.

assumptions_latex: \(P_x:T_xM\to T_xM\) is a smooth field of \(g_x\)-self-adjoint positive-definite linear maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_x(\xi,\eta)=g_x(P_x\xi,\eta)\) is a Riemannian metric and \(\operatorname{grad}_h f=P^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_g f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator representation of smooth problem-adapted metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h\) by \[h_x(\xi,\eta)=g_x(P_x\xi,\eta),\qquad \xi,\eta\in T_xM.\] Smoothness, self-adjointness, and positive definiteness of \(P_x\) make \(h\) a Riemannian metric. For every smooth \(f:M\to\mathbb R\), the gradient identity \[\operatorname{grad}_h f(x)=P_x^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_g f(x)\] follows from the defining gradient pairing. Choosing \(P_x\) to approximate a positive-definite curvature operator yields a problem-adapted metric whose gradient direction acts as intrinsic preconditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem-adapted metric inserts a smooth positive-definite operator into a baseline metric, thereby preconditioning the Riemannian gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Adapted Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operator representation and gradient transformation are correct and fit Problem-Adapted Metrics. The curvature-approximation interpretation is nontrivial and lacks a supporting Riemannian-preconditioning source and locator.

assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\bar M\to M=\bar M/G\) is a smooth quotient by a free proper action, with vertical space \(\mathcal V_{\bar x}=\ker d\pi_{\bar x}\).
\(\bar g\) is a \(G\)-invariant Riemannian metric on \(\bar M\), and \(\mathcal H_{\bar x}=\mathcal V_{\bar x}^{\perp_{\bar g}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\pi(\bar x)}(d\pi\bar\xi,d\pi\bar\eta)=\bar g_{\bar x}(\bar\xi,\bar\eta)\) defines the quotient metric for horizontal lifts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioning metric descending from an invariant total-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=\pi(\bar x)\) and \(\xi,\eta\in T_xM\), let \(\bar\xi,\bar\eta\in\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) be their unique horizontal lifts. The quotient metric is \[g_x(\xi,\eta)=\bar g_{\bar x}(\bar\xi,\bar\eta).\] Invariance of \(\bar g\) makes this definition independent of the representative \(\bar x\). If \(\bar g_{\bar x}(u,v)=\bar g^0_{\bar x}(P_{\bar x}u,v)\), then quotient-metric preconditioning is valid when \(P\) is smooth, positive definite, and equivariant under the group action, so that the metric descends consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant positive-definite metric on a quotient's total space preconditions the quotient geometry through horizontal lifts.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Metric Preconditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The horizontal-lift representation fits quotient-metric preconditioning, but the metric-descent and equivariance conditions need an authoritative quotient-geometry citation with a precise locator.

assumptions_latex: At a critical point \(x_\star\), the Riemannian Hessian under \(g\) is represented by a positive-definite operator \(H_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adapted local curvature operator is \(P_{x_\star}^{-1}H_\star\); ideal conditioning competes with the cost of applying \(P_x^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: Baseline Hessian operator at the critical point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local spectral benefit versus per-iteration metric cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x_\star\), changing from \(g\) to \(h\) represents local curvature by \(P_{x_\star}^{-1}H_\star\). A preconditioner spectrally close to \(H_\star\) can reduce \(\kappa(P_{x_\star}^{-1}H_\star)\), improving the local scaling of gradient-based steps. This benefit must be compared with the work and storage required to form or apply \(P_x^{-1}\), compute metric-dependent projections, and maintain smoothness or invariance constraints. Thus the useful metric minimizes total computational effort, not necessarily the spectral condition number alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger metric preconditioner can improve local curvature conditioning but may increase inverse, projection, storage, and construction costs per iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Conditioning Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local preconditioned-curvature claim is plausible at a critical point and the principle fits the container, but neither the Hessian transformation nor the algorithmic cost tradeoff has cited support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oblique manifold as a product of spheres
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and standard matrix representations of an oblique manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A product of \(k\) spheres is called an oblique manifold. In particular, \(\mathrm{OB}(d,k)=(\mathrm S^{d-1})^k\), and its elements can be represented by matrices in \(\mathbb R^{d\times k}\) whose columns have unit norm, or equivalently by transposed matrices whose rows have unit norm. An analogous construction applies to complex matrices. The complex unit circle \(\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}\) is an alternative representation of \(\mathrm S^1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oblique manifold is a product of spheres. OB(d,k) is the product of k unit spheres in R^d and is commonly represented by matrices with unit-norm columns, or after transposition, unit-norm rows. The analogous complex construction includes the unit-modulus complex circle as a representation of S¹.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm S^{d-1}\) is the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{OB}(d,k)=(\mathrm S^{d-1})^k\cong\{X\in\mathbb R^{d\times k}:\|X_{:j}\|=1\ \forall j\}\), with analogous row-wise and complex representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded-sphere model with the induced Euclidean metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb S^{n-1}\), the tangent space and orthogonal tangent projection are \[T_x\mathbb S^{n-1}=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^n:x^\top\xi=0\},\qquad P_x=I-xx^\top.\] Hence the Riemannian gradient of the restriction of \(f\) is \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla f(x)\). A feasible retraction is \[R_x(\xi)=\frac{x+\xi}{\|x+\xi\|_2},\] defined whenever \(x+\xi\neq0\); it satisfies \(R_x(0)=x\) and \(DR_x(0)\) equal to the identity on \(T_x\mathbb S^{n-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sphere optimization projects the ambient gradient onto the hyperplane orthogonal to the current unit vector and may retract by normalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and differential calculus of the unit sphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space, retraction, projection, and Riemannian-gradient formulas for the unit sphere with its induced metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E\) be a \(d\)-dimensional Euclidean space and \(\mathrm S^{d-1}=\{x\in\mathcal E:\|x\|=1\}\). For \(x\in\mathrm S^{d-1}\), \(\mathrm T_x\mathrm S^{d-1}=\{v\in\mathcal E:\langle x,v\rangle=0\}\) and \(\dim\mathrm S^{d-1}=d-1\). For \(v\in\mathrm T_x\mathrm S^{d-1}\), \(R_x(v)=(x+v)/\|x+v\|=(x+v)/\sqrt{1+\|v\|^2}\) is a retraction. The orthogonal tangent projector is \(\operatorname{Proj}_x(u)=u-\langle x,u\rangle x\). If \(f:\mathrm S^{d-1}\to\mathbb R\) is smooth and \(\bar f\) is a smooth extension to a neighborhood of the sphere, then \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=\operatorname{Proj}_x(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(x))\); consequently, \(x\) is critical for \(f\) if and only if \(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(x)\) is parallel to \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the unit sphere, the tangent space at x is the orthogonal complement of x. Normalization defines a retraction, orthogonal projection removes the component parallel to x, and applying that projection to the gradient of a smooth ambient extension gives the Riemannian gradient. A point is critical exactly when its ambient gradient is parallel to the point.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\) is a \(d\)-dimensional Euclidean space with \(d\geq 1\).
\(v\in\mathrm T_x\mathrm S^{d-1}\) for the retraction formula.
The sphere carries the metric induced by \(\mathcal E\).
\(f:\mathrm S^{d-1}\to\mathbb R\) is smooth and has a smooth extension \(\bar f\) to a neighborhood of the sphere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm T_x\mathrm S^{d-1}=x^\perp\), \(\dim\mathrm S^{d-1}=d-1\), \(R_x(v)=\frac{x+v}{\sqrt{1+\|v\|^2}}\), \(\operatorname{Proj}_x(u)=u-\langle x,u\rangle x\), and \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=\operatorname{Proj}_x(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(x))\), with \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\iff\operatorname{grad}\bar f(x)\parallel x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Great-Circle Descent Algorithm on the Sphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sphere-specific descent iteration using a tangent descent direction and stationary-point line search along a great circle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subset\mathbb{R}^3 be the sphere, let f:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R} be C^2, and let f_S=f|_S. Starting from M_1\in S, at iteration i choose X_i\in T_{M_i}S with df_S(M_i)[X_i]<0. Along the stated great-circle parameterization \gamma_i(t)=M_i\cos t+X_i\sin t, define \varphi_i(t)=f(\gamma_i(t)) for t\ge 0. Choose t_i as the smallest strictly positive solution of \varphi_i'(t)=0 for which \varphi_i(t_i) is a minimum, set M_{i+1}=M_i\cos t_i+X_i\sin t_i, and repeat until the prescribed convergence criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable function restricted to a sphere, start from a point on the sphere, choose a tangent direction having negative directional derivative, search along its stated great-circle curve for the first positive stationary minimizer, update to that point, and repeat until the convergence test is met.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t_i=\min\{t>0:\varphi_i'(t)=0\text{ and }\varphi_i(t)\text{ is a minimum}\},\qquad M_{i+1}=M_i\cos t_i+X_i\sin t_i.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The oblique manifold is the product of \(p\) copies of \(\mathbb S^{n-1}\), represented columnwise. At \(X\in\operatorname{Ob}(n,p)\), \[T_X\operatorname{Ob}(n,p)=\{Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}:\operatorname{diag}(X^\top Z)=0\}.\] Under the Frobenius metric, the orthogonal tangent projection is \[\Pi_X(Z)=Z-X\operatorname{Diag}(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top Z)).\] Thus, for a smooth ambient extension of \(f\), \(\operatorname{grad}f(X)=\Pi_X(\nabla f(X))\); a retraction is obtained by normalizing every nonzero column of \(X+Z\).

assumptions_latex: \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k\mathbb S^{n_i-1}\) carries the product of induced Euclidean metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_xM=\prod_i\{\xi_i:x_i^\top\xi_i=0\}\), and gradients, projections, and componentwise retractions decompose by factor.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite product of possibly different-dimensional unit spheres.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M\), \[T_xM=\prod_{i=1}^k\{\xi_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}:x_i^\top\xi_i=0\},\qquad g_x(\xi,\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^k\xi_i^\top\eta_i.\] The orthogonal projection of an ambient vector \(z=(z_i)\) has components \(z_i-x_i(x_i^\top z_i)\). Consequently, the Riemannian gradient is obtained by factorwise projection. Any collection of sphere retractions \(R^{(i)}\) defines the product retraction \(R_x(\xi)=(R^{(1)}_{x_1}(\xi_1),\ldots,R^{(k)}_{x_k}(\xi_k))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical points of the Brockett cost function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the stationarity equations and preserves the invertibility and distinct-weight boundaries needed for the invariant-subspace and eigenvector conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=A^{T}\), \(N=\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_p)\), and \(f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X^{T}AXN)\) on \(\operatorname{St}(p,n)\). Then \[\operatorname{grad}f(X)=2(I-XX^{T})AXN+X[X^{T}AX,N],\] and \[\operatorname{grad}f(X)=0\iff (I-XX^{T})AXN=0\quad\text{and}\quad[X^{T}AX,N]=0.\] If \(N\) is invertible, these conditions are equivalent to \(\operatorname{span}(X)\) being \(A\)-invariant and \(X^{T}AX\) commuting with \(N\). If, additionally, the \(\mu_i\) are pairwise distinct, criticality is equivalent to the columns of \(X\) being eigenvectors of \(A\). For \(p=n\), the invariant-subspace condition is automatic; with invertible pairwise-distinct weights, the critical points are orthogonal matrices that diagonalize \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Criticality is equivalent to the projected-gradient and commutator equations. Invertible weights yield an A-invariant column space, while the stronger conclusion that every column is an eigenvector requires the weights also to be pairwise distinct. In the square case the invariant-subspace condition is automatic.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ invertible for the invariant-subspace equivalence}
\mu_i\neq\mu_j\text{ for }i\neq j\text{, in addition to invertibility, for the eigenvector-column equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{grad}f(X)=0\iff (I-XX^{T})AXN=0\ \text{and}\ [X^{T}AX,N]=0;\quad N\text{ invertible with pairwise-distinct diagonal entries}\implies\bigl(\operatorname{grad}f(X)=0\iff\text{the columns of }X\text{ are eigenvectors of }A\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stiefel manifold and its weighted PCA formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the real Stiefel manifold and records its projector and weighted principal-component formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers $1\le k\le d$, the Stiefel manifold is $\operatorname{St}(d,k)=\{U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:U^\top U=I_k\}$, an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$. For $U=[u_1,\ldots,u_k]\in\operatorname{St}(d,k)$, $UU^\top$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{span}(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$. If $X\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ with $\alpha_1>\cdots>\alpha_k>0$, weighted $k$-component PCA is $\max_{U\in\operatorname{St}(d,k)}\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i\langle XX^\top u_i,u_i\rangle=\max_{U\in\operatorname{St}(d,k)}\langle XX^\top U,UD\rangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Stiefel manifold consists of real d-by-k matrices with orthonormal columns and is embedded in the ambient matrix space. Such a matrix determines the orthogonal projector onto its column space. Weighted k-component PCA maximizes the stated weighted variance objective over this manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{St}(d,k)=\{U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:U^\top U=I_k\},\quad P_{\operatorname{col}(U)}=UU^\top,\quad \max_{U\in\operatorname{St}(d,k)}\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i\langle XX^\top u_i,u_i\rangle=\max_{U\in\operatorname{St}(d,k)}\langle XX^\top U,UD\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Group and informal Lie-group definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a group algebraically and informally identifies a Lie group as a group with a compatible smooth-manifold structure; the precise smoothness criterion is not part of this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set $G$ with an operation $\cdot:G\times G\to G$ is a group if $a\cdot(b\cdot c)=(a\cdot b)\cdot c$ for all $a,b,c\in G$, there is an identity $e\in G$ satisfying $e\cdot g=g\cdot e=g$ for every $g\in G$, and every $g\in G$ has an inverse $g^{-1}$ satisfying $g\cdot g^{-1}=g^{-1}\cdot g=e$. If $G$ additionally has a compatible smooth-manifold structure, the resulting manifold-group is called a Lie group.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group has an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for every element. Informally, a group with a compatible smooth-manifold structure is a Lie group.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G,\cdot)\text{ is a group exactly when the stated associativity, identity, and inverse axioms hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and connected components of the orthogonal and special orthogonal groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint characterization of the orthogonal-group pair, with child-node specializations for each group's geometry and their orientation-component structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), \(\mathrm O(n)=\{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}:X^\top X=XX^\top=I_n\}\) is an embedded Lie group of dimension \(n(n-1)/2\), and \(T_X\mathrm O(n)=X\operatorname{Skew}(n)\). With the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product, \(\operatorname{Proj}_X(U)=X\operatorname{skew}(X^\top U)\), and for a smooth function with smooth ambient extension \(\bar f\), \(\operatorname{grad}f(X)=X\operatorname{skew}(X^\top\operatorname{grad}\bar f(X))\). The Stiefel Q-factor and polar retractions restrict to \(\mathrm O(n)\). The group \(\mathrm O(n)\) has two connected components distinguished by \(\det X=1\) and \(\det X=-1\); consequently, continuous retraction curves cannot move between them. The special orthogonal group \(\mathrm{SO}(n)=\{X\in\mathrm O(n):\det X=1\}\) is the determinant-positive connected component and an embedded submanifold. It has dimension \(n(n-1)/2\), and for \(X\in\mathrm{SO}(n)\) it has the same tangent-space, projection, and gradient formulas. Retractions on \(\mathrm O(n)\) restrict to \(\mathrm{SO}(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every integer n at least one, the orthogonal matrices form an embedded Lie group of dimension n(n−1)/2. Tangent vectors at X are X times skew-symmetric matrices, which gives explicit orthogonal-projection and Riemannian-gradient formulas under the induced Euclidean metric. The Stiefel Q-factor and polar retractions apply. The orthogonal group has two connected components, distinguished by determinant +1 and −1, so continuous retraction curves remain in their starting component. The determinant-positive component is the special orthogonal group, an embedded submanifold with the same dimension and local geometric formulas; orthogonal-group retractions restrict to it.
assumptions_latex: X\in\mathrm O(n)\text{ for statements about }\mathrm O(n)
f\text{ is smooth and admits the smooth ambient extension }\bar f\text{ when the gradient formula is invoked}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim\mathrm O(n)=\dim\mathrm{SO}(n)=\frac{n(n-1)}2,\quad T_X\mathrm O(n)=X\operatorname{Skew}(n),\quad T_X\mathrm{SO}(n)=X\operatorname{Skew}(n),\quad \operatorname{Proj}_X(U)=X\operatorname{skew}(X^\top U),\quad \operatorname{grad}f(X)=X\operatorname{skew}(X^\top\operatorname{grad}\bar f(X)),\quad \mathrm O(n)=\{\det=1\}\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{\det=-1\},\quad \mathrm{SO}(n)=\{X\in\mathrm O(n):\det X=1\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded and Lie-group geometry of the real orthogonal group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Differentiating \(Q^\top Q=I_n\) yields \[T_QO(n)=\{Q\Omega:\Omega\in\mathfrak o(n)\}=\{Z:Q^\top Z+Z^\top Q=0\}.\] The induced Frobenius metric satisfies \(g_Q(Q\Omega,Q\Lambda)=\operatorname{tr}(\Omega^\top\Lambda)\) and is invariant under both left and right multiplication by elements of \(O(n)\). The orthogonal projection of an ambient matrix \(Z\) is \[\Pi_Q(Z)=Q\operatorname{skew}(Q^\top Z),\qquad \operatorname{skew}(A)=(A-A^\top)/2.\] The group has two connected components distinguished by \(\det Q\in\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal-group tangent vectors are orthogonal matrices times skew-symmetric matrices, and the Frobenius metric is bi-invariant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal matrices and preservation of Euclidean geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and elementary properties of real square orthogonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix $P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal if $P^{T}P=PP^{T}=I$. Then $P^{-1}=P^{T}$, $|\det P|=1$, and the rows and columns of $P$ are orthonormal. For every $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $\|Px\|_{2}=\|x\|_{2}$ and $(Px)^{T}(Py)=x^{T}y$, so orthogonality is preserved under the transformation $x\mapsto Px$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real square matrix is orthogonal when its transpose is its inverse. Its rows and columns are orthonormal, its determinant has absolute value one, and it preserves Euclidean norms, inner products, and orthogonality.
