knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Stationarity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient and minimum-curvature certificates for approximate first- and second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f\in C^2(M)\) and tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H\ge0\), a point \(x\in M\) has an \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-second-order stationarity certificate if
\[
\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_x\le\varepsilon_g,\qquad
\lambda_{\min}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H.
\]
The first inequality alone certifies \(\varepsilon_g\)-first-order stationarity. The second inequality is equivalent to \(g_x(\eta,\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\eta])\ge-\varepsilon_H\|\eta\|_x^2\) for every tangent vector \(\eta\), making the certificate checkable by gradient-norm and minimum-eigenvalue estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small gradient norm certifies approximate first-order stationarity; adding an almost-positive-semidefinite Hessian certifies approximate second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities certify approximate first- and second-order Riemannian stationarity at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Norm induced by the metric at x
Smallest eigenvalue of a self-adjoint tangent-space operator

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional approximate Riemannian stationarity criteria

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Invariance of Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of exact stationarity under smooth Riemannian isometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi:(M,g)\to(N,h)\) be a Riemannian isometry and define \(\widetilde f=f\circ\Phi^{-1}\) for \(f\in C^2(M)\). For \(y=\Phi(x)\),
\[
\operatorname{grad}\widetilde f(y)=D\Phi_x[\operatorname{grad}f(x)],
\]
and the Hessians satisfy
\[
\operatorname{Hess}\widetilde f(y)\circ D\Phi_x
=D\Phi_x\circ\operatorname{Hess}f(x).
\]
Consequently, zero gradient, Hessian positive semidefiniteness, and Hessian eigenvalues are preserved. First- and second-order Riemannian stationarity therefore do not depend on the chosen isometric representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riemannian isometries transport gradients and conjugate Hessians, preserving first- and second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is first- or second-order stationary for \(f\) if and only if \(\Phi(x)\) has the corresponding property for \(f\circ\Phi^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: Differential of the isometry at x
Objective expressed on the isometric representation N

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: naturality of gradient and Hessian under isometries

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Equality-Constraint Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded manifolds defined as regular level sets of smooth equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable with \(m\le n\), and set \(M=c^{-1}(0)\). This is a regular equality-constraint model when \(Dc(x)\) has full row rank \(m\) for every \(x\in M\). Then \(M\) is a smooth embedded submanifold of dimension \(n-m\), and
\[
T_xM=\ker Dc(x),\qquad
N_xM=\operatorname{range}Dc(x)^{\mathsf T},
\]
where the normal space is taken with respect to the Euclidean metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full row rank of the equality-constraint Jacobian makes the feasible level set an embedded manifold with explicit tangent and normal spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=c^{-1}(0)\) is an embedded manifold with \(T_xM=\ker Dc(x)\) and \(N_xM=\operatorname{range}Dc(x)^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: Tangent space to the feasible manifold
Euclidean normal space to the feasible manifold

children.title: Riemannian Multiplier Representation

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Multiplier Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier form of the Riemannian gradient and stationarity on a regular level-set manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:c(x)=0\}\) be regular and carry the induced Euclidean metric, and let \(f\) be differentiable near \(M\). For every \(x\in M\), there is a unique vector \(\lambda(x)\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=\nabla f(x)+Dc(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda(x),\qquad
Dc(x)\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=0,
\]
namely \(\lambda(x)=-(Dc(x)Dc(x)^{\mathsf T})^{-1}Dc(x)\nabla f(x)\). Hence Riemannian stationarity is equivalent to the existence of a multiplier satisfying the ambient equation \(\nabla f(x)+Dc(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a regular equality manifold, the Riemannian gradient is the ambient gradient corrected by a unique normal multiplier term.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in C^1\) and \(Dc(x)\) has full row rank on \(M\).
\(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=0\) if and only if a unique \(\lambda\) satisfies \(\nabla f(x)+Dc(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient on the feasible manifold
Equality-constraint multiplier under the stated sign convention

children.title: Ambient Multiplier Representation
children.top_down_role: Extrinsic multiplier certificates expressed through embedding constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Multiplier Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained representation for a regular embedded level-set manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(\mathcal M=h^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(Dh(x)\) has full row rank at \(x\in\mathcal M\). Then \(T_x\mathcal M=\ker Dh(x)\) and \(N_x\mathcal M=\operatorname{range}Dh(x)^\top\). Consequently,
\[\operatorname{grad}_{\mathcal M}f(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists!\,\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ \nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^\top\lambda=0.\]
Thus the ambient KKT multiplier is the unique coefficient representing \(-\nabla f(x)\) in the constraint-normal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular equality-constrained point, Riemannian stationarity is equivalent to a unique ambient KKT multiplier representing the negative gradient in the normal space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_{\mathcal M}f(x)=0\iff \exists!\lambda:\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^\top\lambda=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the tangent/normal-space identities and unique multiplier correspondence.

children.title: Multiplier Translation Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Projection, normal-space, plus representation choices linking the two multiplier views.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Translation Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit conversion between normal vectors and equality-constraint multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the regular level-set hypotheses, define the normal-coordinate map by
\[\Lambda_x(v)=\bigl(Dh(x)Dh(x)^\top\bigr)^{-1}Dh(x)v,\qquad v\in N_x\mathcal M.\]
It is the inverse of \(\lambda\mapsto Dh(x)^\top\lambda\). Hence the orthogonal normal projection and tangent projection are
\[P_x^N=Dh(x)^\top\bigl(Dh(x)Dh(x)^\top\bigr)^{-1}Dh(x),\qquad P_x^T=I-P_x^N.\]
For a stationary point, the KKT multiplier is \(\lambda=-\Lambda_x(\nabla f(x))\). These formulas translate the intrinsic equation \(P_x^T\nabla f(x)=0\) into its ambient multiplier equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constraint Jacobian and its Gram inverse convert normal vectors into multipliers and translate projected-gradient stationarity into the ambient KKT equation.
assumptions_latex: The metric is induced by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda=-\bigl(Dh(x)Dh(x)^\top\bigr)^{-1}Dh(x)\nabla f(x)\) at stationarity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas and representation role are appropriate, but the inverse-coordinate and projection formulas have no cited source.

children.title: Multiplier Correspondence Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Rank loss, redundant constraints, plus embedding-sensitive correspondence failures.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Correspondence Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank loss destroys unique normal coordinates and may destroy multiplier existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full-row-rank hypothesis is essential. Redundant constraints can destroy uniqueness: for \(h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\), \(h(t)=(t,t)\), the feasible set is \(\{0\}\), while every pair satisfying \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2=-f'(0)\) represents stationarity. More severely, let \(h(t)=t^2\) and \(f(t)=t\). The feasible set \(\mathcal M=\{0\}\) is a zero-dimensional manifold, so \(\operatorname{grad}_{\mathcal M}f(0)=0\); however, \(Dh(0)=0\), and the ambient equation \(f'(0)+Dh(0)^\top\lambda=0\) becomes \(1=0\). Thus rank loss can eliminate both uniqueness and existence of corresponding multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without constraint regularity, redundant equations make multipliers nonunique, while singular equations can make intrinsic stationarity hold although no ambient multiplier exists.
assumptions_latex: Equality constraints are allowed to have rank-deficient Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint-Jacobian rank loss can invalidate one-to-one or even existential multiplier correspondence.

notation.meaning: feasible set equipped with its intrinsic manifold structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both counterexamples are internally correct and fit a failure-boundary leaf, but neither is supported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: First-Order KKT Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Stationarity, feasibility, multiplier, plus constraint-qualification interfaces at first order.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order KKT Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order equivalence for smooth regular equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, and suppose \(\mathcal M=h^{-1}(0)\) is regular at \(x\). If \(x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) on \(\mathcal M\), then
\[Df(x)[d]=0\quad\text{for every }d\in T_x\mathcal M.\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{grad}_{\mathcal M}f(x)=0\), and there exists a unique \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^\top\lambda=0,\qquad h(x)=0.\]
Thus intrinsic first-order stationarity and the ambient equality-constrained KKT system describe the same regular critical points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular equality-constrained local minimizer is Riemannian stationary, equivalently satisfying the ambient first-order KKT equations with a unique multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Df(x)|_{T_x\mathcal M}=0\iff \operatorname{grad}_{\mathcal M}f(x)=0\iff \exists!\lambda:\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^\top\lambda=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regular equality-constrained first-order theorem is standard and correctly scoped, but no authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Second-Order KKT Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Curvature-sensitive necessary or sufficient optimality interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order KKT Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order equality-constrained conditions for a regular embedded level-set manifold with the induced Euclidean metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable, let \(\mathcal M=h^{-1}(0)\) carry the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product, and let \(x\in\mathcal M\) satisfy that \(Dh(x)\) has full row rank. Suppose \((x,\lambda)\) satisfies \(\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^\top\lambda=0\), and define \(L(y,\lambda)=f(y)+\lambda^\top h(y)\). Then
\[\langle d,\operatorname{Hess}_{\mathcal M}(f|_{\mathcal M})(x)[d]\rangle=d^\top\nabla^2_{yy}L(x,\lambda)d\qquad\text{for every }d\in T_x\mathcal M.\]
If \(x\) is a local minimizer of \(f|_{\mathcal M}\), this quantity is nonnegative for every \(d\in T_x\mathcal M\). Conversely, if it is strictly positive for every nonzero \(d\in T_x\mathcal M\), then \(x\) is a strict constrained local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a regular Euclidean level-set manifold, the Riemannian Hessian quadratic form equals the Lagrangian Hessian restricted to tangent directions; nonnegativity is necessary at a local minimizer, and positive definiteness is sufficient for strict local minimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) are twice continuously differentiable.
\(x\in\mathcal M=h^{-1}(0)\) and \(Dh(x)\) has full row rank.
\(\mathcal M\) has the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(d\in T_x\mathcal M\), \(\langle d,\operatorname{Hess}_{\mathcal M}(f|_{\mathcal M})(x)[d]\rangle=d^\top\nabla^2_{yy}L(x,\lambda)d\); nonnegativity is necessary, while strict positivity on nonzero tangent directions is sufficient for strict local minimality.

notation.meaning: Riemannian Hessian of the restricted objective

children.title: Critical-Cone Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from first-order feasibility to second-order curvature assessment.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Cone Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition from equality-constrained tangent spaces to multiplier-dependent critical cones when smooth inequalities are added.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) be twice continuously differentiable, and consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le 0\). Let \((x,\lambda,\mu)\) be a KKT point with \(\mu\ge0\), and define \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:g_i(x)=0\}\). The multiplier-dependent critical cone is
\[\mathcal C(x,\mu)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d=0\ \text{for }i\in I(x)\text{ with }\mu_i>0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\ \text{for }i\in I(x)\text{ with }\mu_i=0\}.\]
For an equality-only regular model, the corresponding critical directions form \(T_x\mathcal M=\ker Dh(x)\), where \(\mathcal M=h^{-1}(0)\). Thus active inequalities replace the tangent-space domain of the second-order Lagrangian test by the generally nonsymmetric, multiplier-dependent cone \(\mathcal C(x,\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a KKT point with active inequalities, second-order tests use a multiplier-dependent critical cone; in a regular equality-only model, the corresponding direction set is the tangent space.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) are twice continuously differentiable.
\((x,\lambda,\mu)\) satisfies the KKT feasibility, stationarity, dual-feasibility, and complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Active inequalities replace the equality-only tangent space \(T_x\mathcal M\) by the multiplier-dependent critical cone \(\mathcal C(x,\mu)\) as the direction set for second-order KKT tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Irregular-Constraint Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where a constraint presentation ceases to define the intrinsic geometry reliably.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a level-set model \(\mathcal F=h^{-1}(0)\), the regular interface requires locally constant full row rank of \(Dh\). If this fails, \(\ker Dh(x)\) need not equal the geometric tangent space, multipliers need not exist or be unique, and Lagrangian-Hessian tests may depend on the chosen constraint representation. For example, \(h(t)=t^2\) has \(\mathcal F=\{0\}\), whose tangent space is \(\{0\}\), but \(\ker Dh(0)=\mathbb R\). Hence the Jacobian-based ambient model introduces spurious linearized directions and cannot be translated mechanically into intrinsic manifold optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At rank-deficient constraints, the Jacobian kernel can differ from the true tangent space, so multiplier and Hessian translations may fail.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is presented as \(h^{-1}(0)\).
No constant-rank or full-row-rank condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without constraint regularity, \(\ker Dh(x)\) may not represent the intrinsic tangent space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-deficient example and failure-boundary role are appropriate, but the claims concerning multiplier and Hessian representation dependence lack an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesically convex subsets of a Riemannian line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-level geodesic convexity and the interval consequence for a complete Riemannian line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) is geodesically convex in \((\mathbb R,g)\) if, for every \(x_1,x_2\in A\), there exists a geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) such that \(\gamma(0)=x_1\), \(\gamma(1)=x_2\), and \(\gamma([0,1])\subseteq A\). If \((\mathbb R,g)\) is complete, then every interval in \(\mathbb R\) is geodesically convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of a Riemannian line is geodesically convex when each pair of its points can be joined by a geodesic segment that remains in the subset. If the Riemannian line is complete, every real interval is geodesically convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is geodesically convex}\iff \forall x_1,x_2\in A\;\exists\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\text{ geodesic},\ \gamma(0)=x_1,\ \gamma(1)=x_2,\ \gamma([0,1])\subseteq A;\quad (\mathbb R,g)\text{ complete}\Rightarrow\text{ every interval is geodesically convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product Decomposition from a Critical-Point-Free Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global product topology determined by any nonempty level hypersurface of the convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature $K\le 0$. If $f:M\to\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ convex function with $\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\varnothing$, then for every $c\in f(M)$, setting $L=f^{-1}(c)$, the manifold $M$ is diffeomorphic to $L\times\mathbb R$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a complete nonpositively curved Riemannian manifold admits a twice continuously differentiable convex function without critical points, then it is diffeomorphic to the product of any of that function's level hypersurfaces with the real line.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian representation of symmetric geodesic second differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the symmetric geodesic second difference with the second derivative along a geodesic and gives its minimum-Hessian representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be an open totally convex subset of a Riemannian manifold, let \(x\in A\), and let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\) be of class \(C^2\) at \(x\). For a unit vector \(X\in T_xM\) and the geodesic \(\gamma\) satisfying \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma(0)=X\),
\[
C_f(x;X)=(f\circ\gamma)''(0)=\operatorname{Hess}f_x(X,X),
\]
and
\[
C_f(x)=\min_{\substack{X\in T_xM\\\|X\|=1}}\operatorname{Hess}f_x(X,X).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function that is twice differentiable at x on an open totally convex set, the symmetric second difference in a unit geodesic direction equals the second derivative along that geodesic and the Hessian quadratic form. Its infimum over unit directions is attained as the minimum Hessian value.
assumptions_latex: A\subset M\text{ is open and totally convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_f(x;X)=(f\circ\gamma)''(0)=\operatorname{Hess}f_x(X,X),\qquad C_f(x)=\min_{\substack{X\in T_xM\\\|X\|=1}}\operatorname{Hess}f_x(X,X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Exponential Parameterization and Contraction of a Regular Superlevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extraction's inconsistent degree-symbol notation is normalized to the closed superlevel set, as required by the assertion that the map fixes its boundary level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature $K\le 0$, let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be a nonconstant $C^2$ convex function, and let $c$ be a noncritical value of $f$. Set $L=f^{-1}(c)$ and ${}^{c}M=f^{-1}([c,\infty))$. The normal exponential map restricts to a diffeomorphism from the positive normal half-bundle $NL^+$ onto ${}^{c}M$, with the zero section $L$ fixed. The resulting geodesic deformation of ${}^{c}M$ onto $L$ is length-nonincreasing. If $K<0$, it is length-decreasing except on curves contained in $L$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete nonpositively curved Riemannian manifold, a regular level set of a nonconstant twice continuously differentiable convex function normally parameterizes its closed superlevel side. The induced deformation onto the level set does not increase curve lengths; under strictly negative curvature, it decreases them except for curves lying in the level set.

c\text{ is a noncritical value of }f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric geodesic second-difference quantities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a lower symmetric second difference along a unit-speed geodesic and its infimum over unit tangent directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in A\subset M\), let \(X\in T_xM\) satisfy \(\|X\|=1\), and let \(\gamma:(-a,a)\to A\) be a geodesic with \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma(0)=X\). For a continuous function \(f:A\to\mathbb R\), define

\]

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence-based geodesic convexity for subsets of a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold. A set \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is geodesically convex if, for every \(x,y\in C\), there exists a minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\) such that \(\gamma(0)=x\), \(\gamma(1)=y\), and \(\gamma(t)\in C\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). It is strongly geodesically convex if this minimizing geodesic is unique and lies in \(C\). This record uses the existence convention for “geodesically convex”; requiring every connecting minimizing geodesic to remain in \(C\) is a distinct stronger convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is geodesically convex when each pair of its points can be joined inside it by a minimizing geodesic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative interior of a geodesically convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic relative interior defined by backward extension of every in-set connecting geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a geodesically convex set in a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\). The relative interior \(\operatorname{relint}S\) consists of those \(x\in S\) such that, for every \(y\in S\) and every geodesic \(c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\) connecting \(c(0)=x\) to \(c(1)=y\) with image in \(S\), there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(c\) extends to a geodesic on \([-\varepsilon,1]\) whose image remains in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the relative interior of a geodesically convex set if every geodesic in the set from that point to any other point can be extended a positive distance backward while remaining a geodesic inside the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{relint}S\iff \forall y\in S\ \forall c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M,\ \bigl(c(0)=x,\ c(1)=y,\ c([0,1])\subseteq S\bigr)\Rightarrow\exists\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }c\text{ extends geodesically to }[-\varepsilon,1]\text{ with image in }S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-coercive convex-function criterion for g-connectedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition applicable without completeness of the ambient manifold and without compact closure of the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, not necessarily complete, and let $D\subset M$ be a domain. Suppose $D$ supports a positive convex function $f$ such that (i) $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\partial D$, and (ii) for every $c\in\mathbb R$ and every closed bounded set $B\subset D$, the set $B\cap f^{-1}([0,c])$ is compact. Then $D$ is $g$-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain in a possibly incomplete Riemannian manifold is g-connected if it supports a positive convex function that diverges at the boundary and whose nonnegative sublevel sets have compact intersections with every closed bounded subset of the domain.

f:D\to\mathbb R\text{ is positive and convex}
\forall c\in\mathbb R\ \forall B\subset D\text{ closed and bounded}:\ B\cap f^{-1}([0,c])\text{ is compact}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is }g\text{-connected}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesic convexity of sublevel-set intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geodesic convexity of intersections of convex-function sublevel sets, including the quasiconvexity converse boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an arbitrary index set. For each \(i\in I\), let \(f_i:S\to\mathbb{R}\) be geodesically convex and let \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x\in S:f_i(x)\leq\alpha_i\}\) is geodesically convex. In particular, every sublevel set and the set of global minimizers of a geodesically convex function are geodesically convex. The converse need not hold: convexity of all sublevel sets characterizes geodesic quasiconvexity, not geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary intersection of sublevel sets of geodesically convex functions is geodesically convex. Thus individual sublevel sets and global-minimizer sets are geodesically convex. The converse fails: convex sublevel sets imply only geodesic quasiconvexity.

\forall i\in I,\ f_i:S\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is geodesically convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i\in I}\{x\in S:f_i(x)\leq\alpha_i\}\text{ is geodesically convex; the converse from convex sublevel sets to geodesic convexity fails.}

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity along all geodesic segments contained in the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a geodesically convex subset of a Riemannian manifold and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is geodesically convex on \(C\) if, for every geodesic segment \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\),
\[f(\gamma(t))\le (1-t)f(\gamma(0))+t f(\gamma(1))\qquad\text{for all }t\in[0,1].\]
If \(f\) is differentiable and the relevant minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\) is represented by \(\gamma(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\xi)\), this implies
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\rangle_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is geodesically convex when its restriction to every admissible geodesic segment is an ordinary convex function of the segment parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ\gamma\) is convex on \([0,1]\) for every geodesic segment \(\gamma\) in \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent, but quantifying over every contained geodesic segment is convention-sensitive and the first-order consequence has no authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global normalized-gradient flow and divergence of a convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here the normalized-gradient field is considered away from the critical set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a $C^2$ convex function. Set $U=\operatorname{grad}f/\|\operatorname{grad}f\|$ on $M\setminus\operatorname{Crit}(f)$. For every $x_0\in M\setminus\operatorname{Crit}(f)$, the field line $\alpha$ of $U$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0$ is defined for every $t\in[0,\infty)$; moreover, $f\circ\alpha$ is strictly increasing and convex, and $\lim_{t\to\infty}f(\alpha(t))=+\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete Riemannian manifold, the normalized-gradient trajectory of a twice continuously differentiable convex function starting outside its critical set exists for all nonnegative time. Along it, the function is strictly increasing and convex and tends to positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha\text{ exists on }[0,\infty),\quad f\circ\alpha\text{ is strictly increasing and convex},\quad \lim_{t\to\infty}f(\alpha(t))=+\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order characterizations of geodesic convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order equivalences for differentiable geodesic convexity, strong convexity, and strict convexity along every geodesic segment in a geodesically convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S be a geodesically convex subset of a Riemannian manifold \mathcal M, and let f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R be differentiable on a neighborhood of S. For every geodesic segment c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M contained in S, set x=c(0). Then f|_S is geodesically convex if and only if
\[\forall t\in[0,1],\quad f(c(t))\geq f(x)+t\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),c'(0)\rangle_x.\]
For \mu>0, f|_S is geodesically \mu-strongly convex if and only if
\[\forall t\in[0,1],\quad f(c(t))\geq f(x)+t\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),c'(0)\rangle_x+\frac{\mu t^2}{2}L(c)^2.\]
Finally, f|_S is geodesically strictly convex if and only if, for every such c with c'(0)\neq0,
\[\forall t\in(0,1],\quad f(c(t))>f(x)+t\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),c'(0)\rangle_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a geodesically convex set, differentiable geodesic convexity is equivalent to the supporting-gradient inequality along every geodesic segment. Strong convexity adds the stated quadratic length term. Strict convexity is equivalent to strict inequality on every nonconstant segment at positive parameter values.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable on a neighborhood of }S
c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\text{ is a geodesic segment contained in }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f|_S\text{ satisfies the stated necessary-and-sufficient first-order inequalities for geodesic convexity, }\mu\text{-strong convexity, and strict convexity.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Hessian criteria for geodesic convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order characterizations of geodesic convexity and strong geodesic convexity, plus a sufficient but nonnecessary condition for strict geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S be an open geodesically convex set, and let f:S\to\mathbb R be twice differentiable. Then, with each pointwise condition understood to hold for all x\in S,
\[f\text{ is geodesically convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succeq0,\]
\[f\text{ is geodesically }\mu\text{-strongly convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succeq\mu\operatorname{Id},\]
and
\[\bigl(\forall x\in S,\ \operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succ0\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ is geodesically strictly convex}.\]
The last condition is sufficient but not necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable function on an open geodesically convex set is geodesically convex exactly when its Riemannian Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere. It is geodesically mu-strongly convex exactly when the Hessian is everywhere bounded below by mu times the identity. An everywhere positive-definite Hessian implies strict geodesic convexity, but the converse need not hold.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is open and geodesically convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is geodesically convex}\iff\forall x\in S,\ \operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succeq0;\quad f\text{ is geodesically }\mu\text{-strongly convex}\iff\forall x\in S,\ \operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succeq\mu\operatorname{Id};\quad (\forall x\in S,\ \operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succ0)\Rightarrow f\text{ is geodesically strictly convex, but not conversely.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized-gradient-flow representation of convex sublevel sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The flow parameter runs backward from a regular level set to the corresponding closed sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a $C^2$ convex function with $\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\varnothing$. For every $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $f^{-1}(c)\neq\varnothing$, the level set $f^{-1}(c)$ is a hypersurface in $M$. If $\Phi$ is the flow of $U=\operatorname{grad}f/\|\operatorname{grad}f\|$, then the restriction $\Phi\vert_{f^{-1}(c)\times(-\infty,0]}$ is a diffeomorphism from $f^{-1}(c)\times(-\infty,0]$ onto $f^{-1}(( -\infty,c])$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable convex function without critical points on a complete Riemannian manifold, every nonempty level set is a hypersurface, and backward normalized-gradient flow gives a diffeomorphic product representation of the associated closed sublevel set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, Strictly Convex, Concave, and Affine Functions Along Geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-convexity notions on a totally convex manifold domain, quantified over every connecting geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subseteq M\) be totally convex and \(f:A\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is convex if, for all \(x,x'\in A\), every geodesic \(\gamma_{xx'}\) joining them, and every \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f(\gamma_{xx'}(t))\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(x').\] It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict for \(x\ne x'\) and \(t\in(0,1)\). It is concave, respectively strictly concave, if \(-f\) is convex, respectively strictly convex. It is affine if it is both convex and concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity requires the convex interpolation inequality along every connecting geodesic. Strict convexity makes it strict for distinct endpoints and interior parameters. Concavity is convexity of the negative, and being both convex and concave is called affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ has the stated convexity, strict-convexity, concavity, or affine classification exactly when the corresponding conditions hold}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesically convex program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and immediate feasible-set and local-to-global consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathcal M\) be geodesically convex. If \(f,f_1,\ldots,f_m:S\to\mathbb R\) are geodesically convex, \(g_1,\ldots,g_p:S\to\mathbb R\) are geodesically linear, and \(\alpha_i,\beta_j\in\mathbb R\), then \(\min_{x\in S}f(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq\alpha_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(g_j(x)=\beta_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\) is a geodesically convex program. Each equality is equivalent to \(g_j(x)\leq\beta_j\) and \(-g_j(x)\leq-\beta_j\); therefore its feasible set \(S'\) is geodesically convex, and every local minimizer of \(f|_{S'}\) is global.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geodesically convex program minimizes a geodesically convex objective over a geodesically convex set subject to geodesically convex inequalities and geodesically linear equalities. Replacing each equality by two convex inequalities shows that the feasible set is geodesically convex, so every constrained local minimizer is global.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S'=\{x\in S:f_i(x)\leq\alpha_i\ \forall i,\ g_j(x)=\beta_j\ \forall j\}\text{ is geodesically convex, and every local minimizer of }f|_{S'}\text{ is global.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesically convex and strictly convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies over every ambient geodesic segment contained in the geodesically convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S\subseteq\mathcal M$ be geodesically convex. A function $f:S\to\mathbb R$ is geodesically convex if, for every geodesic segment $c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M$ with $c([0,1])\subseteq S$, the function $f\circ c$ is convex; equivalently, $$f(c(t))\leq (1-t)f(c(0))+tf(c(1))\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,1].$$ It is geodesically strictly convex if, for every such segment with $c(0)\neq c(1)$, the inequality is strict for all $t\in(0,1)$. In Euclidean space these notions coincide with ordinary convexity and strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a geodesically convex domain is geodesically convex when its restriction to every contained geodesic segment is convex. It is strictly geodesically convex when the chord inequality is strict at interior parameters whenever the endpoints differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(c(t))\leq(1-t)f(c(0))+tf(c(1))\quad\forall t\in[0,1],\quad\text{and strictly }<\text{ for }t\in(0,1)\text{ when }c(0)\neq c(1)\text{ in the strictly convex case}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone-differential characterization of geodesic convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order monotonicity criterion along geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subset M\) be open and totally convex and let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^1\). knowledge_statements.title: Strong Geodesic Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric strong convexity along minimizing geodesic segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be geodesically convex and let \(\mu>0\). A function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is \(\mu\)-strongly geodesically convex if every constant-speed minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\) satisfies
\[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+t f(\gamma(1))-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\gamma(1))^2\]
for every \(t\in[0,1]\). When \(f\) is differentiable and \(y=\operatorname{Exp}_x(\xi)\) along such a segment, the equivalent first-order inequality is
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\rangle_x+\frac{\mu}{2}d(x,y)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong geodesic convexity adds a uniform quadratic distance term to the ordinary convexity inequality along every minimizing geodesic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ\gamma\) obeys the displayed \(\mu\)-strong convexity inequality on every admissible geodesic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-convexity inequality is standard under the stated constant-speed minimizing-geodesic convention, but the definition and claimed first-order equivalence require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality from strong geodesic convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient domination on a closed geodesically convex set under positive strong geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty, closed, geodesically convex subset of a complete manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable on a neighborhood of \(S\). If \(f|_S\) is geodesically \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\), and \(x_\star\) is its minimizer, then \[\forall x\in S,\qquad f(x)-f(x_\star)\le \frac{1}{2\mu}\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_x^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive strong geodesic convexity implies that the objective gap is at most the squared Riemannian gradient norm divided by twice the strong-convexity parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathcal M\) is closed and geodesically convex.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in S,\ f(x)-f(x_\star)\le (2\mu)^{-1}\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_x^2.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geodesic strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The one-dimensional strong-convexity modulus along each segment is scaled by the squared segment length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mu>0$. A function $f:S\to\mathbb R$ is geodesically $\mu$-strongly convex if $S$ is geodesically convex and, for every geodesic segment $c:[0,1]\to\mathcal M$ with $c([0,1])\subseteq S$, $$f(c(t))\leq(1-t)f(c(0))+tf(c(1))-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)L(c)^2\quad\forall t\in[0,1],$$ where $L(c)=\|c'(0)\|_{c(0)}$ is the length of the geodesic segment. Equivalently, $f\circ c$ is $\mu L(c)^2$-strongly convex in the ordinary one-dimensional sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is geodesically mu-strongly convex when every restriction to a contained geodesic segment satisfies the strong chord inequality with a curvature term equal to mu times the squared segment length. Equivalently, that restriction has strong-convexity modulus mu times the squared length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(c(t))\leq(1-t)f(c(0))+tf(c(1))-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)L(c)^2\quad\forall t\in[0,1],\qquad f\circ c\text{ is }\mu L(c)^2\text{-strongly convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact sublevels and uniqueness under strong geodesic convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness consequences of strong geodesic convexity on a closed geodesically convex subset of a complete manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty, closed, geodesically convex subset of a complete manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable on a neighborhood of \(S\). If \(f|_S\) is geodesically \(\mu\)-strongly convex for some \(\mu>0\), then every sublevel set of \(f|_S\) is compact and \(f|_S\) has exactly one global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonempty, closed, geodesically convex subset of a complete manifold, a differentiable function that is strongly geodesically convex has compact sublevel sets and a unique global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathcal M\) is closed and geodesically convex.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(c\in\mathbb R\), \(\{x\in S:f(x)\le c\}\) is compact, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\) contains exactly one point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear convergence of exponential-map gradient descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-value and distance convergence for constant-step Riemannian gradient descent on a complete manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and geodesically convex on a complete manifold \(\mathcal M\). Given \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), set \(S_0=\{x\in\mathcal M:f(x)\le f(x_0)\}\). Assume \(\operatorname{grad}f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(S_0\), and \(f|_{S_0}\) is geodesically \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\). For \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{Exp}_{x_k}(-L^{-1}\operatorname{grad}f(x_k))\) and \(\kappa=L/\mu\ge1\), \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x_\star\), every iterate lies in \(S_0\), and for every \(k\ge0\), \[f(x_k)-f(x_\star)\le\left(1-\frac1\kappa\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f(x_\star)\bigr),\] \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,x_\star)\le\left(\sqrt{1-\frac1\kappa}\right)^k\sqrt\kappa\,\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x_\star).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponential-map gradient descent with step size 1/L remains in the initial sublevel set and converges linearly to the unique minimizer when the objective has an L-Lipschitz gradient near that set and is positively strongly geodesically convex on it.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and geodesically convex on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x_\star\), \(x_k\in S_0\) for every \(k\ge0\), and the stated function-gap and distance bounds hold for every \(k\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convexity of retraction pullbacks on tangent-space domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a retraction on a Riemannian manifold, let \(x\in\mathcal M\), and let \(U_x\subseteq T_x\mathcal M\) be convex, contain \(0_x\), and lie in the domain of \(R_x\). A function \(f\) is retraction-convex at \(x\) on \(U_x\) if the pullback \(\widehat f_x=f\circ R_x\) is convex on \(U_x\); equivalently,
\[f(R_x((1-t)\xi+t\eta))\le(1-t)f(R_x(\xi))+t f(R_x(\eta))\]
for all \(\xi,\eta\in U_x\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). Retraction convexity is relative to both the chosen retraction and tangent-space neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retraction convexity means that composing the objective with a chosen retraction produces an ordinary convex function on a convex tangent-space neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(U_x\subseteq T_x\mathcal M\) is convex and contains \(0_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ R_x\) is convex on \(U_x\).

notation.meaning: retraction restricted to the tangent space at x
retraction pullback of f at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Pullback convexity is a coherent definition and fits the leaf, but retraction-convexity terminology is convention-dependent and no citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Retraction-convex sets and functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convexity induced by the curves of a fixed retraction and records the exponential-retraction specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathrm R\) be a retraction on a manifold \(\mathcal M\). A set \(S\subseteq\mathcal M\) is retraction convex if, for every \(x,y\in S\), there exists \(v\in T_x\mathcal M\) such that \(c(t)=\mathrm R_x(tv)\) satisfies \(c(0)=x\), \(c(1)=y\), and \(c([0,1])\subseteq S\). A function \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) is retraction convex if \(f\circ c\) is convex for every retraction curve \(c\) contained in \(S\). For the exponential retraction, these notions reduce to geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed retraction, a set is retraction convex when each pair of its points can be joined within the set by a retraction curve. A function is retraction convex when its composition with every retraction curve contained in the set is convex. For the exponential retraction, this reduces to geodesic convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a manifold and \(\mathrm R\) is a retraction on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated curve conditions define retraction convexity of \(S\) and \(f\); for the exponential retraction, retraction convexity reduces to geodesic convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Retraction convexity on a subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convexity along unit-direction retraction segments whose entire image up to each endpoint remains in the specified subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a Riemannian manifold, \(R\) a retraction on \(M\), \(S\subset M\), and \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is retraction convex with respect to \(R\) in \(S\) if, for every \(x\in M\), every \(\eta\in T_xM\) with \(\|\eta\|_x=1\), and every \(t\ge 0\) such that \(R_x(\tau\eta)\in S\) for all \(\tau\in[0,t]\), the scalar function \(\tau\mapsto f(R_x(\tau\eta))\) is convex on \([0,t]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is retraction convex with respect to R in S if its restriction to every unit-direction retraction segment is convex whenever that entire segment lies in S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau\mapsto f(R_x(\tau\eta))\text{ is convex on }[0,t]

children.title: Local Geodesic Convexity
children.top_down_role: Convex behavior restricted to suitable geodesic neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Geodesic Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise local version of geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\). The function \(f\) is locally geodesically convex at \(x\) if there exists a strongly geodesically convex neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) such that, for every minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to U\),
\[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+t f(\gamma(1))\qquad(t\in[0,1]).\]
It is locally geodesically convex on a set \(C\) if this property holds at every \(x\in C\), with neighborhoods allowed to depend on \(x\). No global geodesic connection between arbitrary points of \(C\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is locally geodesically convex when it is convex along minimizing geodesics inside some strongly geodesically convex neighborhood of each point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Near each designated point, \(f\) restricts to a geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex neighborhood.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise local definition is coherent and matches the leaf, but its strongly geodesically convex-neighborhood convention lacks an authoritative citation.

children.title: Retraction–Geodesic Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Local regimes where retraction-based structure agrees with geodesic structure.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold and \(R:T\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\) is a second-order retraction.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(x\in\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Hess}(f\circ R_x)(0_x)=\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\), so their quadratic convexity tests at \(x\) coincide.

notation.meaning: retraction restricted to the tangent space at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order agreement between a retraction pullback and the exponential-map model at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order retraction satisfies \(R_x(0_x)=x\), \(\mathrm D R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\), and zero covariant acceleration at \(t=0\) for \(t\mapsto R_x(t\xi)\). Consequently, for every \(\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\), \[\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}f(R_x(t\xi))\right|_{t=0}=\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}f(\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\xi))\right|_{t=0}=\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\xi],\xi\rangle_x.\] Thus the pullback Hessian at the origin equals the Riemannian Hessian, although convexity away from the origin need not agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order retraction and the exponential map give the same second-order objective model at their base point, but their finite-neighborhood convexity may differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Retraction–Geodesic Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the compatibility leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports the precise second-order-retraction and pullback-Hessian claims. The explanatory derivation is proof text and should be removed after sourcing.

children.title: Local Convexity Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood, curvature, plus retraction effects that prevent local convex organization.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a smooth retraction on a Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal M,g)\).
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive Riemannian Hessian does not ensure convexity of \(f\circ R_x\) away from \(0_x\) when the retraction acceleration term is nonzero.

notation.meaning: retraction curve generated by a tangent vector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the acceleration term that can destroy local retraction convexity beyond base-point agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(c(t)=R_x(t\xi)\), the pullback curvature satisfies \[\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}f(c(t))=\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(c(t))[\dot c(t)],\dot c(t)\rangle_{c(t)}+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(c(t)),\nabla_{\dot c(t)}\dot c(t)\rangle_{c(t)}.\] The second term vanishes along geodesics but generally not along retraction curves. Hence even if \(\operatorname{Hess}f\) is positive semidefinite on a neighborhood, \(f\circ R_x\) can lose convexity where the acceleration term is sufficiently negative. Second-order compatibility controls this term only at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retraction curves have an acceleration contribution absent from geodesics. Away from the base point, that contribution can overturn positive Riemannian curvature and destroy pullback convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Convexity Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the acceleration identity is plausible, but its regularity and sign-based breakdown claim require an authoritative locator. The derivation is proof text.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is connected, compact, and has no boundary.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable and geodesically convex along every geodesic segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is constant on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact boundaryless-manifold obstruction for globally defined smooth geodesically convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Geodesic convexity implies \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\), and therefore \(\Delta f(x)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\geq0\). On a compact manifold without boundary, \(\int_{\mathcal M}\Delta f\,\mathrm dV=0\); hence \(\Delta f=0\). Positive semidefiniteness together with zero trace gives \(\operatorname{Hess}f=0\). Since \(f\) attains a maximum and is harmonic, it is constant on connected \(\mathcal M\). Thus nonconstant globally geodesically convex smooth objectives require a restricted domain or different global geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every smooth function convex along all geodesics of a connected compact boundaryless manifold is constant, obstructing nontrivial global geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Geodesic-Convexity Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-manifold obstruction fits the topic and appears standard, but no source supports the exact hypotheses and conclusion. The Laplacian and maximum-principle argument is proof text.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local minimizers of geodesically convex functions are global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An optimality-landscape consequence of geodesic convexity on the function's geodesically convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $f:S\to\mathbb R$ is geodesically convex, then every local minimizer of $f$ on $S$ is a global minimizer of $f$ on $S$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every local minimizer of a geodesically convex function is also a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_\star\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\text{ on }S\implies x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x).
