knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot-Based Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian finite-sum SVRG using a periodically refreshed full-gradient snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose a snapshot \(\tilde x\), compute \(\tilde g=\operatorname{grad}f(\tilde x)\), and initialize \(x_0=\tilde x\). At inner iteration \(t\), sample \(i_t\) uniformly and set
\[v_t=\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(x_t)-\mathcal T_{\tilde x\to x_t}\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(\tilde x)+\mathcal T_{\tilde x\to x_t}\tilde g,\qquad x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t).\]
After a prescribed inner-loop length, select the next snapshot from the inner iterates, recompute its full gradient, and repeat. Output the final snapshot or an iterate sampled according to the convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-gradient snapshot supplies a transported control variate that is periodically refreshed during stochastic inner iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction and \(\mathcal T\) maps the required tangent vectors.
Snapshot epochs and stepsizes are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\) with periodically refreshed \((\tilde x,\tilde g)\).

notation.meaning: vector transport from \(T_y\mathcal M\) to \(T_x\mathcal M\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the snapshot-based leaf and the displayed estimator is a recognizable Riemannian SVRG form, but no cited algorithm specifies the transport, snapshot-selection rule, or output convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive-Estimator Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian SARAH/SPIDER-type recursion with periodic batch recalibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0\in\mathcal M\) and compute \(v_0\) from a full or large-batch gradient at \(x_0\). For \(t\ge1\), either recalibrate \(v_t\) from a fresh batch at \(x_t\), or sample a batch \(B_t\) and set
\[v_t=\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_t)+\mathcal T_{x_{t-1}\to x_t}\left(v_{t-1}-\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_{t-1})\right).\]
Then update \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\). Stop after the prescribed oracle budget and output the designated final or randomly selected iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transported gradient-difference recursion updates the estimator cheaply between periodic large-batch recalibrations.
assumptions_latex: The same sampled batch is used in both component-gradient sums.
\(R\) and \(\mathcal T\) are defined along every update.
Recalibration times, batch sizes, and stepsizes are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_t\) follows the transported recursive difference rule and drives \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\).

notation.meaning: vector transport between consecutive tangent spaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the recursive-estimator leaf, but the record blends SARAH/SPIDER-style variants without a source fixing the recursion, recalibration rule, batch model, and output convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Table-Based Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian SAGA-type estimator maintaining one stored component gradient per finite-sum term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), store pairs \((\alpha_i,y_i)\) with \(y_i=\operatorname{grad}f_i(\alpha_i)\). At iterate \(x_t\), sample \(i_t\) uniformly and form
\[v_t=\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(x_t)-\mathcal T_{\alpha_{i_t}\to x_t}y_{i_t}+\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathcal T_{\alpha_j\to x_t}y_j.\]
Set \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\), replace \((\alpha_{i_t},y_{i_t})\) by \((x_t,\operatorname{grad}f_{i_t}(x_t))\), and leave other entries unchanged. Stop after the prescribed iteration or oracle budget and output the designated iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transported gradient table supplies a SAGA-type control variate while one component entry is refreshed per iteration.
assumptions_latex: Each stored vector can be transported from its reference point to \(x_t\).
The component index is sampled uniformly.
The retraction update is defined for the chosen stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_t\) is the table-corrected estimator and exactly one table entry is refreshed at iteration \(t\).

notation.meaning: reference point and stored component gradient

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the table-based leaf, but the transported SAGA formula and one-entry refresh convention require a specific Riemannian SAGA source; none is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Transported Variance-Control Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Places control-variate terms from different base points in the current tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,y\in\mathcal M\), let \(I\) be a sampled index, and let \(c_I(y)\in T_y\mathcal M\) have mean \(c(y)=\mathbb E_I[c_I(y)]\). A transported control-variate estimator at \(x\) has the form
\[v(x,y,I)=g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}c_I(y)+\mathcal T_{y\to x}c(y)\in T_x\mathcal M.\]
If \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\) is deterministic conditional on \((x,y)\) and linear, then
\[\mathbb E_I[v(x,y,I)]=\mathbb E_I[g_I(x)].\]
Thus transport makes the subtraction tangent-space consistent while preserving the estimator mean under these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector transport moves a control variate and its mean into the current tangent space, preserving unbiasedness when transport is fixed and linear.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\) is deterministic conditional on \((x,y)\) and linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_I[v(x,y,I)]=\mathbb E_I[g_I(x)]\) and \(v(x,y,I)\in T_x\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: vector transport from the reference tangent space to the current one

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent under fixed linear transport and matches the leaf, but no source supports it as the intended transported variance-control mechanism in this taxonomy.

children.title: Transport Bias
children.top_down_role: Systematic estimator error introduced by approximate or incompatible vector transport.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies bias introduced when implemented transport differs from the transport required by the control variate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an ideal estimator use a linear transport \(\mathcal P_{y\to x}\), while its implementation uses \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\):
\[v_{\mathcal T}=g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}c_I(y)+\mathcal P_{y\to x}c(y).\]
Conditional on \((x,y)\), with \(\mathbb E_I[c_I(y)]=c(y)\), its transport bias relative to \(\mathbb E_I[g_I(x)]\) is
\[b_{\mathrm{tr}}(x,y)=(\mathcal P_{y\to x}-\mathcal T_{y\to x})c(y).\]
Consequently \(\|b_{\mathrm{tr}}(x,y)\|\le\|\mathcal P_{y\to x}-\mathcal T_{y\to x}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|c(y)\|\); persistent transport mismatch can prevent an unbiased convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using mismatched transports for a sampled control variate and its mean creates bias controlled by the transport-operator error.
assumptions_latex: Both transports are linear maps from \(T_y\mathcal M\) to \(T_x\mathcal M\).
The mean term is transported by \(\mathcal P_{y\to x}\) while the sampled term uses \(\mathcal T_{y\to x}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_{\mathrm{tr}}=(\mathcal P_{y\to x}-\mathcal T_{y\to x})c(y)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebra is correct for the deliberately mismatched sampled-term and mean-term transports, but that convention is specialized and uncited. A source must establish that this is the intended transport-bias boundary rather than an artificial implementation mismatch.

children.title: Estimator Drift
children.top_down_role: Accumulating mismatch between recursive estimates plus current gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimator Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes accumulation of recursive-estimator error between exact or large-batch recalibrations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_t\in T_{x_t}\mathcal M\) estimate \(\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\), and define \(e_t=v_t-\operatorname{grad}f(x_t)\). Suppose a transported recursive update satisfies
\[\mathbb E[\|e_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\le(1+\rho_t)\|e_{t-1}\|^2+q_t.\]
Iterating this inequality gives
\[\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\le\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^t(1+\rho_j)\Bigr)\mathbb E\|e_0\|^2+\sum_{k=1}^t q_k\prod_{j=k+1}^t(1+\rho_j).\]
Estimator drift occurs when these accumulated amplification and innovation terms exceed the variance budget required by the convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive estimator errors drift when multiplicative amplification and per-step innovations accumulate beyond the admissible variance budget.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional second-moment recursion holds.
All products and sums are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\) obeys the displayed accumulated-drift bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accumulated scalar recursion follows from the assumed one-step inequality and the failure-boundary role fits, but no Riemannian estimator analysis is cited for that recursion or the stated variance-budget interpretation.

children.title: Snapshot Separation Effects
children.top_down_role: Bias or variance growth as reference points become geometrically distant.

knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot Separation Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates snapshot distance to the conditional variance of a transported control-variate estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[v=g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}g_I(y)+\mathcal T_{y\to x}\operatorname{grad}f(y),\]
where \(I\) is sampled uniformly. If component gradients satisfy the transported mean-square Lipschitz condition
\[\mathbb E_I\|g_I(x)-\mathcal T_{y\to x}g_I(y)\|^2\le L_{\mathcal T}^2d(x,y)^2,\]
then
\[\mathbb E_I\|v-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|^2\le L_{\mathcal T}^2d(x,y)^2.\]
Hence variance control deteriorates quadratically with snapshot separation under this condition, motivating bounded epoch lengths or snapshot refresh when \(d(x,y)\) becomes large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under transported mean-square smoothness, the control-variate variance grows at most quadratically with distance from the snapshot.
assumptions_latex: The transported mean-square Lipschitz inequality holds.
The estimator uses the exact full gradient at snapshot \(y\).
The sampled component gradient is unbiased at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_I\|v-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|^2\le L_{\mathcal T}^2d(x,y)^2\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian distance from snapshot to current point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variance conclusion is plausible under the displayed transported mean-square condition and appropriate unbiasedness at both points, but the condition and its applicability to the intended estimator need a specific source.

children.title: Estimator Recalibration
children.top_down_role: Refresh, correction, plus synchronization regimes limiting persistent estimator error.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimator Recalibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resets a drifting variance-reduced estimator using an exact or fresh large-batch gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose recalibration times \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots\), batch sizes \(B_k\), and stepsizes \(\eta_t\). At time \(t=\tau_k\), draw a fresh batch \(S_k\) and set
\[v_t=\frac1{B_k}\sum_{i\in S_k}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_t),\]
using the full index set when exact recalibration is required. For \(\tau_k<t<\tau_{k+1}\), update \(v_t\) by the prescribed transported recursive or control-variate rule. In every iteration set \(x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(-\eta_t v_t)\). Stop at the prescribed budget and output the designated iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At scheduled times, replace the accumulated estimator by a fresh batch or full gradient, then restart the variance-reduced recursion.
assumptions_latex: Recalibration times and batch sizes are fixed or chosen by a stated stopping rule.
Fresh recalibration samples are conditionally independent of the past.
The intervening estimator update and retraction are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\tau_k}=B_k^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_k}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_{\tau_k})\) resets accumulated estimator error.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits estimator recalibration, but the record combines exact and large-batch resets with unspecified intervening recursions and schedules. A cited algorithm is required to fix the intended variant.

assumptions_latex: The algorithm accesses individual summands only through the stated oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\) measures component-oracle calls needed for expected \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity.

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient of component i at x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\) on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\). An incremental first-order oracle queried at \((i,x)\) returns \((f_i(x),\operatorname{grad}f_i(x))\), possibly together with prescribed retraction or transport operations not charged as oracle calls. For a randomized algorithm producing \(X\), its incremental oracle complexity at tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is the least number \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\) of component queries sufficient to ensure \[\mathbb E\!\left[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2\right]\leq \varepsilon^2.\] The expectation includes all algorithmic sampling and output randomization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental complexity counts component value-gradient queries required to return a point whose expected squared Riemannian gradient norm is at most the prescribed tolerance squared.

children.title: Full-Gradient Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting for complete finite-sum gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Gradient Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts evaluations of the complete finite-sum Riemannian gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), a full-gradient oracle queried at \(x\in\mathcal M\) returns \(F(x)\) and \[\operatorname{grad}F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x).\] If an algorithm returns a random point \(X\), its full-gradient complexity \(Q_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)\) is the number of such complete-gradient evaluations required to guarantee \(\mathbb E[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2]\leq\varepsilon^2\). Component evaluations used internally to assemble one complete gradient are not counted separately under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-gradient complexity counts complete finite-sum gradient evaluations needed to achieve expected Riemannian stationarity.
assumptions_latex: Every component gradient belongs to the common tangent space \(T_x\mathcal M\) at the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One full-gradient call returns the average of all \(n\) component gradients at a common point.

children.title: Component-Gradient Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Gradient Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts individual finite-sum Riemannian gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A component-gradient query selects \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\) and returns \(\operatorname{grad}f_i(x)\), optionally with \(f_i(x)\). For an algorithm returning \(X\), the component-gradient complexity \(Q_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon)\) is the total number of such queries required to ensure \[\mathbb E\!\left[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2\right]\leq\varepsilon^2.\] Repeated queries, minibatch members, and all components used to form a complete gradient are counted individually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component-gradient complexity counts every sampled component gradient, including each member of minibatches and full-gradient sweeps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minibatch of size \(b\) costs \(b\) component-gradient queries under this convention.

children.title: Oracle-Cost Conversion
children.top_down_role: Dataset-size plus batching regimes translating between the two cost measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Cost Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact accounting conversion when full gradients are assembled componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an execution makes \(q_f\) full-gradient calls and \(q_c\) additional component-gradient calls for a finite sum with \(n\) components. If every full gradient is assembled by querying each component once at the same point, then its equivalent component-oracle cost is exactly \[q_{\mathrm{eq}}=nq_f+q_c.\] Consequently, any guarantee stated as \((Q_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon),Q_{\mathrm{comp}}^{\mathrm{extra}}(\varepsilon))\) implies the component-query bound \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\leq nQ_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)+Q_{\mathrm{comp}}^{\mathrm{extra}}(\varepsilon)\). This conversion excludes parallel-time discounts and unequal component costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each assembled full-gradient call by exactly n component calls, then add all other component calls.
assumptions_latex: A full gradient uses all \(n\) components exactly once.
All component queries have equal unit oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_{\mathrm{eq}}=nq_f+q_c\).

children.title: Mixed-Oracle Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued accounting for algorithms using full and component gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm attaining \(\mathbb E[\|\operatorname{grad}F(X)\|^2]\leq\varepsilon^2\), its mixed-oracle complexity is the ordered pair \[\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)=\bigl(Q_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon),Q_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon)\bigr),\] where the second coordinate counts only component queries not already charged inside the first. Given nonnegative unit costs \(c_f\) and \(c_c\), the corresponding scalar resource cost is \[C_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)=c_fQ_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)+c_cQ_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon).\] Reporting the pair preserves information that a single scalar count loses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed complexity records full-gradient and additional component-gradient calls separately, with optional conversion to a weighted scalar cost.
assumptions_latex: The two oracle classes and the no-double-counting convention are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is vector-valued, while \(C_{\mathrm{mix}}\) depends on the chosen cost model.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory–Computation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting principle for finite-sum variance-reduction state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each stored tangent vector require \(d\) scalars. A table method retaining one transported or reference-point component gradient per summand uses \(\Theta(nd)\) scalar memory and can update only sampled entries. A refresh method retaining a reference full gradient and \(O(1)\) working tangent vectors uses \(\Theta(d)\) scalar memory but must periodically spend \(n\) component queries to rebuild that reference. Thus oracle complexity comparisons must report both query counts and stored state; neither memory profile alone implies a universally smaller query count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient tables spend linear-in-sample memory to reuse components; refresh schemes use dimension-scale memory but periodically pay for complete component sweeps.
assumptions_latex: Stored vectors have \(d\) scalar coordinates in a fixed representation.
Transport metadata and indices require lower-order storage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representative storage costs are \(\Theta(nd)\) for a component table and \(\Theta(d)\) for a refresh state.

notation.meaning: number of scalars per represented tangent vector

A source covering the relevant algorithm classes and storage models is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Dependent Finite-Sum Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions delimiting when Euclidean-style finite-sum bounds transfer to a manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-sum complexity guarantee is geometry-uniform on a region \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal M\) only if its constants can be chosen uniformly over \(\mathcal U\). A standard sufficient regime requires: component gradients are retraction-smooth with a common constant \(L\); the retraction differential and chosen vector transport have uniformly bounded distortion; and all iterates remain in \(\mathcal U\), where curvature and injectivity or retraction radii admit uniform bounds. If any required bound varies with \(x\), the resulting oracle estimate is geometry-dependent and must display the corresponding supremum or local constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum rates are geometry-uniform only when smoothness, retraction, transport, curvature, and iterate-region constants are uniformly controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal U\) contains every iterate and every retraction curve used by the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform geometric constants yield a uniform regime; point-dependent constants yield a geometry-dependent complexity statement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the proposed sufficient regime, and the necessary retraction, transport, curvature, and radius assumptions vary materially by algorithm and theorem. A manifold finite-sum complexity source is needed before fixing this condition statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Manifold Coordinate Adaptivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise adaptive scaling intrinsic to a fixed product decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M=\mathcal M_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal M_m\) with product metric, retractions \(R^{(j)}\), and stochastic gradient blocks \(g_{t,j}\in T_{x_{t,j}}\mathcal M_j\). Initialize \(x_0\in\mathcal M\) and \(v_{0,j}=0\). For \(t\geq1\), set \[v_{t,j}=\beta v_{t-1,j}+(1-\beta)\|g_{t,j}\|^2,\qquad x_{t+1,j}=R^{(j)}_{x_{t,j}}\!\left(-\alpha_t\frac{g_{t,j}}{\sqrt{v_{t,j}}+\delta}\right).\] Stop under a prescribed iteration, gradient, or budget rule and return the selected iterate. Each scalar accumulator is attached to a manifold factor, not to coordinates within that factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain one squared-gradient accumulator per product factor and retract a separately scaled stochastic-gradient step on each factor.
assumptions_latex: The product decomposition and product metric are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is invariant under factorwise isometries but generally depends on the chosen product decomposition.

notation.meaning: stochastic gradient block on factor j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blockwise update is a plausible product-manifold adaptive algorithm, but no source identifies this exact variant. Its claimed invariance additionally requires equivariance of the stochastic-gradient rule and factor retractions under the admitted factorwise isometries, which is not stated.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Adaptive Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-free preconditioning by positive bundle endomorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An intrinsic adaptive scaling at \(x_t\in\mathcal M\) is a positive-definite, self-adjoint linear map \(A_t:T_{x_t}\mathcal M\to T_{x_t}\mathcal M\) defined from geometric data and transported optimization history. Given a stochastic gradient \(g_t\in T_{x_t}\mathcal M\), the scaled step is \[\eta_t=-\alpha_t A_t^{-1/2}g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(\eta_t).\] Intrinsicness requires equivariance: for every relevant Riemannian isometry \(\phi\), the transformed rule satisfies \(A_t^{\phi}=D\phi_{x_t}A_tD\phi_{x_t}^{-1}\). Hence the update represents the same tangent vector independently of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic adaptivity scales gradients with a positive geometric operator whose transformation law makes the resulting tangent step coordinate-independent.
assumptions_latex: \(A_t\) is invertible, self-adjoint, and positive definite under the Riemannian metric.
The history used to construct \(A_t\) is compared through specified vector transports.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivariance of \(A_t\) makes \(\eta_t\) coordinate-independent under the admitted isometries.

notation.meaning: differential of an isometry at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operator formulation is plausible, but no source establishes this definition or its admitted transformation class. Equivariance under relevant isometries supports invariance under those isometries, not unrestricted coordinate independence without a more general bundle-coordinate transformation statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Momentum Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Momentum recursion with tangent-space transport between iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), set \(m_0=0\in T_{x_0}\mathcal M\), and fix a retraction \(R\) with associated vector transport \(\mathcal T\). After observing \(g_t\in T_{x_t}\mathcal M\), form \[m_t=\beta_t\mathcal T_{x_{t-1}\to x_t}(m_{t-1})+(1-\beta_t)g_t,\qquad \eta_t=-\alpha_t A_t^{-1/2}m_t,\qquad x_{t+1}=R_{x_t}(\eta_t).\] Here \(A_t\) is a positive-definite adaptive scaling on \(T_{x_t}\mathcal M\). Stop by a prescribed budget or stationarity rule and return the designated iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transport old momentum into the current tangent space, combine it with the new gradient, scale it adaptively, and retract.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T_{x_{t-1}\to x_t}\) maps the previous tangent space into the current one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every term in \(m_t\) lies in the common tangent space \(T_{x_t}\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: vector transport associated with the update

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Transporting momentum into the current tangent space is structurally correct, but the exact transport-and-scaling recursion has no source. The initialization also does not specify how the displayed recursion begins, since its first indexed use requires both a previous and current iterate.

children.title: Coordinate Dependence
children.top_down_role: Adaptive behavior that changes under chart or local-coordinate choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of coordinatewise adaptive scaling under a rescaled chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R\), an objective \(f\), and the coordinatewise normalized update \(x^+=x-\alpha g_x/\sqrt{g_x^2}\) for \(g_x\neq0\). Under the reparameterization \(y=ax\) with \(a>0\), the Euclidean coordinate gradient is \(g_y=g_x/a\). Applying the same formula in the \(y\)-coordinate and mapping back gives \[x^+=x-\frac{\alpha}{a}\frac{g_x}{|g_x|},\] whereas applying it directly in the \(x\)-coordinate gives \(x^+=x-\alpha g_x/|g_x|\). For \(a\neq1\), the iterates differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized coordinatewise update changes under simple coordinate rescaling, so its trajectory is not intrinsically defined.
assumptions_latex: Both coordinate formulas use the same numerical stepsize \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adaptive update is not invariant under the coordinate change \(y=ax\).

notation.meaning: coordinate gradients in the x and y parameterizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rescaling calculation is directly checkable and the counterexample kind fits Coordinate Dependence, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale. Evidence is therefore required before candidate-review acceptance.

children.title: Representation Dependence
children.top_down_role: Adaptive behavior that changes across embeddings, quotients, or equivalent parameterizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance boundary for ambient coordinatewise preconditioners.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the Euclidean manifold \(\mathbb R^d\), let an ambient adaptive direction be \(U(g)=D(g)g\), where \(D(g)=\operatorname{diag}((\delta+g_1^2)^{-1/2},\ldots,(\delta+g_d^2)^{-1/2})\) and \(\delta>0\). Two orthonormal representations related by \(Q\in O(d)\) describe the same direction only if \[U(Qg)=QU(g).\] For a general non-permutation rotation \(Q\) and unequal nonzero coordinates of \(g\), this equality fails. Therefore ambient coordinatewise adaptation depends on the chosen orthonormal representation unless its scaling rule is orthogonally equivariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise ambient scaling generally changes after rotating the representation; invariance requires the preconditioner to commute with the representation change.
assumptions_latex: \(d\geq2\), \(\delta>0\), and \(Q\) is a non-permutation orthogonal transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of \(D(Qg)Q=QD(g)\) implies representation-dependent adaptive directions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivariance test is appropriate for Representation Dependence, and coordinatewise scaling generally fails it, but no cited source or standard-field rationale supports the generic rotation claim and stated failure boundary.

children.title: Reparameterization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of scaling, momentum, plus convergence behavior to equivalent variable descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reparameterization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of scalar coordinatewise normalization under a rescaled chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two scalar coordinates represent the same point by \(x=cz\), where \(c>0\). Consider the adaptive coordinate increment \(\Delta x=-\alpha g_x/(\sqrt{v_x}+\varepsilon)\), with \(v_x>0\). Tensorial transformation of the derivative and its squared scale gives \(g_z=cg_x\) and \(v_z=c^2v_x\). Applying the same coordinate formula in \(z\) and mapping the increment back gives \(c\Delta z=-\alpha c^2g_x/(c\sqrt{v_x}+\varepsilon)\), which generally differs from \(\Delta x\). Thus even this elementary reparameterization changes the represented tangent step unless the stepsize or preconditioner is transformed appropriately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinatewise adaptive step generally changes under coordinate rescaling, so it does not define an intrinsic manifold update without an appropriate transformation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[c\Delta z\ne\Delta x\quad\text{in general}.\]

notation.meaning: gradient coordinate and adaptive squared scale

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the scalar rescaling calculation is internally consistent. No citation is supplied for interpreting this calculation as the invariance boundary of manifold adaptive methods, so the record requires an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Intrinsic-Invariance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric constructions that reduce coordinate or representation sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic-Invariance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance condition for intrinsic stochastic adaptive updates under Riemannian isometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:(\mathcal M,g)\to(\mathcal N,h)\) be a Riemannian isometry. An adaptive update \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(U(x_k,G_k,S_k))\) is intrinsically invariant when its stochastic gradient, state, update map, and retraction satisfy \(G_k^{\mathcal N}=D\Phi_{x_k}G_k^{\mathcal M}\), \(S_k^{\mathcal N}=\Phi_*S_k^{\mathcal M}\), \(U(\Phi(x),\Phi_*G,\Phi_*S)=D\Phi_xU(x,G,S)\), and \(R^{\mathcal N}_{\Phi(x)}(D\Phi_x\eta)=\Phi(R^{\mathcal M}_x(\eta))\). With correspondingly coupled randomness and states, the iterates obey \(y_k=\Phi(x_k)\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive method is intrinsic when every state and update is isometry-equivariant and the retraction commutes with the isometry; then transformed runs have matching trajectories.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:(\mathcal M,g)\to(\mathcal N,h)\) is a Riemannian isometry.
The two runs use correspondingly coupled stochastic samples and initial states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y_0=\Phi(x_0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_k=\Phi(x_k)\ \text{for all }k\ge0.\]

notation.meaning: differential of the isometry at the current point
retraction used to map a tangent update to the manifold

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits an intrinsic-invariance regime, and the stated equivariance conditions plausibly imply conjugate trajectories. However, the adaptive-state pushforward \(\Phi_*S\) is not defined for a specified state space, and no source supports this particular invariant adaptive-method framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Riemannian Quasi-Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transported inverse-BFGS scheme using stochastic Riemannian gradient differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), a retraction \(R\), vector transport \(\mathcal T\), and positive-definite \(H_0:T_{x_0}\mathcal M\to T_{x_0}\mathcal M\), sample a gradient estimate \(g_k\), set \(\eta_k=-\alpha_kH_kg_k\), and update \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\). Form \(s_k=\mathcal T_{\eta_k}\eta_k\) and a matched-sample difference \(y_k=g_{k+1}-\mathcal T_{\eta_k}g_k\). Transport \(H_k\) to \(\widetilde H_k\) on \(T_{x_{k+1}}\mathcal M\). If \(\langle s_k,y_k\rangle>0\), let \(\rho_k=\langle s_k,y_k\rangle^{-1}\) and apply \(H_{k+1}=(I-\rho_ks_k\otimes y_k)\widetilde H_k(I-\rho_ky_k\otimes s_k)+\rho_ks_k\otimes s_k\); otherwise damp or skip the update. Stop at a prescribed stochastic stationarity tolerance or sampling budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method transports an inverse-Hessian approximation between tangent spaces and updates it from matched-sample stochastic gradient differences satisfying a curvature test.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction and \(\mathcal T\) is a compatible vector transport.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\alpha_kH_kg_k).\]

notation.meaning: inverse-Hessian approximation on the current tangent space
vector transport along the accepted step
transported displacement and stochastic secant difference

children.title: Subsampled Riemannian Newton Methods
children.top_down_role: Newton families using sampled gradient or Hessian information.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsampled Riemannian Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized tangent-space Newton iteration using sampled gradients and Hessians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-sum objective \(f(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x)\) on a Riemannian manifold, choose samples \(G_k\) and \(H_k\), form \(g_k=|G_k|^{-1}\sum_{i\in G_k}\operatorname{grad}f_i(x_k)\) and \(B_k=|H_k|^{-1}\sum_{i\in H_k}\operatorname{Hess}f_i(x_k)\), and select \(\lambda_k\ge0\). Compute an exact or inexact solution of \((B_k+\lambda_kI)\eta_k=-g_k\), require a descent or residual safeguard, and set \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\alpha_k\eta_k)\). Stop when a prescribed sampled or independently validated stationarity criterion is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subsampled Riemannian Newton method solves a regularized tangent-space Newton system built from sampled component gradients and Hessians, then retracts the step.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice Riemannian differentiable for every \(i\).
\(R\) is a retraction on the iterates' tangent spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(B_k+\lambda_kI)\eta_k=-g_k,\qquad x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\alpha_k\eta_k).\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and finite-sum tangent Newton system match the terminal container. The descent or residual safeguard and validation criterion remain generic, and no source is supplied for the sampled Riemannian gradient/Hessian scheme.

children.title: Subsampled Riemannian Trust-Region Methods
children.top_down_role: Trust-region families using sampled tangent-space models.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsampled Riemannian Trust-Region Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampled quadratic model with tangent trust region and stochastic acceptance test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x_k\in\mathcal M\), construct sampled estimates \(g_k\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) and self-adjoint \(B_k:T_{x_k}\mathcal M\to T_{x_k}\mathcal M\). Approximately minimize \(m_k(\eta)=\widehat f_k+\langle g_k,\eta\rangle+\tfrac12\langle\eta,B_k\eta\rangle\) subject to \(\|\eta\|\le\Delta_k\). Using a sufficiently accurate estimate of actual reduction, compute \(\rho_k=(\widehat f_k(x_k)-\widehat f_k(R_{x_k}(\eta_k)))/(m_k(0)-m_k(\eta_k))\). Accept \(R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\) when \(\rho_k\) exceeds the acceptance threshold, otherwise retain \(x_k\), and update \(\Delta_k\) from \(\rho_k\). Stop at a validated stationarity tolerance or budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method minimizes a sampled quadratic model inside a tangent trust region and accepts the retracted step when estimated actual and predicted reductions agree sufficiently.
assumptions_latex: The reduction estimate and sampled model meet the prescribed accuracy event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{k+1}\in\{x_k,R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\},\qquad \|\eta_k\|\le\Delta_k.\]

source_refs.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

The cited deterministic Euclidean trust-region section does not support the subsampled Riemannian or stochastic-accuracy aspects. In addition, \(\widehat f_k\) is used both as the model constant and as a function evaluated at two points; a domain-specific source is needed before fixing that estimator convention.

children.title: Curvature-Sample Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Sampling regimes governing Hessian-model fidelity plus step reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Sample Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-norm accuracy requirement for sampled Riemannian Hessians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_k\) be a sampled self-adjoint curvature operator on \(T_{x_k}\mathcal M\), and let \(H_k=\operatorname{Hess}f(x_k)\). A deterministic accuracy event is \(\|B_k-H_k\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon_{H,k}\). For a step-scaled second-order model, the sufficient form \(\varepsilon_{H,k}\le c_H\max\{\|\eta_k\|,\epsilon\}\) bounds curvature-induced model error by \(\tfrac12\varepsilon_{H,k}\|\eta_k\|^2\). In a stochastic regime the event must hold conditionally on the past with probability at least \(1-\delta_k\), where the sequence \((\delta_k)\) is chosen to support the desired aggregate guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature sample is accurate when its operator-norm error is controlled, possibly relative to step size, with a specified conditional failure probability.
assumptions_latex: \(B_k\) and \(H_k\) are self-adjoint operators on the same tangent space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left|\tfrac12\langle\eta_k,(B_k-H_k)\eta_k\rangle\right|\le\tfrac12\varepsilon_{H,k}\|\eta_k\|^2.\]

notation.meaning: operator norm induced by the Riemannian metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the accuracy container, and the displayed operator-norm inequality correctly yields the quadratic-form error bound. The step-scaled tolerance, conditional probability event, and claim about supporting an aggregate guarantee require a specific source and a stated condition on \((\delta_k)\).

children.title: Sample-Reuse Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fresh-sample, shared-sample, plus persistent-sample choices for curvature models.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Reuse Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity conditions for fresh, fixed-block, and independently validated curvature samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_k\) contain all iterates and samples revealed before iteration \(k\). Fresh sampling permits conditional statements such as \(\mathbb E[B_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\operatorname{Hess}f(x_k)\). If a sample \(S_j\) is reused over a block \(k=j,\ldots,j+q-1\), this conditional unbiasedness generally disappears because \(x_k\) depends on \(S_j\); validity must instead follow from a uniform event \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal U_j}\|B_{S_j}(x)-\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon_j\) containing the block iterates. Alternatively, acceptance or stopping may be certified using a sample independent of the construction sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh samples support conditional unbiasedness; reused samples require uniform accuracy over the visited region or independent validation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_k\) records the algorithmic history before sampling at iteration \(k\).
Every reused-block iterate lies in \(\mathcal U_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{reuse requires uniform control or independent validation, not pointwise conditional unbiasedness alone}.\]

notation.meaning: region containing all iterates in the reuse block

The cited general stochastic-optimization chapter does not specifically support reused Riemannian curvature samples, the proposed uniform event, or the alternative certification rule.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Cubic-Regularization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian cubic model using stochastic gradient and Hessian estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), a retraction \(R\), and \(\sigma_0>0\), sample \(g_k\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) and a self-adjoint \(B_k\). Compute an approximate global minimizer or certified sufficient-decrease step for \(m_k(\eta)=\widehat f_k+\langle g_k,\eta\rangle+\tfrac12\langle\eta,B_k\eta\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|\eta\|^3\). Set the trial point to \(R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\), estimate its actual reduction using prescribed samples, and accept it when the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio exceeds a threshold. Decrease \(\sigma_k\) after reliable success and increase it after failure. Stop using an independently reliable first- or second-order stationarity test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method minimizes a stochastic cubic tangent model, retracts the step, and adapts regularization according to estimated actual versus predicted reduction.
assumptions_latex: Gradient, curvature, and reduction estimates satisfy the algorithm's stated accuracy events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\eta_k\approx\arg\min_{\eta\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M}m_k(\eta),\qquad x_k^+=R_{x_k}(\eta_k).\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the cubic-regularization method container. The model is plausible, but the sufficient-decrease certificate, sampling rules, reduction estimator, parameter updates, and reliable stopping test are not specified precisely enough to identify one established stochastic Riemannian algorithm, and no source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy-Curvature Failure Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missed negative curvature can produce false second-order termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the Euclidean manifold \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x_1^2-\tfrac12x_2^2\). At \(x=0\), \(\nabla f(0)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(0)=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), so the point is a strict saddle. Suppose a noisy curvature oracle returns \(B=I\) with positive probability. On that event, the cubic model \(m(\eta)=\tfrac12\langle\eta,B\eta\rangle+\tfrac{\sigma}{3}\|\eta\|^3\) has its unique minimizer at \(\eta=0\). A method that terminates from the sampled gradient and sampled minimum eigenvalue can therefore declare second-order stationarity at a strict saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If noise hides a negative Hessian eigenvalue, a stochastic curvature method can return a zero step and falsely certify a strict saddle.
assumptions_latex: The curvature oracle returns \(B=I\) with positive probability at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lambda_{\min}(B)>0\quad\text{while}\quad\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(0))=-1.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind correctly fits the failure-regime container. The Euclidean example is internally consistent and shows that a sampled positive-definite curvature matrix can conceal a strict saddle, but the record has no cited evidence as required for this nontrivial failure claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Subdifferential Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic Fréchet and limiting subdifferentials for lower-semicontinuous manifold functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous on a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold. For \(f(x)<+\infty\), the intrinsic Fréchet subdifferential consists of vectors \(v\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,\log_x y\rangle+o(d(x,y))\) as \(y\to x\) within a normal neighborhood. The intrinsic limiting subdifferential \(\partial f(x)\) consists of limits \(v=\lim_j\mathcal T_{x_j\to x}v_j\), where \(x_j\to x\), \(f(x_j)\to f(x)\), and each \(v_j\) is a Fréchet subgradient at \(x_j\). Intrinsic stationarity means \(0_x\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic subgradients are defined through first-order geodesic support inequalities and transported limits, without choosing an ambient representation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\ \text{is intrinsically stationary}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0_x\in\partial f(x).\]

notation.meaning: local inverse exponential vector at x
parallel transport along the local minimizing geodesic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the intrinsic-interface container, and the finite-dimensional Fréchet and limiting constructions are plausible. A variational-analysis source is required to support the exact little-o formulation, transported-limit definition, and use of local parallel transport.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intrinsic subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both the pointwise set of intrinsic subgradients and the resulting set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\) be convex and let \(x\in A\). The subdifferential of \(f\) at \(x\) is
\[
\partial f(x):=\{\omega_x\in T_x^*A:\omega_x\text{ is a subgradient of }f\text{ at }x\}.
\]
The set-valued map
\[
\partial f:x\mapsto\partial f(x)
\]
is called the subdifferential of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential at x is the set of all subgradients of f at x. The assignment mapping each point to this set is the subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\omega_x\in T_x^*A:\omega_x\text{ is a subgradient of }f\text{ at }x\},\qquad \partial f:x\mapsto\partial f(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded Tangent–Normal Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient limiting-subgradient stationarity for a smooth embedded manifold constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a smooth embedded manifold and let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper near \(x\in\mathcal M\). The embedded tangent–normal stationarity condition is \(0\in P_{T_x\mathcal M}\partial F(x)\). Equivalently, there exists \(v\in\partial F(x)\) with \(v\in N_x\mathcal M\), or \(0\in\partial F(x)+N_x\mathcal M\). Under a subdifferential chain rule that identifies the intrinsic subdifferential of \(F|_{\mathcal M}\) with \(P_{T_x\mathcal M}\partial F(x)\), this condition is equivalent to intrinsic stationarity of the restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embedded stationarity requires an ambient subgradient to be normal to the manifold; equivalence with intrinsic stationarity needs an appropriate chain-rule qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a smooth embedded manifold.
The selected ambient subdifferential \(\partial F(x)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in P_{T_x\mathcal M}\partial F(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\partial F(x)\cap N_x\mathcal M\ne\varnothing.\]

notation.meaning: orthogonal projection onto the tangent space
normal space of the embedded manifold

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the stationarity container. The projection, normal-intersection, and normal-sum formulations are equivalent for the selected set-valued subdifferential, but equivalence with intrinsic stationarity depends materially on which limiting subdifferential and chain-rule qualification are used. No supporting source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Stationarity Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retraction-based proximal-gradient residual for a smooth-plus-nonsmooth composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=f+h\) on a Riemannian manifold, with \(f\) differentiable and \(h\) proper, choose \(t>0\) and a retraction \(R\). Define \(\eta_t(x)\) as a selected minimizer of \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2t}\|\eta\|^2+h(R_x(\eta))\) over \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\), and define the composite stationarity measure \(\mathcal G_t(x)=\|\eta_t(x)\|/t\). If the subproblem is locally well posed and the limiting-subdifferential chain rule applies at \(\eta=0\), then \(\mathcal G_t(x)=0\) implies \(0_x\in\operatorname{grad}f(x)+\partial h(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The norm of a retraction-based proximal tangent step, divided by its stepsize, measures composite stationarity and vanishes only at a qualified stationary point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(h\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
The proximal tangent subproblem has a selected minimizer and satisfies the stated chain rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal G_t(x)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad0_x\in\operatorname{grad}f(x)+\partial h(x).\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the stationarity-measure container, and the one-way zero-residual implication is appropriately qualified. A source is needed for this particular retraction-based proximal subproblem, its existence assumptions, and the limiting-subdifferential chain rule yielding the stated stationarity condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Nonsmoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why smoothness is preserved only under regular coordinate changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=|x|\), and parameterize \(x\) by \(P(u)=u^2\). The original objective \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x=0\), whereas the represented objective satisfies \((f\circ P)(u)=u^2\) and is smooth at \(u=0\). This does not contradict coordinate invariance of smoothness: \(P\) is not a local diffeomorphism at \(u=0\), since \(DP(0)=0\). Thus a singular or noninjective representation may conceal nonsmooth stationarity and cannot be treated as a smooth manifold chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonsmooth function |x| becomes the smooth function u² under x=u² because that parameterization is singular, not a valid local coordinate change at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(P(u)=u^2\) is used as a representation of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\notin C^1\) at \(0\), while \(f\circ P\in C^\infty\), because \(DP(0)=0\).

notation.meaning: Possibly singular parameterization of the represented variable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct, matches the representation-dependent nonsmoothness leaf, and is appropriately classified as a counterexample. However, it has no citation or explicit standard-field rationale, so its claims about singular parameterizations and invalid manifold charts lack the required evidence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riemannian Multi-objective Optimization Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the problem class only; no particular ordering, Pareto concept, or solution method is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multi-objective optimization problem on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\) seeks to minimize or maximize multiple objective functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\), with \(m\ge 2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-objective optimization problem on a Riemannian manifold seeks to minimize or maximize two or more objective functions whose common domain is the manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The simultaneous optimization of }(f_1,\ldots,f_m)\text{ over }\mathcal M\text{ is a Riemannian multi-objective optimization problem.}

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-plus-Regularizer Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the basic composite objective on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold. A smooth-plus-regularizer model is the problem \[\min_{x\in\mathcal M} F(x):=f(x)+h(x),\] where \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable and \(h:\mathcal M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, but may be nonsmooth or extended-valued. Its effective feasible set is \(\operatorname{dom}h=\{x\in\mathcal M:h(x)<+\infty\}\). A first-order composite method separately accesses the Riemannian gradient of \(f\) and a proximal or generalized-subdifferential interface for \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold composite objective is the sum of a differentiable function and a proper lower-semicontinuous regularizer, which may encode nonsmooth penalties or constraints.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
\(f\in C^1(\mathcal M)\) and \(h\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f+h\) is a smooth-plus-regularizer model with effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}h\).

notation.meaning: Set on which the regularizer is finite.
Riemannian gradient of the smooth term.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Regularizer Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes a regularizer from an embedding space to the manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be an embedded submanifold of a Euclidean space \(E\), with inclusion \(\iota:\mathcal M\hookrightarrow E\), and let \(H:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. The ambient-regularizer restriction is \[h:=H\circ\iota,\qquad h(x)=H(x)\quad(x\in\mathcal M).\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}h=\mathcal M\cap\operatorname{dom}H\). Ambient convexity or proximal tractability of \(H\) does not by itself imply geodesic convexity or an explicitly computable intrinsic proximal mapping for \(h\), because manifold distance and feasible geodesics differ from their ambient Euclidean counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambient regularizer restricts to the embedded manifold by evaluation on manifold points; ambient convexity and easy Euclidean proximal steps need not survive intrinsically.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset E\) is an embedded submanifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h=H|_{\mathcal M}\) and \(\operatorname{dom}h=\mathcal M\cap\operatorname{dom}H\).

notation.meaning: Inclusion of the manifold into the ambient space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restriction formula and effective-domain identity are correct and fit a definition container. The additional claims about failure of ambient convexity and Euclidean proximal tractability to imply intrinsic properties are nontrivial manifold claims with no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Geodesically Convex Composites
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines geodesic convexity for a composite objective on a geodesically convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathcal M\) be geodesically convex: every \(x,y\in D\) are joined by a minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to D\). A composite \(F=f+h:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is intrinsically geodesically convex when, for every such \(x,y,\gamma\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[F(\gamma(t))\le (1-t)F(x)+tF(y).\] It is a geodesically convex smooth-plus-regularizer composite when \(f\in C^1(D)\) and both \(f\) and the proper lower-semicontinuous function \(h\) satisfy this inequality. The definition uses manifold geodesics rather than chords in an embedding space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite is intrinsically convex when its value along every minimizing geodesic is bounded by the linear interpolation of endpoint values.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a geodesically convex subset of \((\mathcal M,g)\).
\(f\in C^1(D)\) and \(h:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f+h\) is geodesically convex on \(D\) when both summands are geodesically convex there.

notation.meaning: A minimizing geodesic joining two points of the domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits a definition container and states a coherent strong form of geodesic convexity quantified over the relevant minimizing geodesics. An authoritative source is needed to confirm that this quantifier convention and the extended-valued composite formulation match the intended local terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Tractability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates well-posed proximal models from computationally accessible ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal M\) and \(\lambda>0\), define the intrinsic proximal set \[\operatorname{Prox}_{\lambda h}(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal M}\left\{h(y)+\frac{d(x,y)^2}{2\lambda}\right\}.\] The regularizer is proximally tractable on \(D\subseteq\mathcal M\) only if this set is nonempty for every requested \(x\in D\), a minimizer can be computed to the accuracy required by the outer method, and the cost of doing so is controlled. Proper lower semicontinuity may give existence under additional compactness or coercivity, but it does not supply computability, uniqueness, or an efficient oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold regularizer is proximally tractable only when its distance-regularized subproblem is solvable to controlled accuracy and cost, not merely mathematically well posed.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a complete Riemannian manifold with distance \(d\).
\(h:\mathcal M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is proximally tractable on \(D\) only when \(\operatorname{Prox}_{\lambda h}(x)\neq\varnothing\) and admits a controlled-cost accuracy oracle for requested \((x,\lambda)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Space Proximal Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the standard local composite model in one tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x\in\mathcal M\), let \(R_x:T_x\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\) be a retraction and let \(L>0\). The tangent-space proximal model for \(F=f+h\) is \[m_x(\eta)=f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x+\frac{L}{2}\|\eta\|_x^2+h(R_x(\eta)),\qquad \eta\in T_x\mathcal M.\] A proximal direction is any \(\eta_x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in T_x\mathcal M}m_x(\eta)\), and the trial point is \(x^+=R_x(\eta_x)\). This model linearizes only the smooth term and retains the regularizer through its pullback.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent proximal model linearizes the smooth term, adds a quadratic metric penalty, and evaluates the regularizer after retracting the tangent displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_x\in\operatorname*{argmin}m_x\) defines the trial point \(x^+=R_x(\eta_x)\).

notation.meaning: Retraction based at the current point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind and tangent-space model match the leaf. Because the precise pullback model, retraction update, and proximal-direction convention are specialized Riemannian composite-optimization constructions, a source with a theorem, definition, or algorithm locator is required.

children.title: Intrinsic Proximal Methods
children.top_down_role: Proximal constructions based on intrinsic distance or manifold geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Proximal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the exact distance-based proximal-point iteration on a manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a complete Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal M,g)\), a proper lower-semicontinuous objective \(F:\mathcal M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), an initial point \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and parameters \(\lambda_k>0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), choose \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal M}\left\{F(y)+\frac{d(x_k,y)^2}{2\lambda_k}\right\}.\] Stop when a prescribed stationarity, displacement, or objective-decrease tolerance is met; otherwise continue. The construction is intrinsic because its regularization uses only the Riemannian distance and requires no embedding or retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic proximal point iteration minimizes the objective plus squared Riemannian distance from the current iterate, stopping under a specified tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Each displayed proximal subproblem has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname{Prox}_{\lambda_k F}(x_k)\) until the chosen stopping rule is satisfied.

notation.meaning: Positive proximal parameter at iteration k.

children.title: Retraction-Based Proximal Methods
children.top_down_role: Proximal constructions using tangent models plus retraction mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction-Based Proximal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a proximal update through a tangent model and retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), a retraction \(R\), parameters \(L_k>0\), and \(F=f+h\) with \(f\in C^1(\mathcal M)\). At iteration \(k\), compute \[\eta_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M}\left\{\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_k),\eta\rangle_{x_k}+\frac{L_k}{2}\|\eta\|_{x_k}^2+h(R_{x_k}(\eta))\right\},\] and set \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\). Stop when \(\|\eta_k\|_{x_k}\) or another declared stationarity measure is below tolerance. A line search may increase \(L_k\) until sufficient decrease holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retraction-based proximal method solves a regularized tangent model and maps its direction back to the manifold, optionally using backtracking.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^1(\mathcal M)\), while \(h\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(R\) is a retraction and each tangent subproblem is solvable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k)\), with termination governed by the declared stationarity tolerance.

notation.meaning: Proximal direction in the current tangent space.
Retraction used to update the iterate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the retraction-based proximal-method leaf and its variables and update are explicit. The tangent subproblem, stopping measure, and optional sufficient-decrease backtracking are specialized claims for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Proximal-Construction Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Local regimes where intrinsic plus retraction-based constructions agree.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Construction Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when intrinsic and tangent proximal subproblems are exactly the same.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathcal M\) and a normal neighborhood \(U\) on which \(\exp_x:T_x\mathcal M\supset V\to U\) is a diffeomorphism. For any proper \(h:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\lambda>0\), the change of variables \(y=\exp_x(\eta)\) gives \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in U}\left\{h(y)+\frac{d(x,y)^2}{2\lambda}\right\}=\exp_x\!\left(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in V}\left\{h(\exp_x\eta)+\frac{\|\eta\|_x^2}{2\lambda}\right\}\right).\] The equality is local and requires minimizing geodesics to remain inside the normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside a normal neighborhood, the intrinsic distance-based proximal problem equals its tangent-space pullback under the exponential map.
assumptions_latex: \(\exp_x:V\to U\) is a diffeomorphism onto a normal neighborhood.
Every relevant minimizing geodesic from \(x\) remains in \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intrinsic proximal minimizers on \(U\) are exponential images of the corresponding tangent-space minimizers on \(V\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the correspondence leaf, and the local change-of-variables identity is plausible under the stated normal-neighborhood assumptions. A source is required to support the exact distance identity, domain restrictions, and set-valued argmin correspondence.

children.title: Retraction-Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometry or step-size regimes where retraction-based proximal models lose fidelity.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction-Approximation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks the local order at which a retraction approximates exponential geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a retraction. For fixed \(x\), it satisfies \(R_x(0_x)=x\) and \(DR_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\), so \(R_x(t\eta)\) and \(\exp_x(t\eta)\) agree to first order as \(t\to0\). Consequently, replacing \(\exp_x\) by an arbitrary retraction preserves only first-order local constructions in general. Second-order model or acceleration claims require a second-order retraction, namely zero covariant acceleration of \(t\mapsto R_x(t\eta)\) at \(t=0\). Without that condition, quadratic geometric error terms can change second-order proximal models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every retraction matches the exponential map to first order; second-order proximal or acceleration claims require a second-order retraction or explicit error control.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction on a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First-order agreement holds for any retraction, whereas second-order agreement is not guaranteed unless \(R\) is second order.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf, and first-order agreement follows from the retraction axioms. The broader assertion that second-order model or acceleration claims require a second-order retraction is context dependent and may admit explicit-error alternatives, so an authoritative source is needed to delimit the claim precisely.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Proximal Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the geometric data required by an accelerated composite iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An accelerated proximal interface maintains iterates \(x_k\in\mathcal M\), extrapolated points \(y_k\in\mathcal M\), and weights \(t_k\ge1\). Given a declared extrapolation map \(E\), set \[y_k=E(x_{k-1},x_k,\beta_k),\qquad \beta_k=\frac{t_{k-1}-1}{t_k},\] compute a proximal-gradient step \(x_{k+1}=\mathcal P_{L_k}(y_k)\), and update \(t_{k+1}=(1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2})/2\), unless a restart rule resets \(t_{k+1}=1\). The interface must specify how tangent vectors are transported or compared, the domain of \(E\), the proximal model \(\mathcal P_{L_k}\), and the stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accelerated manifold proximal method needs explicit geometric extrapolation, tangent comparison, proximal-step, weight-update, restart, and stopping interfaces.
assumptions_latex: The extrapolation map \(E\) and proximal map \(\mathcal P_{L}\) are well defined on all generated points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration produces \(y_k\), \(x_{k+1}\), and \(t_{k+1}\) by the displayed extrapolation, proximal, and weight updates.

notation.meaning: Declared proximal-gradient update with parameter L.
